content.framing: Shown with consequences; fights celebrated as skill and joy, cruelty condemned

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)

delivery.evidence: Capoeira history is explained in story chapters (ch. 6, 10-11, 24, 27); villains get backstories (B.J., Tetsuma); a reviewer says the series reflects little on violence (MyAnimeList).
delivery.note: The love of capoeira is the clearest "message"; moral judgments come through who protects and who uses people.

personified.ideology: Money and revenge; others must lose so I am fine
Protective strictness born of a criminal past

105774.dominant: Expressive individualism (freedom and joy, affirmed), Might makes right (the Inheritance War, critiqued), Communitarianism and Traditionalism (the roda and the mestres' lineage, affirmed).

33633.heading: Beast Master
33633.label: From summaries
33633.life_message: Look past a frightening surface to the person underneath, and learn that real love calms and frees someone instead of smothering them.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; Leo's rages treated as a condition to be calmed; attempts on his life condemned

delivery.evidence: Classmates' fear of Leo is shown as a natural first reaction that changes once they know him; the relatives are unseen, one-note villains (Soliloquy in Blue: the attacker is never named).
delivery.note: The message of acceptance is carried by the romance and by Yuiko's choices, not by speeches.

personified.ideology: See past appearances; love without smothering
Gentle nature in a frightening shell

108115.heading: Beast Tamer
108115.label: From summaries
108115.life_message: Kindness and respect are the real strength: people treated as partners rather than tools become a family, while pride, envy and contempt for others destroy those who hold them.

delivery.evidence: Arios is drawn as wholly arrogant and contemptuous of commoners and tamers (Japanese Wikipedia); the townspeople themselves say the beast tamer is more useful than the Hero.
delivery.note: The moral (kindness over pride) is carried by contrast between Rein and Arios rather than by speeches; the genre makes the arrogant rival a clear foil.

personified.ideology: Pride and contempt for the weak

108115.dominant: Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Strength rules (critiqued), Liberalism (rights and consent).

160880.heading: Beat & Motion
160880.label: From summaries
160880.life_message: Dreams are worth chasing again after failure and ridicule; mocking other people's dreams is the real waste, and two people who believe in each other can both start over.

content.framing: Mixed: comic, and tied to hidden pain

delivery.evidence: The theme is stated outright in ch. 1 (Nico's outburst against mocking dreams) and then carried by the plot. Tatsuhiko's cynicism is given a real cause (childhood mockery, a failed band) rather than mocked (Mangapedia).
delivery.note: A drama of setbacks and encouragement; conflicts are aired and resolved within a few chapters (MyAnimeList reviews).

personified.ideology: Cynicism about dreams, then renewed effort

160880.dominant: Expressive individualism (pursue your dream), Existentialism (meaning chosen after cynicism), Classical virtue ethics (perseverance), Communitarianism (friends who help).

45355.heading: Before Dawn and the End of the World
45355.label: From summaries
45355.life_message: Ordinary lives are full of disappointment, loneliness and dreams that faded, but people keep going, and small moments of light and the chance of a new morning are reason enough.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers stress that meaning comes from the characters' own experience rather than any sermon from the author (AniList review 24222) and that endings are open (AniList review 2168).
delivery.note: Quiet vignettes leave the meaning to the reader; there is no opposing worldview to treat fairly or unfairly.

personified.character: The letter writer (What a Wonderful World)
The woman on her day off

45355.dominant: Existentialism (finding meaning in an ordinary life), Secular humanism (hope carried by people and small moments).

101625.heading: Berserk of Gluttony
101625.label: From summaries
101625.life_message: The despised can rise and protect the people they love, but power fed by killing has a terrible cost and must be held in check by love and purpose; cruelty that comes from rank is the real evil.

content.framing: Mixed: killing monsters endorsed; a revenge killing presented as earned; its cost to Fate kept in view
Chaste romance; sexual exploitation of a child planned and stopped, condemned

delivery.evidence: ANN's Eisenbeis: most elites are cruel, nobles especially, with Roxy the exception; the Vlericks are drawn as one-note bullies. Eris's sacrifice argument is given a hearing before it is rejected.
delivery.note: The anti-caste message is plain and the villains are cartoon-cruel; the moral tension lives inside Fate, whose power keeps the story from being a simple revenge fantasy.

personified.ideology: The despised rising through power that costs him
Merit over birth; nobility as service
Privilege of rank and cruelty to the skill-less

101625.dominant: Might makes right (explored: the strong rule, and Fate becomes strongest), Critical theory (a birth-based caste system condemned), Bushido / honor code (the good knight's code, kept by Roxy and betrayed by most holy knights).

30002.heading: Berserk (Kentaro Miura)
30002.label: From summaries
30002.life_message: A good life is a stubborn struggle: you keep fighting against fate, cruelty and your own rage, and you choose to protect the people beside you rather than sacrifice them for a dream.

content.framing: Mixed: rape and abuse condemned and shown as trauma; consensual sex and nudity neutral; some scenes eroticized

delivery.evidence: Themes of fate, free will and religion are argued through characters (Guts, Griffith, Mozgus, Farnese; Wikipedia themes); Mozgus is deliberately one-sided (Miura via Wikipedia), while Griffith is given a strong case.
delivery.note: Ideas are dramatized rather than preached, with a few statements by Guts and the Skull Knight; the church is drawn more harshly than other views.

personified.ideology: A dream that justifies any sacrifice

30002.dominant: Existentialism, Might makes right (critiqued), Nihilism (explored), Pagan/occult, Christian (critiqued institution), Communitarianism.

126135.heading: Bibliomania
126135.label: From summaries
126135.life_message: Perfect wish-worlds, whether fantasies, games or endless reading, can quietly devour a person, and a hunger to consume everything, even knowledge, becomes a monster; the imperfect real world, with its small joys and real people, is worth more than any dream that eats you.

content.framing: Condemned (cycles of revenge); monstrous devouring shown as horror

delivery.evidence: The serpent's defense of staying (the real world is pain) is given strongly by the guests themselves (ch. 5), and Alice answers it; the twist then turns her answer against her.
delivery.note: The message is carried by allegory and a final reveal rather than by narration; readers are invited to re-read.

personified.ideology: Love of the real world, then the hunger to know everything
A perfect family instead of a real one
The real world is only pain

126135.dominant: Hedonism (critiqued), Nihilism (explored), Existentialism, Buddhist ideas (craving), Postmodernism (the book that writes people).

31409.heading: Biomega
31409.label: From summaries
31409.life_message: One loyal protector and a few companions can carry hope for human beings through the end of the world, and no power has the right to force a "new humanity" on everyone else.

content.framing: Neutral (action spectacle); the DRF's mass killing condemned

delivery.evidence: The DRF is drawn as a menacing, cult-like power with little explanation; reviewers note Nihei rarely explains anything (Thompson; ANN vol. 4).
delivery.note: The message is carried by action and imagery; the story almost never states a lesson, and the villains' case for a "new human race" is barely argued.

personified.ideology: Loyal protection of humanity's slim hope
Remake humanity by force; immortality; hatred of the non-organic
Devotion and reason of a made mind

102043.heading: BL Metamorphosis
102043.label: From summaries
102043.life_message: It is never too late or too odd to love what you love, and a shared passion can turn two lonely people of very different ages into true friends who help each other grow.

delivery.evidence: Publishers Weekly notes an "unhurried pace"; SOLRAD and Comics Beat describe a tranquil story where the message comes through small scenes; no character argues against the friendship, and Urara's shame is answered by example rather than lecture.
delivery.note: A quiet slice of life whose message is shown in what the two women do together.

personified.ideology: Enjoy what you love openly, at any age
Fear of judgment, then courage to create

102043.dominant: Expressive individualism (liking what you like without shame), Communitarianism (friendship and fan community).

33116.heading: Black Bird
33116.label: From summaries
33116.life_message: Devoted love and family are worth any danger: a girl who accepts the demon who has always protected her, and a mother who chooses her child even at the risk of her own life, are rewarded with a family.

content.framing: Mixed: Kyo's killings framed as protection; Sho's cruelty condemned

33116.dominant: Traditionalism (bride, heir, clan), Pagan/occult (yokai world), Might makes right (rivals fight for the bride), Communitarianism (the tengu village).

delivery.evidence: The romance carries the message without lectures; the one strong opposing voice, the exorcist Raikoh, is shown as obsessive and dangerous rather than given a fair hearing (Wikipedia; VIZ vol. 8).
delivery.note: The story's view that Kyo's devotion is true love is presented through Misao's growing trust rather than argued; critics say the series never questions it (Dacey; ANN vol. 11).

personified.ideology: Cruelty and resentment; rule by fear
Humans and demons must stay apart

30040.heading: Black Cat
30040.label: From summaries
30040.life_message: A person shaped to kill can choose a free, merciful life; revenge and the hunger to rule others are rejected, and a chosen family is worth protecting.

content.framing: Mixed: action played as exciting; killing for its own sake and revenge rejected

delivery.evidence: The no-kill and anti-revenge lessons are taught through events (the paralysis bullet lesson, v7; taking Creed alive, VIZ v20); Creed is given a backstory of abuse but no persuasive case (fan wiki).
delivery.note: Both the ruling organization and the revolutionaries are shown as dangerous, with the hero standing apart from each; the message is carried by action and comedy rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Revolution, contempt for the weak, immortality through force
World peace through a secret ruling organization
Live freely and give everyone a second chance

30040.dominant: Libertarianism (freedom from controlling institutions), Expressive individualism, Transhumanism (critiqued), Strength rules (critiqued).

86123.heading: Black Clover
86123.label: From summaries
86123.life_message: A good life is earned by effort, not birth: you refuse to give up, you lift up the people others look down on, and you build a family out of misfits.

delivery.evidence: Asta and Yuno tell Lucius that a true Wizard King is one everyone admires, and Asta says his imperfect life belongs to him (fan wiki); no review opened addresses preachiness.
delivery.note: Asta and his allies state the never-give-up and anti-discrimination themes aloud, while some snobbish rivals are later partly redeemed.

personified.ideology: Effort and loyalty can beat birth

86123.dominant: Progressivism (anti-discrimination), Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Pagan/occult (as fantasy setting), Critical theory (class), Patriotism / nationalism (service to the kingdom).

31600.heading: Black Jack
31600.label: From summaries
31600.life_message: Every life is worth fighting for with all one's skill, whatever the law, the price or the odds, yet medicine cannot conquer death, and pride, greed and cruelty are the real diseases.

delivery.evidence: Each story ends on a moral turn; Tezuka stated the series is about doctors' dilemmas (Japanese Wikipedia); Kiriko is given real reasons for euthanasia.
delivery.note: Reviewers call some stories heavy-handed but say that suits Tezuka's young readers (Manga Bookshelf roundtable).

personified.ideology: A doctor must fight for every life

31600.dominant: Secular humanism, Classical virtue ethics, Duty ethics, Existentialism.

30735.heading: Black Lagoon
30735.label: From summaries
30735.life_message: It holds up no settled good life: in a world without law the strong and the clever survive, but Rock's stubborn empathy argues that a person can keep some humanity, and even change others' fates for the better, without pretending the darkness away.

content.framing: Stylized and often relished as action; atrocities (torture, child killers, terror) shown as horror
Abuse condemned as the root of monsters; fan service and the sex trade shown without judgment

delivery.evidence: Rock and Revy argue morality openly (ch. 9-10, 15), and Rock and Chang argue fate and God (ch. 116); ANN's Matthew Roe says the anime rarely over-explains and leaves viewers to judge; Santos (ANN) thinks it fails to explore its controversial subjects.
delivery.note: Its question of how far an ordinary person sinks is carried by Rock's arc and by debates between characters, with no narrator or arc that settles it.

personified.ideology: Empathy and a stubborn hope for good endings
Nihilism: only money and guns protect you
Killing as the law of the world, learned through abuse

30735.dominant: Nihilism (explored and argued against), Might makes right (explored), Existentialism, Pragmatism.

50375.heading: Black Paradox
50375.label: From summaries
50375.life_message: The wish to die can give way to a reason to live, and every soul is precious; people and societies that treat souls as a resource to be mined bring ruin on themselves.

content.framing: Suka's seduction and forced kiss condemned
Shown with sympathy; the wish to die fades, though not through help

delivery.evidence: No speeches; the message comes through consequences (explosions, Piitan's death) and Marusou's closing prophecy. CBR notes the themes are shown through visuals rather than stated.
delivery.note: The story never lectures about suicide or greed; reviewers differ on whether it resolves its ideas (ANN: uneven; Anime Corner: little resolution).

personified.ideology: Fear of the future turned to acceptance
Progress at any cost; using people
Beauty and money as reasons to live

50375.dominant: Existentialism (why go on living), Nihilism (critiqued), Utilitarianism and Consumerism (critiqued in the soul-energy plot).

126768.heading: Black Sesame Salt and Custard Pudding
126768.label: From summaries
126768.life_message: Love can grow after commitment: a hasty marriage between two very different people becomes real through patience, respect and everyday care.

content.framing: Neutral (the drunken start is played for comedy)

delivery.evidence: A rom-com; the blurbs and tags suggest the message is carried by the couple's daily life (Love After Marriage, Cohabitation). No review was opened.
delivery.note: Delivery cannot be judged from blurbs; to verify on a full read.

126768.dominant: Traditionalism (love built inside marriage), Expressive individualism (an unconventional couple).

101746.heading: Black Summoner
101746.label: From summaries
101746.life_message: Strength is won by seeking out ever-stronger opponents, and power is good when it protects the household you have gathered; those who use power to enslave, brainwash or torment others are the real villains.

content.framing: Endorsed (fighting as joy); villains' cruelty condemned
Mixed: the hero's harem endorsed; villains' sexual slavery condemned

delivery.evidence: Kelvin's creed (seek stronger foes; get strong before trying to change the world) is stated in nearly every J-Novel Club blurb; villains such as Clive are cartoonish, raving that he is the protagonist (ch. 37).
delivery.note: The message is stated openly in Kelvin's catchphrases and carried by battle; no character challenges the slave system.

personified.ideology: Strength and the joy of battle; protect the household

101746.dominant: Might makes right, Hedonism (the joy of battle), Expressive individualism, Pagan/occult.

98148.heading: Black Torch
98148.label: From summaries
98148.life_message: Kindness to an outcast is repaid with loyalty, and an outsider earns belonging by protecting others and by treating a dangerous partner as an equal rather than a tool; power used to dominate the weak destroys the one who seeks it.

content.framing: Neutral (battle action); cruelty and predation by villains condemned

delivery.evidence: Amagi is given a full backstory as a protector god betrayed by fear and war (ch. 18), and ANN notes the series questions the Bureau's own account of the war; Jiro's view wins without speeches.
delivery.note: The message is carried by choices in battle (Rago's sacrifice, Jiro's refusal to see Rago as a tool) rather than stated.

personified.ideology: Compassion and loyalty across the human-spirit divide
The strong should rule the weak
Protect the family from the spy's life

98148.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (loyalty, compassion, courage), Might makes right (critiqued in Amagi), Communitarianism (the squad as found family), Pagan/occult (a world of spirits).

30736.heading: Blade of the Phantom Master
30736.label: From summaries
30736.life_message: Justice for the oppressed and loyalty to those you love are worth any cost, but a hero who fights evil with deceit and cruelty carries guilt for it, and peace is won only through sacrifice.

content.framing: Villains' cruelty condemned; the hero's ruthless killing left morally open
Sexual violence condemned; some fan-service imagery

delivery.evidence: Bang Ja and Sando voice the case against Munsu's methods and are not mocked; Aji Tae and the corrupt lords are drawn as monstrous.
delivery.note: The message emerges from episodic cases and Munsu's guilt rather than speeches; the creator's notes explain Korean legends and history.

personified.ideology: Justice by any means; loyalty to a dead king
The inspectors' ideals: justice with virtue

30736.dominant: Confucian ethics, Might makes right (critiqued), Utilitarianism, Classical virtue ethics.

30149.heading: BLAME!
30149.label: From summaries
30149.life_message: Keep going and keep protecting the fragile spark of human life, even in a vast world that no longer cares whether people exist; persistence and care for the next generation matter more than understanding everything.

delivery.evidence: Opus notes it avoids manifestos and heavy philosophizing; Thompson notes the sparse dialogue and unanswered questions.
delivery.note: Meaning comes through images of scale and decay and through what Killy does, with almost no speeches.

personified.ideology: Law without purpose; credentials over people
Seizing transcendence for one's own kind

103192.heading: blanc
103192.label: From summaries
103192.life_message: Love that lasts is chosen again and again through doubt, grief and family rejection; two people who stand by each other, with friends around them, can make a marriage even where the law does not.

delivery.evidence: The case is made through events (caregiving, the funeral, the wedding); the father's objection is voiced but cast as harm (Anime Feminist); the legal gap is raised by Sajō's own doubts.
delivery.note: A quiet relationship drama with a clear point of view on same-sex marriage, carried by family scenes rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Duty and doubt, then committed love

103192.dominant: Expressive individualism (choosing one's own life and love), Progressivism (affirming same-sex marriage), Communitarianism (chosen family at the wedding).

74307.heading: Blank Canvas: My So-Called Artist's Journey
74307.label: From summaries
74307.life_message: Skill is built by showing up and drawing every day; the people who push us hardest may love us most, and gratitude left unsaid turns into regret, so honor your teachers while you can.

content.framing: Mixed: played as loving strictness and comedy; later dropped

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)

delivery.evidence: The narrator states her regrets directly (a panel calls herself greedy and self-centered; Agency for Cultural Affairs feature); Hidaka's mantra is repeated throughout.
delivery.note: An honest memoir: the author judges her younger self openly, but through comedy and story rather than lectures.

personified.ideology: Talent and self-interest, slowly replaced by effort and gratitude

74307.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (diligence and gratitude), Confucian ethics (honor for the teacher), Expressive individualism (following a dream), Pragmatism (practice over theory).

45205.heading: Blast of Tempest
45205.label: From summaries
45205.life_message: Grief and the wish for revenge can blind you, but the people we lose would want us to live on; the story should end as a comedy, not a tragedy, and the way there is friendship, honest reasoning and letting go.

content.framing: Framed as sacrifice; grief shown with consequences

delivery.evidence: Characters quote Hamlet and The Tempest and argue the theme aloud; ANN notes a long debate at the Tree of Exodus; Samon's opposing view is given reasons and partly vindicated (Wikipedia; fan wiki).
delivery.note: The revenge-versus-forgiveness question is debated openly in dialogue, but the answer is shown through what happens rather than preached.

45205.dominant: Existentialism (choosing against an imposed fate), Utilitarianism (sacrifice for the world, explored), Duty ethics (promises kept), Stoicism (acceptance of loss).

30012.heading: Bleach
30012.label: From summaries
30012.life_message: A good life is spent protecting the people you love and following your own heart even when the authorities, or would-be gods, are wrong; fear of death is part of being human, and it is what gives courage and hope their meaning.

content.framing: Neutral (sword combat as the story's main action); atrocities condemned

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)

delivery.evidence: Aizen and Yhwach get long, serious speeches (ch. 178, 686); Kubo said he never thought of Ichigo as a hero (VIZ interview via ComicBook.com, 2023).
delivery.note: Its themes of resolve, loyalty and defiance of corrupt authority come through battles and the villains' arguments, which are partly left standing.

personified.ideology: Protect loved ones and follow your own heart
Human will should take the empty place of heaven
A founder who gives and takes power by blood
The law must be kept, even against family

30012.dominant: Existentialism, Classical virtue ethics, a critique of Might makes right and of Collectivism/authoritarianism, Bushido / honor code, with Buddhist ideas and Shinto folk belief as setting.

42994.heading: Blood Blockade Battlefront
42994.label: From summaries
42994.life_message: In a world gone mad, ordinary courage, decency and loyalty to your friends hold things together; a true gentleman uses great strength with restraint, and even the weakest member of the team has something to give.

content.framing: Neutral (comic and heroic action); villains' cruelty condemned; mass casualties often treated as background

delivery.evidence: ANN calls it a very moral work under its madcap street antics; Klaus's virtue is shown in action, not speeches; villains like Femt are cartoon tyrants.
delivery.note: The message rides on character and comedy; no lectures. Nightow sees Leo as the one who watches the city with an ordinary person's eyes (Wikipedia, Leonardo Watch).

42994.dominant: Communitarianism (Libra as a found family), Classical virtue ethics and an honor code (Klaus's chivalry), Absurdism (life goes on in a mad city).

51614.heading: Blood Lad
51614.label: From summaries
51614.life_message: Owning a wrong you caused and keeping your promise to the person you failed matters more than power or status; caring for someone means asking their consent and, in the end, being willing to let them go.

delivery.evidence: The moral rides on Staz's vow and on gags; villains such as Braz get motives and partial redemption, while Akim is a monster.
delivery.note: A parody action-comedy; its point about promises and letting go is shown through the quest, not stated.

personified.ideology: Live for your hobbies, but keep your promise
Cold calculation; the ends justify the means
Honor among rivals; strength by effort

51614.dominant: Pagan/occult (a comic demon world), Might makes right (a world run by the strongest, questioned), Expressive individualism (the otaku hero).

98397.heading: Blood on the Tracks
98397.label: From summaries
98397.life_message: A child is not his parent's possession: a good life begins when you face the truth about the people who shaped you, take back your own self, and can then meet even a parent who harmed you with clear eyes and some mercy.

content.frequency: Recurring undertone; one sexual scene between 14-year-olds
content.framing: Shown as disturbing and confused, not as titillation

delivery.evidence: Oshimi drew strictly from Seiichi's perspective (ANN interview) and later gives Seiko's own past (v16); Comics Beat says the book avoids demonizing either character.
delivery.note: The message is carried by atmosphere, point of view and slowly revealed memory, with almost no stated moral.

personified.ideology: Possessive love; the child as part of oneself
Keeping the peace by not seeing
A self struggling to belong to itself

98397.dominant: Existentialism, Confucian ethics (filial duty, explored), Nihilism (explored, then moved past), Buddhist ideas (by echo).

35627.heading: Bloody Monday
35627.label: From summaries
35627.life_message: Loyalty to family and friends, and skill used to protect others, can stop fanatics who believe destruction brings rebirth; but trust is costly, because anyone, even a friend, may be the enemy.

content.framing: Neutral (thriller action); terror and cruelty condemned
Mixed: harassment condemned; seduction used by villains

delivery.evidence: K's doctrine is shown only through fanatical followers, and her own aide calls her a blind believer; the state's torture and tracking are not questioned (Japanese Wikipedia).
delivery.note: The thriller form carries the message; the story rarely pauses to argue, and its villains are given motives (Hosho's brother, Maya's upbringing) more than arguments.

personified.ideology: Faithless rivalry; life as a game

86218.heading: Bloom Into You
86218.label: From summaries
86218.life_message: A good life is lived as your true self, not as the person others expect, and real love lets the other person change and grow rather than freezing them in place.

content.framing: Endorsed; consent in early kisses debated by critics

delivery.evidence: Nakatani says she avoided a story about the social obstacles to same-sex love and focused on the characters' flaws (Wikipedia, Production). The play inside the story states the theme openly (choose to be yourself).
delivery.note: The message is carried by the characters' inner lives and by the school play, which mirrors Touko's choice; the adult couple and Maki are drawn to make the point that love is real and that a life without romance can be full.

personified.ideology: Living as someone else versus becoming yourself

164708.heading: Blooming Love
164708.label: From summaries
164708.life_message: Two people who are each "half-fledged" can grow into skilled, whole people by honoring each other's craft, helping where the other is weak, and choosing each other's good over their own comfort.

delivery.evidence: Sportskeeda describes a slow, character-focused romance about personal growth; the lesson (help each other where you are weak) is shown in shared projects, not stated in lectures.
delivery.note: The values come through work scenes and small choices; the study-abroad offer in vol. 7 sets career against staying near family and partner without a stated answer in sources.

personified.ideology: Art as a calling; gentle persistence

164708.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (craft excellence), Communitarianism (family workshop and friends), Traditionalism (an inherited craft).

86890.heading: Blue Giant
86890.label: From summaries
86890.life_message: Love what you do with your whole heart, practice every day, and play with honest feeling; greatness is built from stubborn effort, humility before criticism, and the people who believe in you.

content.framing: Neutral (part of jazz-bar life); not glamorized

delivery.evidence: Dai states his goal openly and gives one short speech on letting beginners into jazz (v5-6); the critics he faces are drawn fairly and often proved right. Reviewers describe the music conveyed through faces and layout rather than lectures (ANN; Publishers Weekly).
delivery.note: The message is carried by practice scenes and performances, and by the future interviews at the end of each volume, not by lectures.

personified.ideology: High standards that serve the art
A teacher who gives his skill away

86890.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (excellence through practice), Expressive individualism (honest self-expression), Communitarianism (family and band).

146203.heading: BLUE LOCK -EPISODE NAGI-
146203.label: From summaries
146203.life_message: Talent only comes alive when you want something for yourself; a friendship built on one person's dream has to become two people's dreams, even if that means parting.

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)

delivery.evidence: The Blue Lock creed of ego is stated outright; Baro argues the lone-king view against Nagi and Reo's partnership (ch. 9); Chigiri recasts the team's goal as what each player wants (ch. 29).
delivery.note: The philosophy is spoken in match speeches and inner monologues, but carried by sports action; the partnership ideal is given real weight through Reo's grief.

personified.ideology: Shared dreams; possession of a partner's talent
The lone king who needs no one
Instinct that despises rules and right and wrong

146203.dominant: Expressive individualism (ego and desire), Existentialism, Strength rules (elimination).

106130.heading: Blue Lock
106130.label: From summaries
106130.life_message: Find what only you can do and pursue it without apology: hunger to win, honest self-analysis and constant adaptation make you great, rivals are there to learn from and "devour," and teamwork is valuable when it serves the strongest individual.

content.frequency: Pervasive outside the book; recurring inside

delivery.evidence: Ego states the thesis in direct speeches; Common Sense Media says self-centered ego themes overshadow the positives; The Daily Campus calls it propaganda for hyper-competition. The Side-B arc (vol. 39) is the first sustained voice for the other side.
delivery.note: The teamwork view is voiced mostly by players who are eliminated, though the story refines "ego" into self-knowledge and lets rivals combine.

personified.ideology: Japan needs egoists; cooperation is weakness
Team play; Blue Lock as inhumane

106130.dominant: Expressive individualism, Existentialism (self-creation), Pragmatism, Might makes right (as "skill makes right"), Classical virtue ethics; Communitarianism and Confucian harmony critiqued.

107237.heading: Blue Period
107237.label: From summaries
107237.life_message: A good life is one you choose and work for: find what moves you, put in the hours, be honest about yourself, and let others be who they are.

content.framing: Neutral (artistic nudity); crude jokes shown as immature

delivery.evidence: Yatora's mother's worries about money are presented as reasonable (Anime Feminist); Yuka's family is the clearest negative portrayal (ANN). Lessons about art are taught openly by teachers, which ANN's Silverman sometimes finds too informative (via Wikipedia).
delivery.note: The art lessons are explicit; the moral themes (honesty, acceptance) are carried by character moments rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Effort and method can make an artist
A safe career for a family without money

107237.dominant: Expressive individualism, Existentialism, Classical virtue ethics, Secular humanism, Pragmatism.

86279.heading: Boarding School Juliet
86279.label: From summaries
86279.life_message: Love and friendship that cross a hostile divide, held with courage and finally made public, can change a prejudiced world: the enemies' children end as reformers whose wedding stands for peace.

content.framing: Mixed: slapstick brawling played as comedy; cruelty condemned
Mixed: fan service as comedy; the assault attempt condemned

delivery.evidence: Early volumes carry the theme lightly (ANN reviewers found the feud thinly developed in vol. 1); TV Tropes' YMMV page says the message grows heavier near the end, with Westerners on the class trip drawn as racists easily beaten. The main segregationist, Reon, is given a sympathetic backstory and redemption.
delivery.note: The anti-prejudice message rides on a romantic comedy and becomes open politics in the election and class-trip arcs (ch. 79-108).

personified.ideology: love and coexistence across the divide
segregation and hatred of the other nation
family honor and keeping to one's own

personified.character: Western racists on the class trip

86279.dominant: Progressivism (ending segregation and prejudice), Expressive individualism (love chosen against the group), Patriotism / nationalism (critiqued), Feminism (a woman's right to lead).

111258.heading: Bocchi the Rock!
111258.label: From summaries
111258.life_message: Small, frightening steps toward other people, taken with friends who accept you as you are, let a lonely person's gift be shared; you grow by practice and courage, not by becoming someone else.

content.framing: Played for comedy, with costs shown; minors do not drink

delivery.evidence: 4-koma gags carry the story; there are no villains, and the one critic of the band (Poison Yami) is given a real point before she changes her mind (Wikipedia). Rival Yoyoko's ambition is treated with sympathy.
delivery.note: Growth through shared music is shown in comic episodes and a few serious full-page moments, and left for readers to infer.

111258.dominant: Expressive individualism, Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics.

30670.heading: Bokurano: Ours
30670.label: From summaries
30670.life_message: Everyone dies and goodness does not spare anyone; what matters is what you do with the time you have, and whether you will give your life for people you will never meet.

content.framing: Condemned in its cost; some killings presented as necessary

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)
content.framing: Condemned: abuse shown as crime and lasting harm
Shown with consequences; some suicides framed as sacrifice

delivery.evidence: Each arc tests a different view of life and death through a child's choices; TV Tropes notes authorial lectures on caring for strangers and criticism of the United States; Kirie argues about whether films in which extras die can be called happy (TV Tropes).
delivery.note: Mostly carried by events, but characters debate the ethics of their war openly, and the author's views surface in later volumes.

personified.ideology: The individual serves the whole; honesty

30670.dominant: Existentialism (meaning chosen in the face of certain death), Utilitarianism (lives weighed against lives and worlds), Communitarianism (protecting strangers), Nihilism (explored and resisted).

168468.heading: Boruto: Two Blue Vortex
168468.label: From summaries
168468.life_message: Doing right and protecting the people you love matters even when no one believes you; truth and loyalty outlast a lie the whole world has accepted.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; fighting framed as protecting others

delivery.evidence: Ikemoto said he could not write villains with explained backstories the way Kishimoto did, so his antagonists may seem more unreasonable (Wikipedia); Kawaki and Jura, however, are given reasons and feelings (ch. 26, 38).
delivery.note: Loyalty under slander is carried by Boruto's actions rather than speeches; memory-manipulating and devouring foes stand for the opposing view.

personified.ideology: Protect the family at any cost, even by imprisoning it

168468.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (loyalty, perseverance), Communitarianism (village), Might makes right (critiqued), Transhumanism

114027.heading: Boy Meets Maria
114027.label: From summaries
114027.life_message: Love means seeing the real person behind the roles people play, and healing from harm takes time, honesty and people who stay.

delivery.evidence: SOLRAD describes the message as carried by art and layout (a bedroom echoing the trans flag colors, a mirror contrast, panel breakdowns during stage panic) and by both boys' gradual disclosures; the bullies voice opposing views and are shown as harmful.
delivery.note: The theme of roles and real selves is built into the drama-club plot rather than stated by a narrator, per the reviews opened.

personified.ideology: Performed identity as refuge; gender left open

114027.dominant: Expressive individualism (affirmed, with an open ending), Progressivism (inclusion of gender variance), Existentialism (roles versus a real self), Feminism and Critical theory only in the SOLRAD reading.

187624.heading: Boyish Girlfriend
187624.label: From summaries
187624.life_message: Loving someone means delighting in who they really are, in every style, and letting them open up at their own pace.

delivery.evidence: Siliconera finds an acceptance message in Daichi's compliments across styles; The Outer Haven finds mostly repeated dress-up comedy; neither mentions lecturing.
delivery.note: Any point about gender expression is left to the comedy.

187624.dominant: Expressive individualism (acceptance of a partner's style); light romance.

30877.heading: Boys Over Flowers
30877.label: From summaries
30877.life_message: Self-respect is not for sale: an ordinary girl who refuses to be bullied or bought wins respect and love across class lines, and love is shown changing a spoiled, violent boy (a change many modern readers question).

content.framing: Mixed: bullying condemned; Tsukushi's and Tsukasa's own violence often played as spirit or comedy

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)
content.framing: Mixed: assaults by strangers condemned; Tsukasa's attempt in ch. 16 followed by romance; chastity kept by the leads

delivery.evidence: The message is carried by melodrama and comedy; the class snobs are drawn broadly, but Kaede and Sakurako get backstories and reconciliation (Wikipedia; fan wiki).
delivery.note: No one lectures; Tsukushi's speeches against being bought (ch. 4) and against bullying (ch. 3) are the closest to stated themes.

personified.ideology: Integrity and self-respect of the ordinary person

30877.dominant: Might makes right (critiqued), Expressive individualism, Consumerism (explored), Classical virtue ethics, Traditionalism (critiqued).

114972.heading: Boys Run the Riot
114972.label: From summaries
114972.life_message: Living as your true self is worth the fear of being seen, and friends who accept you, and work you make together, can carry you through a world that does not yet understand you.

content.framing: Condemned (bullying and attacks); one fight shown as defense

delivery.evidence: Transphobic voices are mostly mocking classmates, a book that calls Ryo ill (vol. 1) and a classmate who calls the brand a gimmick (vol. 4); WING is a more rounded voice who argues identity should be the selling point (SOLRAD).
delivery.note: The message is stated in the brand's name and Ryo's choices; the author's own experience shapes it (SOLRAD, citing the vol. 1 interview). The story rarely lingers on argument and spends most pages on school life and the business.

100209.heading: Breasts Are My Favorite Things in the World!
100209.label: From summaries
100209.life_message: A good life follows your own desires and quirks without shame, and the right friend will accept them and may become the person you love.
100209.dominant: Hedonism, Expressive individualism, Progressivism (all my own framing; no source applies these labels).

delivery.evidence: The title and premise state the theme outright; the AniList reviewer calls it "a tribute to breasts." No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The series argues for nothing beyond its own premise; acceptance of desire and same-sex love is shown, not argued.

118730.heading: Brutal
118730.label: From summaries
118730.life_message: When the law fails the victims, a hidden killer who punishes the guilty in kind feels like justice; the story invites readers to cheer him and seldom asks what that makes him, or them.

content.framing: Sexual violence condemned (perpetrators punished) but shown
Shown with consequences for victims; the hero's own pathology unexamined

delivery.evidence: Targets are drawn as unredeemable and gloating (MAL reviewers: one-dimensional villains); the lawful alternative (Mamiya) is admiring rather than argued.
delivery.note: The story never states a thesis; it builds each case so the reader wants the punishment, then delivers it.

personified.ideology: Retribution in kind when the law fails; private judgment

118730.dominant: Might makes right (a hidden hunter of predators), Liberalism (critiqued: due process shown failing), Christian imagery (confession without repentance), Utilitarianism.

64377.heading: Brynhildr in the Darkness
64377.label: From summaries
64377.life_message: Keeping your promises and protecting people the powerful treat as disposable is worth any cost; no institution has the right to rank human lives and use them as tools.

content.framing: Mixed: harem fan service played as comedy; coercion by villains condemned

delivery.evidence: The lab's utilitarian logic is voiced by Chisato and Miki and given real stakes (Miki's case that all witches must die to save the world, Wikipedia), but the top villains (Takachiho, Makina, Onodera) are drawn as monstrous.
delivery.note: The anti-experimentation message is carried by the plot of sheltering escapees rather than by speeches; the harem comedy runs alongside it without comment.

personified.ideology: Protect every life; reason and promise-keeping
Science without ethics; people ranked by usefulness
Sacrifice the few to save the many

64377.dominant: Transhumanism and Utilitarianism (critiqued), Duty ethics, Strength rules (critiqued), Communitarianism.

50593.heading: Btooom!
50593.label: From summaries
50593.life_message: Trust and cooperation, not killing, are the way to survive a world built to make people kill each other, and even a shut-in can change by choosing to protect someone.

content.framing: Neutral (survival action); murder for gain condemned
Sexual violence condemned; fan service neutral (male gaze)
Condemned (killing for gain); survival violence neutral

delivery.evidence: ANN (vol. 1) found Ryōta's moral musings heavy-handed, like the author's agenda; most villains are one-dimensional (ANN anime review via Wikipedia), but Kira is given a backstory and a redemption.
delivery.note: The trust-versus-killing theme is stated often by Ryōta and carried by the game rules themselves.

personified.ideology: Trust and protect; do not kill for gain
Elite rule through a virtual world

50593.dominant: Might makes right (critiqued: the island's rules), Communitarianism (trust and alliances), Critical theory (elites who use people).

31111.heading: Buddha
31111.label: From summaries
31111.life_message: Suffering is not answered by revenge, privilege or self-torment, but by seeing that all life is connected and meeting every being with compassion, along a middle way.

content.framing: Neutral (nudity as everyday dress); temptation resisted

delivery.evidence: Tricycle finds it seldom preachy, though the Buddha's later speeches set out core doctrine; Thompson praises a message carried by characters and drama. Opposing views get full arcs: Dhepa's asceticism, Tatta's revenge, Devadatta's will to power, the Brahmins' caste teaching.
delivery.note: Teaching scenes grow longer in later volumes (v4-8), as the emphasis shifts from the Buddha's life to his teachings (Tricycle).

personified.ideology: Humans are meant to suffer; self-torment brings insight

31111.dominant: Buddhist ideas (affirmed), Pacifism / nonviolence (affirmed), Hindu ideas (explored; caste critiqued), Environmentalism (animals as kin).

164961.heading: Bug Ego
164961.label: From summaries
164961.life_message: Shortcuts that bend the rules of reality come with a price, and the real prize is the slow work of becoming someone's friend.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers note it asks many questions and offers few answers (ANN); consequences come from the hacks' rules, not from lectures.
delivery.note: The point (shortcuts cost; friends matter) is shown through what happens, not stated.

33468.heading: Bunny Drop
33468.label: From summaries
33468.life_message: Family is made by choosing to care for someone day after day, not by blood or by what relatives think proper; the series carries that idea to an ending in which the girl and the man who raised her choose to marry, which most readers rejected.

content.framing: Endorsed: the guardian-ward romance is the happy ending

delivery.evidence: Reviewers describe quiet, awkward slice-of-life with thoughts shown rather than lectures (Gaffney, vol. 7). The relatives who object to Rin are drawn as cold; Daikichi's own hesitation about the romance is shown (vol. 9), but no character argues the case against it at length (Carlson).
delivery.note: The message is carried by everyday scenes, not speeches; the ending is presented as natural and the objections to it are left to the reader.

personified.ideology: self-reliance; staying with the one who raised her

33468.dominant: Communitarianism (chosen family), Expressive individualism (in the ending), Duty ethics, Confucian ethics.

116827.heading: Burn the Witch
116827.label: From summaries
116827.life_message: Real magic is doing your job well and protecting the people in your care, even when your own bosses would sacrifice them; waiting to be chosen like a fairy-tale princess leads people astray.

content.framing: Neutral (fantasy action); killing of the innocent opposed
Played for comedy; Noel punishes it

delivery.evidence: Ninny states the fairy-tale theme in an opening monologue (ch. 1), but the protect-the-innocent message is carried by plot; the agency directors argue their case and one of them lifts the order (ch. 4).
delivery.note: Light and comic in tone; the message comes through actions, not lectures.

personified.ideology: Protect the people in your care, whatever the rules

personified.character: Top of Horns (Bruno Bangnyfe, Wolfgang Slashhaut)

personified.ideology: Wanting to be special, chosen like a princess

116827.dominant: Pragmatism (work for pay and points), Communitarianism (protecting those in your care), Pagan/occult imagery (witches and spells).

101793.heading: By the Grace of the Gods
101793.label: From summaries
101793.life_message: A kind, hardworking person who was treated badly can build a good life by doing honest work, treating others fairly and learning that he does not have to do everything alone.

content.framing: Neutral (hunting and monster combat); thugs' violence condemned

delivery.evidence: Ryoma models kindness and fair work rather than arguing for them; the villains are minor bullies and a cruel distant god (Wikipedia; fan wiki); Turnaround calls it light-hearted and suitable for new readers of all ages.
delivery.note: Values are shown through daily choices (giving workers days off, cleaning a town, caring for slimes); no opposing worldview is given a fair hearing.

101793.dominant: Moralistic therapeutic deism (kind gods who reward a good man with a happy life), Classical virtue ethics, Pragmatism, Communitarianism.

38341.heading: CØDE:BREAKER
38341.label: From summaries
38341.life_message: Evil must be stopped, but no one has the right to decide who deserves to die; a killer can be changed by someone who refuses to give up on the value of every life.

content.framing: Mixed: executions shown as cool justice early, then questioned and increasingly refused
Played for comedy (groping gags); romance mild and sincere
Mixed: vigilante killing presented as justice, then questioned

delivery.evidence: Sakura and Rei argue about killing in words, again and again (anime ep. 2-5 summaries; ANN: "no easy answers"); Rei states his motto openly; Sakura's view gradually wins.
delivery.note: The debate over killing is the spine of the early volumes; later volumes turn to mystery and power battles, with the moral argument carried by Rei's choices.

personified.ideology: State power that uses people as tools

38341.dominant: Pacifism / nonviolence (Sakura) against retributive justice (Rei); Pagan/occult imagery; Collectivism/authoritarianism critiqued (Eden).

42586.heading: Cage of Eden
42586.label: From summaries
42586.life_message: People stay human under pressure by sticking together, forgiving, protecting the weak and choosing leaders who serve; those who seize power for themselves become the island's worst predators.

content.framing: Mixed: fan service and peeping played as comedy; sexual violence condemned
Endorsed as comedy (peeping); survival risks neutral

delivery.evidence: Akira states his idea of leadership in key speeches (ch. 40); villains like Nishikori are drawn as cartoonish manipulators and misogynists (Wikipedia), while Kouhei and Shuu are given reasons and redemption.
delivery.note: The cooperation theme is carried by the survival plot and a few speeches; ANN found the adults' quick slide into savagery hard to believe.

42586.dominant: Might makes right (critiqued), Communitarianism, Naturalism, Pragmatism.

111233.heading: Call of the Night (Yofukashi no Uta)
111233.label: From summaries
111233.life_message: A good life is one you choose for yourself. Freedom, honesty about your feelings and real connection matter more than fitting in, and love means staying with someone even when it costs you.

content.framing: Mixed: teasing played for comedy; lust distinguished from love

delivery.evidence: ANN's This Week in Anime calls the show a "pseudo-moral argument in favor of truancy"; reviewers otherwise praise its quiet, introspective tone (Aftermath).
delivery.note: Its case for freedom and honest feeling comes through mood and character arcs rather than speeches, while school and parents are mostly absent rather than argued against.

personified.ideology: Freedom and self-discovery outside school norms

111233.dominant: Expressive individualism, Existentialism, Hedonism (explored, then tempered).

98608.heading: Campfire Cooking in Another World with My Absurd Skill
98608.label: From summaries
98608.life_message: A good life is a modest, comfortable one shared with companions over good food: avoid being used by the powerful, work honestly, and be generous with what you have.

content.framing: Neutral (monster hunting played as routine and comic)

delivery.evidence: The kingdom's motives are shown through Mukohda's suspicions and the fan wiki's later reveal rather than argued; Anime Feminist describes a light comedy that pokes fun at its own genre. The gods' greed is satirized but never preached against.
delivery.note: Its preference for a modest, comfortable life is carried by Mukohda's choices and cooking, not by speeches.

98608.dominant: Pragmatism, Hedonism (food as the good life), Pagan/occult (a comic pantheon), Consumerism (explored).

159549.heading: Can I Live With You?
159549.label: From summaries
159549.life_message: A household of people who look after each other can become the family you never had, and every hurt person deserves a home where they are accepted.

content.framing: Mixed: adult nudity and desire presented as appealing; compensated dating treated as a problem to leave (to verify)

delivery.evidence: Every chapter title is a question about life ("What is your dream?", "Won't you try living as yourself?", ch. 1, 13); a MyAnimeList reviewer says Hiromi gives each woman a life tip like a therapist and they accept it too easily.
delivery.note: The found-family message is stated openly through Hiromi's counsel and the question titles, carried by romance and fan service.

personified.ideology: Care and the longing for a happy home
Self-expression and strength through pole dancing

159549.dominant: Communitarianism (found family), Expressive individualism (living as yourself), Traditionalism (explored: marriage and a happy home).

86797.heading: Can You Just Die, My Darling?
86797.label: From summaries
86797.life_message: Love means refusing to harm the person you love even when every impulse pushes you to; it is a choice made again and again.

delivery.evidence: Taku's struggle carries the message; after ch. 10 he speaks of the power of love and friendship (MyAnimeList); the cult and CID are drawn as plain villains.
delivery.note: Resisting inner violence is shown through Taku's choices rather than lectures; the later volumes add shonen speeches about love and friendship.

personified.ideology: The infected must protect each other

86797.dominant: Existentialism, Nihilism (critiqued), Might makes right (critiqued), Secular humanism.

99404.heading: CANDY AND CIGARETTES
99404.label: From summaries
99404.life_message: Loyalty between partners and love of family can hold in a violent world, and an adult owes a child a chance at an ordinary childhood, even when the work they share is killing.

content.framing: Endorsed within the story's logic (the targets are criminals beyond the law's reach); costs to the child raised but rarely followed
Neutral (fan service; not commented on in the story as far as sources show)
Mixed: the child killer is the heroine; the story briefly questions it

delivery.evidence: The publisher copy poses the question of how much blood Raizou will accept, but the AniList reviewer says the story rarely follows up; villains are corrupt elites and crime lords with little sympathy.
delivery.note: The moral questions about a child assassin are raised through situations (Raizou's hesitation, Miharu and another girl assassin) rather than argued, and are mostly left behind as the action escalates.

personified.ideology: Duty to family; protecting a child

99404.dominant: Strength rules (a world of assassins and crime lords), Utilitarianism (killing the guilty for the greater good), Pragmatism, Critical theory (corrupt elites as villains).

87296.heading: Cardcaptor Sakura: Clear Card
87296.label: From summaries
87296.life_message: Love protects best when it is honest and shared: secrets kept "for your own good" cause pain, and kindness, not force, sets everyone free.

delivery.evidence: Values come through character choices (Syaoran's confession, Akiho's reproach of Kaito, Sakura's refusal to fight). Den of Geek called the anime's plot "heavy-handed" (via Wikipedia); Loveridge (ANN) notes there are no traditional villains.
delivery.note: Kaito's scheme is given understandable motives and he is rescued; no worldview is mocked. Manga delivery is judged from summaries only.

personified.ideology: Power over all magic; people as tools

87296.dominant: Communitarianism and Classical virtue ethics (kindness, honesty), Pagan/occult (magic as setting), Expressive individualism (each person's right to choose).

30106.heading: Cardcaptor Sakura
30106.label: From summaries
30106.life_message: Love in all its forms, given freely and never forced, together with kindness and doing your best, carries you through anything; nobody has to be defeated for things to turn out all right.

delivery.evidence: Ohkawa says each relationship is presented without commentary on whether it is right (Wikipedia); there are no villains to argue an opposing view.
delivery.note: The message about love is shown through relationships, not stated as a lesson; the series simply does not question any of them.

30106.dominant: Communitarianism and Expressive individualism (love freely given), Pagan/occult (magic as setting), Progressivism (love without judgment).

104112.heading: Catch These Hands!
104112.label: From summaries
104112.life_message: You do not have to follow the usual adult script to grow up: being honest about who you are, and accepting the other person as they are, can turn an old rivalry into a real partnership.

content.framing: Neutral (slapstick); fighting framed as the pair's way of connecting

delivery.evidence: The theme comes out through the leads' comic failures and one honest conversation (vol. 4); the conventional path of Takebe's friends is shown without mockery.
delivery.note: Okazu, ANN and WWAC describe a comedy carried by character, with the lesson about honesty stated only at the end.

personified.ideology: Prove yourself by winning; later, accept yourself

86778.heading: Cells at Work!
86778.label: From summaries
86778.life_message: Every cell has a job, and life goes on because ordinary workers do theirs faithfully and protect one another; no part is too small to matter.

content.framing: Neutral (defense of the body; framed as necessary)

delivery.evidence: Boxed explanations teach the biology in every chapter (ANN); the cancer cell is given a real argument against the system (BMJ), though he loses.
delivery.note: The teaching is explicit but about biology, not morals; the values of work and teamwork come through the plot.

176740.heading: Centuria
176740.label: From summaries
176740.life_message: Kindness that treats every person as human, even a stranger, is what makes us human; a family is made by those who give themselves for a child, and that love is worth protecting against any king, god or prophecy.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; cruelty condemned, protective violence endorsed with remorse

delivery.evidence: Mira states the moral of ch. 1 aloud, but the rest is carried by events. Villains get some reasons: Elstri fears for the kingdom, the Rummir Empress would sacrifice a child for peace (Wikipedia), Lacrima grieves her brother; Arkos is drawn as pure cruelty, as Kuramori intends (Shonen Jump+ villain interview, via fan wiki).
delivery.note: The message rides on sacrifices and choices rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Protect the child; never forget the debt
Divine right to do anything; cruelty as fun
Kill one child to save the realm

176740.dominant: Communitarianism (found family), Classical virtue ethics, Collectivism/authoritarianism and Might makes right (critiqued), Pagan/occult (invented gods).

105778.heading: Chainsaw Man (Tatsuki Fujimoto)
105778.label: From summaries
105778.life_message: A good life here is an ordinary one: food, a home, a dog, people to eat with, and the freedom to choose your own wants instead of having them chosen for you.

content.framing: Mixed: Denji's lust played for comedy and pathos; coercion and manipulation shown as harmful but rarely judged

delivery.evidence: Morals are never stated; ideas come through absurd events and characters' choices. Makima's case for control and the Church's case for a world without evil are given real force before they fail (ch. 84, 141).
delivery.note: Its ideas come through absurd, violent events and the characters' choices rather than stated morals.

personified.ideology: A better world through total control
Simple desires and living day to day
A cult that uses a hero to start a war

105778.dominant: Existentialism, Absurdism, Pagan/occult imagery, Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Hedonism (explored).

85395.heading: Cheeky Brat
85395.label: From summaries
85395.life_message: A girl who has always put others first learns to be honest about what she wants, and a love that starts out pushy grows into steady, mutual support as both partners mature.

content.framing: Endorsed (romance); the pressured advances are framed as romantic, which critics question
Mixed: played as romantic; reviewers object

delivery.evidence: The theme of honesty about feelings is carried by Yuki's narration and the romance; rivals are given sympathy and graceful exits (Wikipedia; ciatr). No source comments on preachiness.
delivery.note: A character-driven shōjo romance with no stated message; its values show in what the story rewards.

personified.ideology: persistent pursuit of what you want
self-restraint and duty, opening to honesty

85395.dominant: Expressive individualism (learning to voice one's feelings), Communitarianism (team and family), Confucian ethics and Traditionalism (the eldest daughter's duty).

98188.heading: Cheerful Amnesia
98188.label: From summaries
98188.life_message: Love that chooses the same person again, through illness and memory loss, and patience with a partner who has changed are what make a life together.

delivery.evidence: A gag-a-page 4-koma (Asian Movie Pulse); acceptance of the couple is shown through coworkers and friends, and the mother's objection is answered by pressure rather than argument (vol. 4, Outer Haven).
delivery.note: Its message about faithful love is carried by comedy; the opposing view appears briefly in the mother and is overridden.

108946.heading: Cherry Magic! Thirty Years of Virginity Can Make You a Wizard?!
108946.label: From summaries
108946.life_message: Being truly known and loved by someone helps an insecure person accept himself, and a love built on honesty, patience and mutual support is worth committing to for life.

content.framing: Mixed: social drinking neutral; pushing drinks on someone condemned

delivery.evidence: Early volumes carry the message through romance and comedy; vol. 10 states it, with Kurosawa's sister asking why two people who love each other cannot marry (Anime UK News).
delivery.note: Opponents (wary parents, landlords, office rivals) are shown as obstacles to be overcome, with some, like Kurosawa's parents, given room to change.

personified.ideology: Pursue what you want regardless of commitments

108946.dominant: Expressive individualism (self-acceptance), Progressivism and Liberalism (same-sex marriage), Communitarianism (supportive friends, coworkers and family).

30387.heading: Chibi Vampire
30387.label: From summaries
30387.life_message: Giving of yourself rather than taking, honesty and faithful love can heal people and bridge any difference; sometimes loving your family means letting them go.

content.framing: Mixed: chaste central romance endorsed; exploitation and coercion condemned; Ren's womanizing played for comedy

delivery.evidence: Karin's kindness and the family's loyalty carry the message through comedy and melodrama; the villains (Glark, the Brownlicks) are flat, but Yuriya and Elda are drawn with sympathy.
delivery.note: The story rarely lectures; its values show in who gives and who takes.

personified.ideology: Pure-blood pride and fear of hybrids
Use the few to save the many, for profit

30387.dominant: Communitarianism (family loyalty); Pagan/occult (vampire lore and spirits); Expressive individualism (being different accepted); critique of Might makes right and Utilitarianism (the clans' plan to sacrifice Karin).

43245.heading: Chihayafuru
43245.label: From summaries
43245.life_message: Giving your whole self to something you love, with friends and teammates beside you, shapes who you become; courage and honesty matter more than winning, and the people who quietly stand by you deserve to be seen.

delivery.evidence: Rival styles (Shinobu's solitary karuta, Suo's detached tricks) are given real strength and inner life; they are shown as lonely or incomplete, not as villains.
delivery.note: The message is shown through matches, friendships and inner monologue; the poems themselves often carry the meaning.

35655.heading: Children of the Sea
35655.label: From summaries
35655.life_message: Life is one vast, connected mystery that joins the sea, the stars and every living body; it should be met with wonder and humility, not explained away or controlled, and even a lonely, angry girl belongs to it.

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)

delivery.evidence: Competing theories from scientists and from Dede are given room (Garrity); the mysteries are shown, not explained, and volume 5 is nearly wordless (Japanese Wikipedia; Manga Bookshelf).
delivery.note: The spiritual and ecological themes come through images and mood; characters debate them, but the book does not lecture.

personified.ideology: Sea mysticism and life through the female body
Science seeking to explain the boys

35655.dominant: Pantheist/New Age (the sacred, living sea and cosmos), Environmentalism, Pagan/occult (sea myths and rites), Existentialism.

86742.heading: Children of the Whales
86742.label: From summaries
86742.life_message: Feeling everything, grief included, and remembering the dead truthfully is what makes us human; a people that keeps choosing to live together, and tries to understand even its enemies, can outlast an empire that offers peace by taking feeling away.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; the Empire's massacres condemned; self-defense accepted with grief

delivery.evidence: ANN's McNulty saw the series heading toward endorsing free emotion; the Emperor's and Orca's case for a painless world is stated at length (VIZ vols. 15, 21), while Liontari's cruelty is cartoonish (ANN anime review).
delivery.note: The emotion-versus-control argument is carried by events and by Chakuro's archivist narration rather than speeches, but the later volumes argue it openly against the Emperor.

personified.ideology: Emotionless soldier who learns to feel
A world without pain through an apocalypse
Happiness by removing sadness and feeling

86742.dominant: Existentialism, Authoritarianism (critiqued), Stoicism (critiqued), Communitarianism, Pacifism / nonviolence (explored).

107120.heading: Chillin’ in Another World with Level 2 Super Cheat Powers
107120.label: From summaries
107120.life_message: A good life is a peaceful home, honest work and friendship across old enemy lines; great power is best used to protect the people around you and to build bridges between peoples, not to win wars.

content.framing: Mostly one-sided fantasy combat; cruelty and war-mongering condemned; mercy shown
Married love endorsed; fan service and sexual jokes played as comedy

delivery.evidence: Coexistence is shown through the household and Flio's choices rather than speeches; the war-hungry side (the old king, the Blonde Hero, Yuigarde) is played as comic incompetence, while Gholl's reluctant demon rule and the wyverns' different view of life and death get a fairer hearing (vols. 9-10).
delivery.note: The message is clear and gentle: peace and family beat conquest. It is carried by domestic comedy, with occasional serious turns (Rys injured, Wyne's loss, the twins).

personified.ideology: Peaceful home life and coexistence over war
Strength-based demon custom turned to love and protection
War and rule by brute strength

107120.dominant: Communitarianism (affirmed), Pragmatism (affirmed), Pacifism / nonviolence (limited, affirmed), Might makes right (critiqued but relied on).

113647.heading: Chillin' in My 30s After Getting Fired From the Demon King's Army
113647.label: From summaries
113647.life_message: Losing your place can lead you to who you really are; patient, competent care for others, peacemaking across old hatreds, and a family built on love outlast pride and jealousy.

content.framing: Endorsed as comedy; romance leads to marriage

delivery.evidence: Dariel's peacemaking and the human-demon prejudice are shown through events (the mine treaty, Laidy's change of heart); Bashvaza is given a jealous motive and a redemption, not just villainy.
delivery.note: Light comedy carries the message; critics found the lead bland rather than preachy.

personified.ideology: Bloodline supremacy and power through magic
The Hero's duty to kill the Demon King

113647.dominant: Communitarianism, Pacifism / nonviolence (in war), Traditionalism; Might makes right critiqued.

30107.heading: Chobits
30107.label: From summaries
30107.life_message: Real love is a free choice to stay with someone as they are, not ownership or gratification; and machines that only serve us can pull people away from each other.

content.framing: Mixed: sexual comedy and some romances endorsed; exploitation and assault condemned

delivery.evidence: The picture books inside the story state the questions outright (whether a persocom-human bond is one-sided; Wikipedia), and Minoru warns Hideki against loving a persocom (fan wiki). Yumi's and Shimizu's fears are drawn with sympathy; Kojima is the only real villain.
delivery.note: The themes are voiced through the picture books and friends' stories, framed by romantic comedy.

personified.ideology: Love chooses the person, not the use
A made companion cannot replace the dead, until he loves her as herself
Fear of being compared with a perfect machine
Persocoms as things to crack open

30107.dominant: Transhumanism (can a made mind love and be loved?), Consumerism critiqued (people preferring convenient machines to people), Expressive individualism (choosing one's own person), with a Feminist critique turned on the series itself.

156031.heading: Choking on Love
156031.label: From summaries
156031.life_message: Letting someone very different into a carefully planned life can open you to love and to your own creative voice; a good partner pushes you toward your dream instead of away from it.

content.framing: Neutral (adult romance; restraint shown when the couple stops short of sex)
Neutral (the drunken kiss is played as embarrassing)

delivery.evidence: Order versus spontaneity is explored through Hibari's own growth; Gaku's flaws (rudeness, immaturity) are shown and apologized for (reader reviews, vol. 5).
delivery.note: No source comments on preachiness; the message rides on the romance and the art plot.

156031.dominant: Expressive individualism (art and music as self), Communitarianism (band and friends).

103238.heading: Chronicles of an Aristocrat Reborn in Another World
103238.label: From summaries
103238.life_message: Great power is a gift to be used humbly for others, under good rulers and kindly gods; corrupt nobles, tyrants and evil gods are brought down, and peace is better than war.

delivery.evidence: Villains are cartoon figures (Corgino is an overweight buffoon, Wikipedia); the gods comment on Cain's choices comically; ANN calls the tone extremely laid-back.
delivery.note: The message is carried by rescue plots rather than speeches; Cain is lectured often for recklessness, but never for his aims.

103238.dominant: Pagan/occult (a real pantheon), Might makes right (benevolent overpowered hero), Traditionalism (nobility and arranged marriage), Communitarianism.

30338.heading: Chrono Crusade
30338.label: From summaries
30338.life_message: A short life given away in love for others is a full life, and even one born a "demon" can choose to protect rather than destroy.

content.framing: Neutral (demon fights as action); cruelty by demons condemned
Mixed: comic fan service; romance treated tenderly
Mixed: recklessness played for comedy; the demon contract shown with a heavy cost

delivery.evidence: Aion's case against a system that binds each being to a role is given charisma and backstory (fan wiki); the Order is shown with faults (Kate's distrust of Chrono, Remington's secrets) but as good.
delivery.note: Themes of sacrifice and love come through the plot and Rosette's choices; there are no sermons, and the manga's late reveal changes the religious frame quietly.

30338.dominant: Christian (as setting and imagery), Classical virtue ethics (courage and sacrifice), Existentialism (a short life chosen and lived fully), Pagan/occult (demon contracts).

103884.heading: Citrus+
103884.label: From summaries
103884.life_message: Declaring love is the start, not the end: two people have to keep choosing each other in small daily ways, say what they feel, respect each other's plans, and build a future together instead of letting others define it.

content.framing: Endorsed (romance); the first series' coercive advances criticized by others

delivery.evidence: The affirmation is carried by the couple's choices; the doubter Sayaka gets a full arc rather than a strawman, and Goodreads readers praise how her story was handled (vol. 2).
delivery.note: Friends and family appear as meddling advice-givers rather than as a contrary worldview; the one real objection to the couple, Sayaka's, is answered within the story.

personified.ideology: Duty and reserve learning to open up
Rules and doubt about same-sex love

103884.dominant: Expressive individualism (love on your own terms), Progressivism (a same-sex couple accepted), Communitarianism (friends and family around the couple).

30792.heading: City Hunter
30792.label: From summaries
30792.life_message: Behind the clown's mask, a good man protects people who cannot protect themselves; keeping your word to a dead friend and the steady love of a partner can redeem even a violent past.

content.framing: Neutral (action); villains condemned; Ryo's killing of criminals endorsed
Harassment played for comedy and punished by Kaori; not condemned by the story

delivery.evidence: Villains are cartoon predators and drug lords; Ryo's code is shown in action rather than stated.
delivery.note: Episodic action comedy; the values (loyalty, protection) come through what Ryo does when he turns serious.

personified.ideology: Protector's code beneath a lecher's mask
Power through drugs and child soldiers

30792.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (a protector's code), Hedonism (explored as comedy), Duty ethics (keeping a promise), Bushido / honor code (warrior honor).

97700.heading: CITY
97700.label: From summaries
97700.life_message: Ordinary life in a town full of odd, kind neighbors is worth enjoying every day; small kindnesses and friendship are what make a city a home.

delivery.evidence: Episodic gags with no argued message; the closest to a moral is Midori finding every day fun (ep. 13) and the town's habit of rewarding kindness (ep. 4-5).
delivery.note: A gag comedy; values are carried by situations, not speeches.

48200.heading: Classmates (Sotsu gyo sei: Winter and Spring)
48200.label: From summaries
48200.life_message: Honest, patient love can carry two very different people through fear, family illness and diverging dreams; growing up means choosing your own path while keeping faith with the person you love.

content.framing: Endorsed (as committed love); the teacher's attraction to a student shown as uncomfortable but not fully condemned

delivery.evidence: No speeches: the case for the couple is made through daily scenes, illness and graduation. Homophobia stays in the background (AIPT); Hara is drawn sympathetically and uncomfortably at once (AIPT; StoryGraph).
delivery.note: Nakamura aimed for a slow, serious, almost clichéd love story with realistic touches (Wikipedia).

personified.ideology: Duty and caution, learning to trust love
Adult desire that ignores a student's position

48200.dominant: Expressive individualism, Progressivism (affirming same-sex love), Secular humanism.

96798.heading: Classroom of the Elite
96798.label: From summaries
96798.life_message: In a system that rewards only results, the clever rise by reading and using other people; the story asks, without settling it, whether its brilliant, cold hero is a protector or a manipulator.

content.framing: Mixed: bullies and attackers condemned; violence the hero arranges is shown as useful
Mixed: fan service played straight; stalking and false-accusation threats condemned or used as leverage

delivery.evidence: Kinugasa says each class's approach has problems and none is absolutely correct; rivals (Ryuen, Sakayanagi, Ichinose) are given real strengths.
delivery.note: The story shows rather than tells; Ayanokoji's unreliable narration (Wikipedia) leaves the reader to judge him.

personified.ideology: Results over feelings; people as tools

96798.dominant: Might makes right (the school's creed, tested), Pragmatism, Utilitarianism, Critical theory (the ranking system).

30583.heading: Claymore
30583.label: From summaries
30583.life_message: A good life holds onto its humanity under pressure. You stay loyal to comrades and to the dead, refuse to be used as someone else's weapon, and choose solidarity with other outcasts over power or revenge.

content.framing: Mixed: sexual threat and abuse condemned; nudity often uncensored

delivery.evidence: The Organization's motives are revealed through Rubel and Miria's investigation (v15-16) rather than speeches; Isley and Priscilla get sympathetic backstories (Extra Scene 3-4, v14). No review opened calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its themes of humanity and institutional exploitation emerge through plot reveals and characters' choices rather than lectures.

personified.ideology: Loyalty and humanity kept despite a monstrous body
People as weapons; ends justify means
Faith community moving from exclusion to hospitality
Power without restraint, born of trauma

87151.heading: Colette Decides to Die
87151.label: From summaries
87151.life_message: Caring for others is a calling worth keeping, but only if you also rest and let yourself be cared for; good work done with love gives life meaning, and even guilt and death can be met with mercy.

content.framing: Neutral; aggression shown as wrong and apologized for
Endorsed: slow, chaste romance that ends in marriage
Shown with consequences; recovery through rest and purpose

delivery.evidence: Caitlin Moore (ANN) calls it "a touch didactic" for adults but well suited to teens; lessons come through Colette's patients and Hades' example.
delivery.note: Gentle, episodic stories each carry a small lesson about care, rest or forgiveness; no villain argues the other side at length.

personified.ideology: Care for others, balanced by care for yourself
Duty borne quietly; mercy in judgment

87151.dominant: Communitarianism (care for a whole town), Pagan/occult (Greek gods as real), Duty ethics (a healer never abandons a patient), Classical virtue ethics.

107114.heading: COLORLESS
107114.label: From summaries
107114.life_message: Knowledge and loyal protection of the vulnerable, not fanatical faith that demands sacrifice, are the way to restore what a broken world has lost.

delivery.evidence: The publisher frames it as a stylish noir thriller; the cult is a villain, but a MyAnimeList reviewer says the cult and police are not simple villains (to verify).
delivery.note: Sources describe mood, art and mystery rather than an argued message; how the cult's beliefs are presented could not be checked.

personified.ideology: Innocence and the hope of restoration

107114.dominant: Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued, through the cult), Secular humanism (science against fanaticism), Transhumanism (explored).
