101808.heading: Combatants Will Be Dispatched!
101808.label: From summaries
101808.life_message: Results matter more than honor: a cynical, lecherous scoundrel who looks after his comrades does more good than self-righteous heroes, and loyalty to your own crew is the rule that counts.

content.framing: Endorsed as comedy (lechery rewarded with Evil Points); victims object, and the stalker Agent Ten is shown as creepy

delivery.evidence: Knights and heroes (Snow, the kingdom's Chosen One) are shown as vain, greedy or useless; Six's cynicism is never seriously answered; the only steady value is loyalty to comrades.
delivery.note: The story makes no argument; its outlook comes through which jokes it rewards.

personified.ideology: Pragmatic villainy with loyalty to comrades
Honor as a mask for greed

101808.dominant: Pragmatism, Absurdism, Might makes right, Hedonism.

100309.heading: Cooking with Wild Game
100309.label: From summaries
100309.life_message: Good work done with care, shared food and honest dealing can bridge peoples who despise each other; strength should protect the weak, and a community is healthiest when every person's labor is respected.

content.framing: Neutral (hunting and butchery as craft); crimes condemned
Neutral (fan service and comedy); assault condemned

delivery.evidence: Forest's Edge skeptics such as Donda Ruu are given reasons and won over by results; the Suun are drawn as plain villains.
delivery.note: The message is carried by meals and their effects rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Clan pride and suspicion of change
Privilege maintained by crime and fear

99737.heading: Crashout Schoolgirl and Degen Teacher
99737.label: From summaries
99737.life_message: When someone is ready to give up, a person who stays beside them and keeps asking why they want to die can give them reasons to live.

content.framing: Endorsed: the secret relationship between an adult teacher and a high-school student is the story's center and is presented sympathetically
Shown with consequences; partly played as black comedy

delivery.evidence: The premise and the episodic comedy carry the message; no character is reported to argue against the relationship except as a rule to dodge (MyAnimeList reviews; ciatr).
delivery.note: The school's ban on teacher-student relationships appears only as something to hide from, not as a view the story weighs (to verify in print).

personified.ideology: Stay beside the despairing, whatever the rules
Despair, then a reason to live

99737.dominant: Existentialism (reasons to live), Expressive individualism (the forbidden relationship), Absurdism (black comedy).

121971.heading: Crazy Food Truck
121971.label: From summaries
121971.life_message: Freedom to live as you choose, eating good food beside someone who cares for you, is worth more than a long life under someone else's control.

content.framing: Endorsed (action as spectacle); cruelty of the villains condemned
Endorsed (fan service throughout; the sexual relationship is the story's romantic climax)

delivery.evidence: Freedom versus control is carried by plot (Gordon's faked death, Arisa's refusal to return; The Slings and Arrows), not speeches; the villains are cartoonish (Colonel Diego; The Manga Critic finds some villain designs grotesque caricatures).
delivery.note: The message emerges mostly in the last volume; the first two are episodic cooking-and-action chapters.

personified.ideology: Choosing a free life even if short
Duty to the system, then loyalty to Gordon

56857.heading: Creature!
56857.label: From summaries
56857.life_message: When the world ends, love and loyalty to the people beside you are what keep you human; those who rule by fear or treat people as tools destroy themselves, and humanity can survive even its own failures.

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)

delivery.evidence: Action horror with themes carried by events: the teacher's madness and the army's cruelty are shown, not argued; the Earth's-will reveal is delivered by the villain (Japanese Wikipedia).
delivery.note: Little lecturing; the meaning comes from who sacrifices and who exploits.

personified.ideology: Survival at any cost; people as tools

56857.dominant: Might makes right (critiqued), Transhumanism, Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Environmentalism.

31183.heading: Cross Game
31183.label: From summaries
31183.life_message: Grief does not have to stop you: you honor the people you have lost by keeping your promises to them through quiet, patient effort, and you let yourself love again.

delivery.evidence: Wikipedia notes the manga was cited for telling its story in wordless scenes; Coach Daimon is drawn as arrogant and his fall is his own doing (Manga Report), while rivals like Yuhei are treated fairly.
delivery.note: The message is almost never stated: it lives in silences, flashbacks and what characters leave unsaid.

personified.ideology: Talent and pride; grief turned to resentment
Elite talent who learns team loyalty

31183.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Duty ethics (promise-keeping), Stoicism.

109064.heading: Crow Hill: Don’t Be Shy!!
109064.label: From summaries
109064.life_message: Behind a tough reputation, telling the truth about your feelings takes more courage than fighting, and the person who once stood up for you is worth standing beside.

content.framing: Mixed: fights for protection; crime condemned

delivery.evidence: A comedy of misunderstandings; the same-sex romance is presented as normal and is not debated in sources opened.
delivery.note: The message (be honest about your feelings) is carried by gags and the final confession, not speeches.

personified.ideology: Shy love behind a tough reputation
Justice and courage for the weak

109064.dominant: Expressive individualism (be honest about who and what you love), Progressivism (same-sex romance as normal), Communitarianism (guarding the town).

35651.heading: Crows
35651.label: From summaries
35651.life_message: Real strength protects friends and the weak and turns rivals into brothers; those who rule by weapons, numbers or money fall, and the fights of youth end when you grow up and move on.

content.framing: Mixed: fair one-on-one fights endorsed; weapons, ambushes and attacks on the weak condemned
Endorsed (fighting as the path to respect and friendship)

delivery.evidence: Bouya states his creed once (a crow is freer than a caged bird, ch. 1, paraphrased); rivals like Rindaman and the Bitou brothers get real reasons, while Bandou and the Snake Heads are drawn as schemers.
delivery.note: The code is shown in action rather than explained; the comedy keeps the tone light.

35651.dominant: Might makes right (explored), Bushido / honor code, Communitarianism.

44721.heading: D-Frag!
44721.label: From summaries
44721.life_message: Even a self-styled tough guy finds he belongs among friends as odd as he is; rivalries are settled with games, and the series is mostly about laughs.

content.framing: Played for laughs; nobody is seriously hurt

delivery.evidence: Reviewers describe a sketch comedy with little story and no moralizing (ANN vol. 1; A Case Suitable for Treatment; MyAnimeList reviews).
delivery.note: The series offers sketches rather than a message; small lessons (apologize, play fair, look after people) arise from the plots without comment.

44721.dominant: Absurd school comedy; Communitarianism (a found family of misfits).

136899.heading: Daemons of the Shadow Realm
136899.label: From summaries
136899.life_message: No village, clan or prophecy owns a person: the twins refuse to be anyone's tool, choose whom to trust, and hold on to each other and the people who treat them as people.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; killing by villains condemned, defensive killing by heroes accepted

delivery.evidence: Arakawa withholds information so readers share Yuru's confusion (Wikipedia, Production); villains like Gonzo and Yamaha get motives and history, while assassins like Ivan are plain villains.
delivery.note: The message that people are not tools rides on plot twists and Yuru's choices; nobody lectures. Common Sense Media summarizes the lessons as loyalty, honor and not using violence to hold power over others.

personified.ideology: Village tradition and prophecy as a means to power
Use the twins' power for the greater good

136899.dominant: Pagan/occult (folk religion), Traditionalism (critiqued), Expressive individualism (self-determination), Communitarianism (found family).

105263.heading: Dai Dark
105263.label: From summaries
105263.life_message: Even when the whole universe wants to use you, you can stay cheerful, kind and loyal to the friends who stand by you, and refuse to let any power own you.

delivery.evidence: No speeches; the critique of the Solar Mass is shown through its schools, workers and cult rather than argued; enemies are mostly grotesque gags.
delivery.note: The message is carried by the crew's behavior and the comedy; the world's injustices are background jokes with a sharp edge.

personified.ideology: Live cheerfully; trust friends; refuse to be anyone's prize
Freedom and appetite; death as natural
Corporate-religious control in the name of light

105263.dominant: Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued: the Solar Mass), Communitarianism (affirmed: the found family), Pagan/occult (explored: dark magic and a God of Death), Absurdism.

165012.heading: Damedol and the Only Fan in the World
165012.label: From summaries
165012.life_message: Steady, wholehearted support from one person can matter more than talent or popularity, and the one being supported can learn to accept it and give care back.

content.framing: Mixed (devotion shown as sweet; overwork shown with a cost)

delivery.evidence: Kishirimo describes an oshi as someone who brightens your life (Real Sound); the story shows devotion through running gags, not lectures (MyAnimeList reviews).
delivery.note: There is no opposing worldview in the sources opened; the only tension is between Urumin's prickliness and Kimiya's sincerity.

personified.ideology: Wholehearted support for the one you believe in
Insecurity learning to accept being loved

165012.dominant: Consumerism (explored, through oshikatsu), Classical virtue ethics (loyalty and constancy), Communitarianism, Expressive individualism.

37627.heading: Dance in the Vampire Bund
37627.label: From summaries
37627.life_message: Peace between peoples who fear each other needs someone strong enough to shelter the outcasts and to fight the extremists on every side, by ruthless means if necessary; love and a promise kept are what keep that power pointed toward good.

content.framing: Neutral to endorsed (the heroes' killings shown as necessary)
Fan service presented for appeal; assaults by villains condemned
Mixed: fan service unjudged; villains' assaults condemned

delivery.evidence: Mina states her aim of coexistence on live TV (ch. 3-4); human extremists and vampire supremacists are both villains, and a sympathetic bullied boy turns terrorist (Wikipedia; TV Tropes).
delivery.note: A political action story whose views on prejudice come through events; its sexual content is presented as appeal rather than argued.

personified.ideology: Coexistence won by a ruthless protector
A bullied boy seeking power through hate

37627.dominant: Duty ethics (Akira's promise), Authoritarianism and Strength rules (explored through Mina's rule and the lords), Liberalism (a minority's rights and coexistence), Patriotism / nationalism (a homeland for vampires).

132029.heading: Dandadan
132029.label: From summaries
132029.life_message: A good life is lived with kindness toward people, spirits and outsiders alike: stand by your friends, protect the vulnerable, eat well after hard work, and do not let fear or other people's mockery decide who you are.

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)
content.framing: Condemned (assaults, framed as villainy); neutral (gags and fan service)

delivery.evidence: Common Sense Media: friendship should be treasured; Tatsu says the meal scenes give readers hope (Wikipedia). Villains such as the Kito family and the teacher are drawn as plain predators.
delivery.note: Its themes of respect and found family come through comedy and horror episodes; its predatory villains are condemned outright, and the leads' kindness is shown rather than preached.

personified.ideology: Folk practice of coexistence between living and dead
Sacrificing outsiders to keep the village safe
Grief that will not let go

132029.dominant: Pagan / occult (Japanese folk religion), Communitarianism (found family), Classical virtue ethics (kindness and courage), Expressive individualism (outsiders accepted as they are).

109608.heading: Dark Gathering
109608.label: From summaries
109608.life_message: Fear and grief can be faced, and a life that trauma took can be won back, when people who love each other stand together and plan carefully; even a god's claim on a family can be broken.

delivery.evidence: Themes of fear, grief and family loyalty are carried by action and backstory; no reviewer calls it preachy. Ghost backstories give even villains sympathy (fan wiki: the courtesan, the soldier, the castle women).
delivery.note: The story argues through outcomes: planning and loyalty win, predators lose, and tragic spirits are often treated with mercy.

personified.ideology: Reason and resolve; use any means to save family
Courage that grows out of fear
Divine arrogance; beings ranked by power

109608.dominant: Pagan/occult (spirit capture and binding as the heroes' craft), Communitarianism (family and team), Might makes right (explored: power ranks and a god who scorns the weak).

100937.heading: DARLING in the FRANXX
100937.label: From summaries
100937.life_message: Love, loyalty and the freedom to choose your own future are what make people human; a society that trades feeling, family and children for comfort, control and endless life has lost what matters most.

content.framing: Neutral (mecha action); the disposal of children condemned
Endorsed as fan service; romance affirmed

delivery.evidence: The case for love and family is carried by the squad's story; APE's view is voiced briefly by Papa in ch. 60 (fan wiki). MyAnimeList reviewers say the manga trims the anime's thematic and world-building depth for a faster mecha romance.
delivery.note: The message is clear but rides on the romance and battles; the adults are given little case beyond control and escape from the body.

personified.ideology: Escape from the body; order through control
Curiosity about family and children; mercy

78881.heading: Darwin's Game
78881.label: From summaries
78881.life_message: In a game that rewards killing, a clear head and loyalty to the people you protect let you survive and build a safe place for others; cruelty for its own sake is punished, but lethal force against the cruel is shown as necessary.

content.framing: Mixed: villains' cruelty condemned; the heroes' lethal force endorsed
Played for comedy and romance; not judged

delivery.evidence: ANN's finale review: after Shinozuka's murder Kaname becomes efficient and remorseless, then the clan adopts a rule against killing unless necessary. The message is carried by choices in battle, not speeches.
delivery.note: Villains like Wang are drawn as sadists with no case, while the Game Master's greater-good reasoning is given real weight.

personified.ideology: Strength rules, then love and loyalty

78881.dominant: Pragmatism, Might makes right (critiqued), Utilitarianism, Communitarianism.

41896.heading: Dawn of the Arcana
41896.label: From summaries
41896.life_message: Seeing truly, the past, the future and other people's pain, makes peace and equality possible; love grows from respect rather than possession, and a ruler's duty is to serve all the people, including the despised.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; massacres, executions and treaty-breaking condemned
Mixed: possessiveness shown as a flaw Caesar outgrows; marriage and fidelity honored

delivery.evidence: Loki's case for the Ajin is given real weight and Cain's resentment is explained by his own hair-color shame (Japanese Wikipedia), but King Guran and Batal are drawn as plain villains.
delivery.note: Equality is carried by Nakaba's choices and Loki's fate rather than by speeches; the romance carries most pages.

personified.ideology: Peace and equality through truth and mercy
Ajin liberation and self-rule, by force if needed

41896.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (a ruler's prudence and courage), Strength rules (critiqued), Progressivism (ending caste and slavery), Duty ethics.

130837.heading: Days with My Stepsister
130837.label: From summaries
130837.life_message: Honest talk, clear boundaries and respect for the other person's choices can heal the scars of a broken family and let trust, and then love, grow slowly.

content.framing: Mixed: restraint and consent respected; stepsibling romance treated as a serious dilemma; some suggestive framing

delivery.evidence: The pair state their rules and feelings openly in dialogue, inner monologue and Saki's diary (anime ep. 9); no character is mocked for holding a different view.
delivery.note: The message is carried by quiet scenes of chores, meals and talk rather than lectures; ANN reviewers found the restraint slow.

57231.heading: Daytime Shooting Star
57231.label: From summaries
57231.life_message: First love is not always lasting love: real love is honest and between equals, a relationship that has to be hidden is a warning sign, and growing up means choosing what is good for you over what dazzles you.

content.framing: Mixed: the teacher-student romance is shown sympathetically at first, then as unequal and ended; the peer romance endorsed

delivery.evidence: Shishio's side is given at length (he lies that he does not love her to protect her, ch. 47; fan wiki), while reviewers say the series gradually exposes him as manipulative and immature (Silverman; Anna N).
delivery.note: The lesson is carried by Suzume's experience, not by lectures; Silverman notes the series gives the teacher-student issue more thought than many shōjo romances.

personified.ideology: Romantic love that ignores a position of trust

57231.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (honesty), Expressive individualism (tempered), Duty ethics (teacher's duty)

100868.heading: Dead Mount Death Play
100868.label: From summaries
100868.life_message: Reputations lie: a feared "monster" can be the one who rescues children and keeps faith with friends, while those who call themselves righteous can be cruel, so judge people by what they do.

content.framing: Mixed: the hero kills in defense and protection; assassins and killers mostly condemned, but Misaki enjoys killing
Gratuitous (per critics); adult same-sex relationships neutral

delivery.evidence: ANN's reviewers say the theme of assumptions about others comes through character; the Geldwood Church is shown through its worst acts, while Shagrua and the Shinoyamas get more room.
delivery.note: The inversion of hero and villain is built into the premise and backstory rather than stated; the story rarely lectures.

personified.ideology: A feared necromancer who wants peace and protects the weak

100868.dominant: Pagan/occult (necromancy as the hero's craft), Pragmatism, Might makes right (explored), Communitarianism (found family).

126770.heading: Deadpool: Samurai
126770.label: From summaries
126770.life_message: Behind the jokes and the violence, even a mercenary who mocks everything can become a loyal teammate; and nothing, including superheroes and the comics business, should be taken too seriously.

content.framing: Endorsed as comedy; villains' cruelty condemned
Mixed: lewd jokes as comedy; the sexual threat condemned

delivery.evidence: The only sincere statement is Captain America's explanation of Deadpool's grief (ch. 11) and VIZ's vol. 4 blurb on his bond with coworkers; everything else is a gag.
delivery.note: There is almost no preaching: the small moral (loyalty under the jokes) is carried by a few quiet moments in a comedy that mocks everything, including itself.

personified.ideology: Irreverence and self-interest, with buried loyalty

126770.dominant: Postmodernism (meta-comedy), Absurdism, Consumerism (brand crossover), Communitarianism (team bond).

143719.heading: Dealing with Mikadono Sisters Is a Breeze
143719.label: From summaries
143719.life_message: Ordinary kindness and steady effort are a talent too: a family is made by caring for one another, not by being brilliant.

delivery.evidence: The father voices the opposing view ("talentless nobody," episode 5) and is answered by events; Yuu states his mother's wish openly; Sakura argues for effort over genius (episode 10).
delivery.note: Each arc resolves one sister's problem through Yuu's care; the theme of talent versus effort is restated through rivals.

143719.dominant: Communitarianism (found family), Classical virtue ethics (effort), Expressive individualism (self-acceptance).

86511.heading: Death March to the Parallel World Rhapsody
86511.label: From summaries
86511.life_message: A good life after burnout is a calm and generous one: travel, good food and honest work, with great power used quietly to protect and care for the people who join you.

content.framing: Mixed: the hero refuses advances from minors; adult sex off-page; fan service as comedy

delivery.evidence: The message of rest and kindness is carried by episodes of travel, food and rescue; villains (scheming nobles, cultists) are thin (fan wiki; Yen Press synopses).
delivery.note: A comfort story: values are modeled by the hero's behavior rather than argued.

personified.ideology: Rest, kindness and hidden power used well

86511.dominant: Pragmatism (skills and problem-solving), Hedonism (food, travel and rest), Communitarianism (found family), Classical virtue ethics (generosity and prudence).

127819.heading: Death Note Short Stories
127819.label: From summaries
127819.life_message: Power over life and death ruins whoever holds it, whether they call its use mercy, justice or business; the only safe choice is to refuse it, and even the cleverest person cannot outwit death.

delivery.evidence: C-Kira stages a televised debate between pro- and anti-Kira speakers (fan wiki); But Why Tho says a-Kira critiques politics, greed and power without heavy-handed lecturing.
delivery.note: The verdicts come through outcomes (who dies) and Near's brief statements rather than lectures.

personified.ideology: Mercy killing; a wish for significance

30021.heading: Death Note (Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata, 2003-2006)
30021.label: From summaries
30021.life_message: No one may make himself judge of who deserves to live: a life spent seizing that power ends in lies, isolation and a meaningless death. Ohba's own stated takeaway is: "Humans will all eventually die, so let's give it our all while we're alive" (Wikipedia, citing Ohba).

content.frequency: Constant (deaths every few chapters), mostly non-graphic

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)

content.framing: Condemned in story; real-world copying documented

delivery.evidence: Light and L argue openly about justice; Light's final speech (ch. 105) states his case in full before the story rejects it. ANN's Briana Lawrence: two sides that both believe in justice (via Wikipedia).
delivery.note: Ohba said he had no particular theme in mind (Wikipedia); the verdict comes through Light's fall rather than a stated lesson.

personified.ideology: Justice by results; one genius may judge and kill
Rule of law, duty and honesty

30021.dominant: Utilitarianism (critiqued), Strength rules (critiqued), Duty ethics (affirmed through Soichiro and the law), Nihilism (explored), Liberalism (affirmed: due process and rule of law).

43748.heading: Defense Devil
43748.label: From summaries
43748.life_message: Mercy that defends the wrongly condemned is worth more than power, and real strength is kindness and loyalty to friends, not domination.

content.framing: Neutral (battle action); cruelty by demons and angels condemned
Played as comedy (fan service); romance sincere

delivery.evidence: Each case closes on the moral that the accused deserved a hearing; Bichula voices the practical objection that kindness wastes dark matter (AniList), and the villains are mostly power-seekers without much depth (MyAnimeList reviewers).
delivery.note: The message is carried by the case structure and by Kucabara's choices more than by speeches.

43748.dominant: Christian (imagery rearranged: demon hero, corrupt angels, a good God), Pagan/occult (demons, Lilith, contracts and dark matter), Liberalism (due process for the accused), Classical virtue ethics (mercy and loyalty).

108817.heading: Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba - Giyu Tomioka’s Story
108817.label: From summaries
108817.life_message: A parent's love can outlast even the worst loss, and those who are strong are bound to protect the grieving and urge them to keep living.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; demon violence condemned, slaying framed as protection

delivery.evidence: The message comes through action and one line of dialogue (the father's last word), with Giyu's reflection at the end; But Why Tho calls the story simple and brief.
delivery.note: Duty is stated outright in Giyu's closing words to Shinobu, but the life-affirming theme is carried by the plot.

personified.ideology: Vengeance and despair, turned toward life

108817.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Stoicism, Bushido / honor code (the protector's duty), Duty ethics.

118991.heading: Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba - Kyojuro Rengoku's Story
118991.label: From summaries
118991.life_message: Strength exists to protect the weak; a son can honor a failing father by taking up the duty the father laid down, without bitterness and without revenge.

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)

delivery.evidence: Kyojuro states his mother's teaching that the strong must protect the weak, and tells Mitsuri her personality and gifts are her strength (Part 2); Hairo's grievance (guns against swords, Shinjuro's cruelty) is given a hearing before he is defeated.
delivery.note: The message is spoken outright in key scenes, but the story is short and action-driven.

personified.ideology: Duty of the strong to protect the weak

118991.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Duty ethics (deontology), Confucian ethics, Bushido / honor code.

126445.heading: Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba - Stories of Water and Flame
126445.label: From summaries
126445.life_message: The strong exist to protect the weak; you honor your family and your dead by living on and doing your duty, not by revenge or despair.

delivery.evidence: Kyojuro states his mother's teaching that the strong must protect the weak; Shinobu tells Yae to bear her grief; Hairo's grievance (guns against swords, Shinjuro's cruelty) is given a fair hearing before he is defeated.
delivery.note: The message is spoken outright in key scenes, but each story is short and action-driven.

personified.ideology: Duty of the strong to protect the weak

126445.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Confucian ethics, Duty ethics (deontology), Bushido / honor code.

87216.heading: Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba
87216.label: From summaries
87216.life_message: A good life is lived for others. You protect the weak, honor the dead, keep promises, and pass your will to the next generation. A long or powerful life bought by harming others is worth nothing.

delivery.evidence: Tallon (Christian Research Journal): "Humanizing is the goal, instead of demonizing." No review in the entry calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its messages about compassion and duty are spoken in Tanjiro's lines and shown through the demons' backstories.

87216.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Confucian ethics, Communitarianism, Buddhist ideas, Bushido / honor code, Traditionalism, Stoicism.

35255.heading: Dengeki Daisy
35255.label: From summaries
35255.life_message: Love that keeps its promises protects the people we are given to care for, and no one is so guilty that they cannot be forgiven and allowed to be happy.

content.framing: Condemned when done by villains; Kurosaki's fights shown as protective
Shown with consequences; healing through others
Mixed: hacking shown as heroic; Kurosaki's secrecy questioned

delivery.evidence: The forgiveness theme is spoken by characters (Soichiro and Midorikawa's letter, ch. 39) but carried mostly by the thriller and comedy; villains like Mori are thin, while Arai, Takeda and Rena get room to change (fan wiki; Wikipedia).
delivery.note: Kurosaki's restraint and the promise to wait are stated directly late in the series (Special Episode 2), as if answering readers' worries.

personified.ideology: Ends justify means; use of others

35255.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (loyalty, courage, restraint), Communitarianism (found family), Duty ethics (a promise kept to a dying friend).

105790.heading: Destroy All Humans. They Can't Be Regenerated. A Magic: The Gathering Manga
105790.label: From summaries
105790.life_message: A shared passion can turn a rival into a friend and a first love, and the people you meet around a game can matter more than winning it.

content.framing: Fan service of young-teen characters (reader reports); romance sincere and innocent

delivery.evidence: Themes ride on games and romance; Emi's two personas and her mother's view are given room (Goodreads readers; VIZ blurbs).
delivery.note: No source comments on preachiness; the game's history is explained in footnotes and a guide rather than in lectures.

31061.heading: Detective Conan (Case Closed)
31061.label: From summaries
31061.life_message: The truth can always be found by careful reasoning, and it must serve life: murder is never justified, even as revenge, and a detective who corners a culprit and lets them die is no better than a murderer.

content.framing: Condemned (murder is the problem to solve); shown with consequences

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)
content.framing: Chaste romance endorsed; comic leering mocked
Shown with consequences; suicide treated as a failure to prevent

delivery.evidence: Conan states his rule against letting culprits die and repeatedly lectures killers that murder is never justified (DCW); The Escapist notes the anime treats killing as serious. Culprits' grievances are heard in full before the verdict.
delivery.note: The message is carried by the structure of every case: a death, an investigation, the truth spoken aloud and a confession.

personified.ideology: Truth by reason; every life matters

31061.dominant: Duty ethics (murder never justified, truth must be told), Classical virtue ethics, Secular humanism (reason over superstition), Liberalism (rule of law).

98564.heading: Devil-Chi
98564.label: From summaries
98564.life_message: Accepting someone's hidden, different self, keeping a childhood promise and standing by a friend who is bullied are what real affection looks like.

delivery.evidence: No review found; the publisher's pitch is a light, slightly lewd love comedy with a memory-and-fate mystery (GANMA!).
delivery.note: The message about accepting difference grows out of the romance and is not stated as a lesson in any source found.

personified.ideology: The misjudged outsider who wants friends

98564.dominant: Expressive individualism (acceptance of a hidden self), Communitarianism (friendship), Pagan/occult (angels, demons and memory magic, explored).

31474.heading: Devilman
31474.label: From summaries
31474.life_message: Fear and hatred of the other can make people more monstrous than demons; a loving heart is what makes someone human, and war, any war, has no justice.

content.framing: Demon battles played as horror-action; human cruelty condemned
Neutral (nudity as part of the horror); a sexual threat to a minor condemned

delivery.evidence: Characters deliver long speeches on human nature and the coming end (TCJ calls it preachy; a MangaUpdates reader notes drawn-out exposition); Nagai stated the anti-war message directly (Wikipedia). The mob is shown as pure frenzy with no reasoning given (fan wiki), while Satan and the demons get reasons.
delivery.note: The warning is spoken aloud by Ryo and the narration and enacted by the mob in v5; the theology (Satan sympathetic, God as aggressor) is carried by the ending more than by argument.

personified.ideology: Love and a human heart in a demon body
The demons' right to the Earth; humans as the true destroyers
Fear and hatred of anyone different

31474.dominant: Nihilism (apocalypse), Christian imagery inverted (Satan and God), Pacifism / nonviolence (anti-war), Might makes right critiqued.

86648.heading: Devils' Line
86648.label: From summaries
86648.life_message: Love that respects consent and self-control can live with a dangerous nature, and people should be judged by what they do, not by what they were born as; fear and hatred of a minority breed the real monsters.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; terror and murder condemned

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)
content.framing: Mixed: committed adult sex affirmed with consent stressed; assault condemned

delivery.evidence: Fandom Post: both extremes in the conflict are flawed and most devils are peaceful; Otaku USA praises the open handling of consent; the CCC's motives are given (Ushio's pity, Nanako's trauma) but its methods are terrorism.
delivery.note: Themes of prejudice and consent are carried by plot and dialogue; the anti-devil side gets backstories but is not given a fair argument.

personified.ideology: Extermination of devils; ends justify means

86648.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (temperance), Progressivism (minority rights), Liberalism (rights and rule of law), Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued).

88577.heading: Dissolving Classroom
88577.label: From summaries
88577.life_message: Showy apologies and perfect manners can hide real evil: an apology that is a performance, not true repentance, is worse than useless.

delivery.evidence: The apology satire is carried by the plot and by Ito's comic afterword on public apologies (The Beat; Wikipedia); no character argues for or against it.
delivery.note: The point is made through repetition and escalation (each chapter another apology, another melting) rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Hollow apology as devotion to evil

88577.dominant: Pagan/occult (devil worship, critiqued), Absurdism, Nihilism (a world where evil wins).

30648.heading: Dogs: Bullets & Carnage
30648.label: From summaries
30648.life_message: People damaged by a cruel past can still choose to protect the weak and stand together, but the story leaves open whether they can escape the violence that made them.

content.framing: Stylized and celebrated as spectacle; cruelty by villains condemned
Exploitation condemned; a comic "Lolita complex" gag left unjudged

delivery.evidence: Reviewers say action crowds out story (ANN: Story D- for vol. 5); themes surface through backstories rather than speeches.
delivery.note: The villains are monstrous (child experimenters, traffickers), but several (Giovanni, the twins, Richter) get sympathetic pasts.

personified.ideology: Protect the few you love; destroy those who made you
People as material for the ultimate weapon
Cynical faith; guardian of the church

30648.dominant: Transhumanism (critiqued: people engineered as weapons), Might makes right (critiqued), Existentialism (choosing a self against a made past), Communitarianism (found family).

85506.heading: Dolly Kill Kill
85506.label: From summaries
85506.life_message: Even after losing everything, people can refuse despair and fight back together; revenge drives Iruma at first, but protecting others is what makes him a hero.

content.framing: Neutral (monster slaughter as horror); human cruelty condemned

delivery.evidence: Values come through action; the extermination-versus-coexistence split gives the opposing view some voice (MAL review).
delivery.note: Messages are carried by events and end-of-chapter lines that one reviewer calls cheesy (MAL), not lectures.

127778.heading: Don't Blush, Sekime-san!
127778.label: From summaries
127778.life_message: Love sees and treasures the other person's unguarded self, and grows through patience and kindness rather than pressure.

delivery.evidence: A situational comedy with no ideological conflict; the message is shown in the couple's behavior.
delivery.note: No lectures or villains; warmth carries the theme.

127778.dominant: Expressive individualism (the true self behind a public face), Communitarianism (friends and class).

108551.heading: Don't Call It Mystery
108551.label: From summaries
108551.life_message: Look closely and question what everyone takes for granted: careful listening can uncover the truth, protect children from harm, and free people from the stories that trap them.

delivery.evidence: Totonō states his views in long monologues on families, gender, bullying and truth (Japanese Wikipedia; Tamura calls it a manga where the hero just keeps talking); other characters call him annoying and his professor tells him to check his sources, so the story builds in pushback.
delivery.note: The message is spoken outright, but it is tied to solving each case and often helps a specific person, which softens the lecturing.

personified.ideology: Question common sense; truth from close observation
Vigilante justice for a loved one

108551.dominant: Secular humanism, Feminism, Critical theory (explored), Pragmatism.

100664.heading: Don't Toy With Me, Miss Nagatoro
100664.label: From summaries
100664.life_message: A good life is found by letting someone close enough to see your weak points and growing braver through it; honest words, kept promises and effort win out over pride, fear and teasing.

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)
content.framing: Endorsed as comedy and romance; the lie about a nude drawing shown with consequences
Shown with consequences (healed through friendship and love)
Endorsed early; softened; the lie shown with consequences

delivery.evidence: Gaffney (Manga Bookshelf) says the tone softens as the volume goes on; no review found calls the series preachy; the lesson about lying is spelled out by Gamo and Nagatoro's siblings (ch. 150-151).
delivery.note: Its message about courage and honesty grows out of the romance itself, while the early teasing and the nudity are presented with little critique inside the story.

personified.ideology: Quiet growth into courage and honesty
Teasing as a way of showing love

100664.dominant: Expressive individualism, Classical virtue ethics (courage and honesty, late), Hedonism (play and teasing), Duty ethics (keeping promises, not lying).

31133.heading: Dorohedoro
31133.label: From summaries
31133.life_message: A good life is a shared meal, a loyal partner and a job you can keep. The world has no fair rulers, so you stick with your own people, keep your word to them, and laugh at the horror.

delivery.evidence: ANN's Loveridge says it revels in absurdity; WSWS faults its weak social analysis; Anime Feminist stresses heart and whimsy. No reviewer calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The series gives sorcerers, humans and devils each sympathetic and cruel members, and states no message outright.

personified.ideology: Loyalty and finding yourself through friends
Power as amusement; nothing is serious
Grievance of the exploited turned to slaughter

31133.dominant: Pagan/occult (as setting), Absurdism, Communitarianism (found family), Might makes right (as the world's rule).

141262.heading: Doron Dororon
141262.label: From summaries
141262.life_message: Strength is for protecting people, and a friend is a friend whatever kind he is: kindness can be found, trusted and returned even in someone everyone has been taught to hate.

content.framing: Endorsed (protective fighting); killing for its own sake condemned

delivery.evidence: The coexistence theme is carried by Kusanagi's deeds and Dora's trust rather than speeches; the opposing view (all mononoke are enemies) is held by sympathetic samurai, while the villains are, in Screen Rant's words, monsters with little motive beyond causing death.
delivery.note: Sources opened do not say whether the corps ever changes its official view of mononoke; the ending removes the question by sending all of them away.

personified.ideology: Coexistence and kindness between humans and mononoke
Strength used to protect others; promise to a parent

141262.dominant: Communitarianism (teamwork and the corps), Classical virtue ethics (courage and restraint), Duty ethics (a promise kept), Bushido / honor code (samurai framing, explored).

31658.heading: Dororo
31658.label: From summaries
31658.life_message: No one is born whole: a person becomes fully human by reclaiming what was taken, finding a reason to live, and standing with the poor against those who trade other people's lives for power.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; tyranny and cruelty condemned

content.frequency: Occasional, heavy in the Banmon arc

31658.dominant: Existentialism, Might makes right (critiqued), Marxism (class struggle), Communitarianism.

delivery.evidence: Kodansha's blurb calls it an allegory of becoming what one is; Tezuka said the theme of punitive justice and the drama of the non-exploiting class drew him (tezukaosamu.net). Daigo is drawn as cold-blooded but shows a father's alarm when his sons duel (Japanese Wikipedia).
delivery.note: The case against ambition and the sympathy for the poor are carried by the quest; the one explicit lesson is the lute priest's talk on the worth of life.

personified.ideology: Power and conquest bought at any price
Take from oppressive samurai to aid the poor
Life is precious; live for a purpose

35293.heading: Doubt
35293.label: From summaries
35293.life_message: Lies, even small ones, breed suspicion and revenge; the story warns that trust is fragile and that those who punish liars become something worse, but it ends with the manipulator winning and offers no way out.

delivery.evidence: The rule 'the liar must die' is stated by the villains; the book exposes everyone's lie but gives the moral to no hero (Slings & Arrows says the plot both carries and undercuts it).
delivery.note: A plot-driven thriller; the theme of lies and trust is carried by the game's structure, not by speeches.

35293.dominant: Nihilism (explored), Duty ethics (critiqued: an absolute rule against lying turned murderous).

108919.heading: Doughnuts Under a Crescent Moon
108919.label: From summaries
108919.life_message: You do not have to perform someone else's idea of normal; honest words let people find the kind of closeness that truly fits them, and the friends and family who love them can make room for it.

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)

delivery.evidence: ANN's Silverman says it handles its social issues without preaching; the pressure to be normal is carried by ordinary people, not villains.
delivery.note: The message is carried by Hinako's inner monologue and small conversations rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Closeness on her own terms over performing what is called normal
Daughters should marry and fit in

108919.dominant: Expressive individualism, Progressivism, Feminism (women defining their own lives), Communitarianism (found family).

98674.heading: Downfall
98674.label: From summaries
98674.life_message: Success and work cannot fill an inner emptiness, and a man who uses the people around him to escape himself ends up alone; the book shows this as a warning, not a path.

content.framing: Depicted, not endorsed; coercion shown but not condemned by the story's resolution

delivery.evidence: Other voices judge Fukazawa (the former assistant, the college girlfriend's "monster" line), but The Comics Journal says the book keeps his view central without undercutting it, and The Manga Critic says the ending explains his behavior as inevitable.
delivery.note: The book shows and does not tell; its warning comes from the wreckage, not from any lesson stated in the story.

personified.ideology: Work as identity; women as escape; sales as truth

98674.dominant: Nihilism, Consumerism (critiqued, then surrendered to), Existentialism, Hedonism (shown as empty).

30796.heading: Dr. Slump
30796.label: From summaries
30796.life_message: Life is best met with curiosity, play and friendship rather than strain and seriousness; the world is strange and funny, and a loving, oddball household is a good place to be.

content.framing: Endorsed as comedy; schemes usually backfire

delivery.evidence: Pure episodic gag comedy; The Asahi Shimbun (via Wikipedia) contrasts it with manga that glorified endurance and self-discipline.
delivery.note: There is almost no stated message; values come through what is funny and what backfires.

30796.dominant: Absurdism, Postmodernism (metafiction and parody), Hedonism (play), Communitarianism (the village).

112673.heading: Dr. STONE Reboot: Byakuya
112673.label: From summaries
112673.life_message: Love and a kept promise can outlast death and time: careful, patient science and faithfulness to the people you love carry humanity's light forward, even when no one knows you are still there.

content.framing: Neutral (natural disaster; weapons used only to save the Earth)

delivery.evidence: No ideology is argued against; the only disagreement is tactical (Yakov and Shamil versus Byakuya, ch. 1-4), settled by cooperation (fan wiki; TV Tropes).
delivery.note: Values are shown through action and sacrifice, not speeches; Boichi's own comment dedicates the book to "those with patient souls" (fan wiki).

112673.dominant: Secular humanism, Duty ethics, Pragmatism, Naturalism, Transhumanism (explored).

98416.heading: Dr. STONE
98416.label: From summaries
98416.life_message: A good life is spent learning, building and sharing knowledge so that every person can live. Progress is slow, earned step by step through work and cooperation, and it is passed down from parents to children.

delivery.evidence: Common Sense Media lists the value of scientific progress as a theme; Beneath the Tangles notes Senku's stated belief that doing right leads to good results. No review opened calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The pro-science message is spoken openly in Senku's lines and the Science Corner asides, while rival visions get a sympathetic hearing in Tsukasa and a thinner one in Ibara.

personified.ideology: "Pure youth" primitivism and purge of corrupt adults
Village priestess tradition and oral memory

98416.dominant: Secular humanism, Naturalism, Pragmatism; Might makes right and Collectivism/authoritarianism are strongly critiqued.

30229.heading: Dragon Head
30229.label: From summaries
30229.life_message: Fear, more than disaster, is what destroys people; facing it honestly and staying with one another, rather than numbing it, worshipping it or preying on the weak, is the only way to stay human, even with no answers.

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)

delivery.evidence: The bad answers to fear (worship, drugs, mob rule, suicide) are each given a character or group with reasons; Teru's monologues state his resolve, which Thompson finds unconvincing.
delivery.note: The book argues through what happens to people, not through lectures; the meaning of the disaster is never given.

personified.ideology: Surrender to fear and worship of darkness
Freedom from fear by drugs and surgery

30229.dominant: Existentialism, Nihilism (critiqued), Might makes right (critiqued), Pagan/occult (darkness cults, critiqued).

185129.heading: Drama Queen
185129.label: From summaries
185129.life_message: Hatred of a whole people, fed by grievance and the story we tell about our own suffering, passes from person to person and wounds everyone, haters included; no one understands a conflict without the whole truth.

content.framing: Explored from inside the killers' view; the story frames hatred as a cycle

delivery.evidence: The publisher's tagline is that hate brings pain (MangaUpdates); reviewers found early chapters one-sided (Anime Senpai) and later chapters humanizing the aliens (ComicBook.com).
delivery.note: Hatred is embodied by the protagonists rather than lectured against; the author deliberately keeps the tone light and makes Nomamoto twisted (animate Times).

personified.ideology: Revenge-driven hatred of all aliens after personal loss

185129.dominant: Patriotism / nationalism (critiqued, as anti-alien nativism), Critical theory (privilege and immigration satire), Strength rules (critiqued), Absurdism and Nihilism (black comedy).

126543.heading: #DRCL midnight children
126543.label: From summaries
126543.life_message: Fear, prejudice and contagion pass through every rank of society, and they can only be resisted by people who cross the lines of sex, race and class and keep a true record together; a girl the world refuses to see becomes the one who holds the truth.

content.framing: Predation shown as horror; queer attraction neutral to affirmed

delivery.evidence: The prejudice of the school is shown through Mina's experience; the VIZ blurb states the theme of a group that eclipses gender, nationality and station; Taliesin notes that unity is not yet shown in vol. 2. Sakamoto speaks of a mission to revive Stoker's message (ANN interview).
delivery.note: The bullies are shown as flawed people who may change (Arthur's cowardice, Quincey's own mistreatment), not as cardboard villains; the Count is pure, shifting menace.

personified.ideology: Equality through merit; the record as truth

126543.dominant: Feminism (Mina as a new woman), Critical theory (race, class and gender in Victorian England), Christian (protection by cross and hymn), Progressivism and Postmodernism (gender fluidity, unreliable records).

43801.heading: Drifters
43801.label: From summaries
43801.life_message: War is the stage on which people show what they are worth, and the story sides with warriors who keep a code, free the enslaved and protect the weak, against those who use power to persecute or exterminate.

content.framing: Endorsed when the Drifters fight; cruelty by Orte and the Ends condemned
Mixed: sexual slavery condemned; harassment of Olminu played for comedy

delivery.evidence: The Black King and Seimei hold opposed views of humanity and the Black King is given his reasons (fan wiki); Orte's knights are drawn as pure villains (TV Tropes lists Aram as a Complete Monster).
delivery.note: The message is carried by battle and comedy, not speeches; Hirano gives his warriors catchphrases rather than arguments.

personified.ideology: Warrior honor; fight for those who cannot

43801.dominant: Bushido / honor code, Might makes right, Patriotism / nationalism (nation-building), Communitarianism (multiracial alliance).

97675.heading: Drifting Dragons
97675.label: From summaries
97675.life_message: Honest, dangerous work shared with a crew that is your family, and respect for what you hunt by using all of it, make a good life; killing for profit and letting it go to waste does not.

content.framing: Neutral (hunting as work); cruelty and waste condemned

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)

delivery.evidence: Values come through daily work and meals; the Slayers are an opposing ideology given a captain and a contract (v7-9, v14), but no review on delivery was opened (to verify).
delivery.note: The series argues by showing: the Quin Zaza eats and uses what it kills, the Slayers waste it, and the reader is left to weigh them.

personified.ideology: eat what you hunt; passion and skill
kill for profit by any means

97675.dominant: Communitarianism (the crew as family), Environmentalism (no waste, no overhunting), Pragmatism.

106820.heading: Drugstore in Another World: The Slow Life of a Cheat Pharmacist
106820.label: From summaries
106820.life_message: A slower life of honest, useful work for your neighbors is better than the grind that burned you out; small problems solved with care, and friends to share meals with, make a good life.

delivery.evidence: Seven Seas pitches it as a relaxing fantasy; AniList tags it Iyashikei; each chapter is a problem and a remedy, with no lectures reported (ANN Preview Guide; Wikipedia episode summaries).
delivery.note: The slow-life ideal is carried by the setting and the comedy, not argued.

personified.ideology: A calm, useful life after burnout
Pride and conquest, humbled into work
Wealth used to crush small rivals

106820.dominant: Pragmatism (a remedy for every problem), Communitarianism (village and found household), Expressive individualism (choosing one's own pace of life).

143025.heading: Duke Pendragon: Master of the White Dragon
143025.label: From summaries
143025.life_message: A second chance should be used to protect your people and set right what was betrayed: loyalty, hard-won skill and keeping faith with a family's legacy can restore what treachery destroyed.

content.framing: Endorsed (heroic combat and justice for betrayers)

delivery.evidence: No review was found; in the novel's opening, the penal commander and his men are drawn as drunken, abusive brutes (novel ch. 1).
delivery.note: The message of restoration and justice rides on the plot; villains are drawn as plainly corrupt.

personified.ideology: Grit and loyalty; justice for betrayal

143025.dominant: Traditionalism (restoring a noble house), Might makes right (explored), Classical virtue ethics.

102732.heading: Dungeon Builder: The Demon King's Labyrinth is a Modern City! (Maou-sama no Machizukuri!)
102732.label: From summaries
102732.life_message: Building a prosperous home where different peoples can live together beats ruling through fear, and the family you create is worth defending at any cost.

content.framing: Neutral; defensive wars won by the hero
Endorsed as comedy and appeal (fan service)

delivery.evidence: Manga Bookshelf found no clear message in vol. 1 beyond Procel's wish to make the happiest dungeon; later synopses frame the coexistence city against lords who rule by fear and greed.
delivery.note: The coexistence ideal is the premise rather than an argued thesis; rival lords and the church stand for the old way and are fought rather than debated.

personified.ideology: Pride of the traditional demon lord
Experienced mentor of the old order

97999.heading: Dungeon Seeker
97999.label: From summaries
97999.life_message: In a cruel world where even the gods toy with people, the betrayed survive by becoming stronger and paying their enemies back; trust is dangerous, and the strong decide who deserves to die.

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)
content.framing: Mixed: sexual abuse condemned; fan service and sex jokes neutral

delivery.evidence: Villains are drawn as purely evil (a fan review says the villains exist only to be hated); Junpei states his kill-or-be-killed creed outright (Isekai fan wiki quote of the character).
delivery.note: The worldview is stated by the hero and enacted in each arc; Noriko's late regret is the only real complication, and fans call it a retcon.

45805.heading: Dusk Maiden of Amnesia
45805.label: From summaries
45805.life_message: Facing the painful truth of the past and forgiving it frees a person from hatred, and love remembered can hold even across death.

delivery.evidence: The moral emerges through the mystery: each ghost story is a distorted memory of the crime; the villagers are shown as frightened people, and the sister gets a full, sympathetic account (Wikipedia; TV Tropes).
delivery.note: Forgiveness and truth carry the message through mystery and romance rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Hatred and the wish for revenge
Fear of the unknown turned to understanding

45805.dominant: Pagan/occult (ghost lore), Postmodernism (rumor shapes reality), Traditionalism (critiqued: human sacrifice).

137942.heading: Easygoing Territory Defense by the Optimistic Lord: Production Magic Turns a Nameless Village into the Strongest Fortified City
137942.label: From summaries
137942.life_message: Your worth is not set by the gift you were born with: a talent others call useless, used with knowledge, hard work and fairness to everyone, can build a home where outcasts flourish.

content.framing: Endorsed (defense of the town); invaders, bandits and monsters defeated
Neutral (fan service and fawning played for comedy)
Mixed: slavery called wrong but kept for the hero's companion; later confronted

delivery.evidence: Van's father and Arte's mother are blinkered caricatures of magic-snobbery, but Murcia, the king and Arte's mother (who regrets) give the other side some nuance (Wikipedia; Japanese Wikipedia).
delivery.note: The message is shown through what Van builds rather than argued; the slavery question is raised and answered quickly (Friedman).

personified.ideology: Worth through useful skill and fairness
Worth by combat magic and rank

137942.dominant: Pragmatism, Communitarianism; Might makes right critiqued (a family that prizes combat magic is proven wrong).

30731.heading: Eden: It's an Endless World!
30731.label: From summaries
30731.life_message: In a cruel world that keeps going, nothing is simply black and white; people get through by loyalty, love and the choice to keep living in the real world rather than escaping into a painless false paradise.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; killing by heroes left morally gray
Neutral to endorsed for consensual sex; sexual violence condemned
Condemned (drug trade and addiction shown as destructive)

delivery.evidence: ANN (vols. 1-2) finds "mechanical dialogues on religion and philosophy throughout the story"; Jackson P. Brown says Endo refrains from judging characters who enter the Colloid; Dark Horse's fan feature says heroes do bad things and villains are ordinary people.
delivery.note: Characters argue philosophy and religion aloud, which one critic finds heavy-handed, but the plot itself leaves most moral questions open.

personified.ideology: Survival and loyalty in a gray world
Violence as a way of life

101860.heading: EDENS ZERO
101860.label: From summaries
101860.life_message: Friends are family, and every being, human or machine, deserves to be befriended; even the worst enemy can be reached, and a broken world can be restored.

content.framing: Neutral (heroic battle); cruelty by villains condemned
Mixed: fan service endorsed as comedy; sexual violence by villains condemned
Endorsed as comedy (groping, peeking); fighting as heroism

delivery.evidence: Shiki states his creed of friendship often; Mashima says battles are only meant to look cool and carry no message of their own (ComicBook.com, 2021). Villains like Shura and Drakken Joe are flat, but Ziggy, Laguna and Holy get real reasons.
delivery.note: Friendship is spoken aloud in speeches and shown in rescues; the AI-personhood theme is carried by the robots' stories rather than argued.

101860.dominant: Communitarianism (friends as family, affirmed), Transhumanism (robot and AI personhood, explored), Environmentalism (Earth ruined and restored, affirmed), Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued).

30933.heading: Elfen Lied
30933.label: From summaries
30933.life_message: Cruelty breeds monsters and only love and acceptance can break the cycle; the story holds up kindness to the rejected, while showing at length how abuse and discrimination destroy children.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; cruelty condemned, though Lucy's killings are drawn with relish
Abuse condemned; nudity and sexual comedy treated as fan service

delivery.evidence: Wikipedia lists discrimination, prejudice, revenge, abuse and the value of humanity as themes, and the anime's director said he meant to question how people divide each other; But Why Tho notes the nature-versus-nurture question is left open.
delivery.note: Its message that cruelty makes monsters is carried by backstories and flashbacks rather than speeches, though characters state it outright at times.

personified.ideology: Love and kindness to the rejected
Vengeance born of abuse; humans are not people
Eugenics; a god of a new race
Duty to the institute against a father's love

30933.dominant: Critical theory (discrimination and othering), Transhumanism (critiqued: eugenics and playing God), Naturalism (nature versus nurture), Nihilism (critiqued).

66903.heading: Emanon Wanderer
66903.label: From summaries
66903.life_message: Every life is a short link in a chain that began billions of years ago; meaning comes from tending life forward and from brief, kind meetings, not from holding on.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers describe atmospheric, mostly wordless sequences and quiet conversations; the series poses questions without answers (AIPT; Manga News; Otaku USA on the first book).
delivery.note: The outlook (continuity of life, impermanence) is carried by mood, landscape and Emanon's choices, not by speeches.

personified.ideology: Memory and continuity of life; wandering

30729.heading: Emma
30729.label: From summaries
30729.life_message: Love, honest work and quiet dignity are worth more than rank, and kindness can cross class lines, though crossing them has real costs.

content.framing: Neutral (nudity as everyday life; marital intimacy honored)

delivery.evidence: Mori lets wordless scenes carry the story (Good Comics for Kids: many of the strongest scenes are wordless); class codes are shown as real pressures with reasons (Richard's fear for his family; Aurelia's history), though the viscount is drawn as a near-pure villain (Gaffney).
delivery.note: The message is carried by quiet scenes and character, not speeches.

30729.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Expressive individualism (love chosen over family plans), Traditionalism (explored), Progressivism.

69325.heading: Erased
69325.label: From summaries
69325.life_message: Courage means reaching out to a child who is alone; one person who refuses to look away, joined by friends and family who believe in him, can change what seemed fixed.

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)

delivery.evidence: Satoru's courage is the plain message, voiced in phrases about believing in people and being brave (the nickname "Yuuki," courage, for Jun; Wikipedia); the killer is given a full backstory chapter (ch. 32) but no excuse.
delivery.note: The message is carried by suspense and by what Satoru does; the story spells out its theme of courage and trust a few times.

personified.ideology: Courage to reach out to the lonely
Predatory emptiness behind a trusted mask
Abuse passed from parent to child

69325.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (courage), Communitarianism, Might makes right (critiqued).

122180.heading: Even Given the Worthless "Appraiser" Class, I'm Actually the Strongest
122180.label: From summaries
122180.life_message: Those the world calls worthless may hold great worth; strength is for protecting people, and even those who wronged you can be given the chance to change.

content.framing: Neutral (monster fights); murder and cruelty condemned
Played for comedy (harem jokes and fan service); romance endorsed

delivery.evidence: Nigun argues that sacrificing a few saved hundreds and Ein admits he is unsure what is right before the story rejects the bargain (ep. 8); Zoid claims Ein is as evil as he is (ep. 6). Villains are otherwise thin (ANN; MyAnimeList readers).
delivery.note: Lessons come through plot outcomes (mercy rewarded, abusers punished or reformed) rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Kindness and refusal to sacrifice anyone
Sacrifice the few for the many

122180.dominant: Might makes right (explored and partly critiqued), Classical virtue ethics, Duty ethics (no sacrificing the innocent), Pagan/occult (World Tree spirits).

122069.heading: Even Given the Worthless 'Blacksmith' Class, I'm Still the Strongest
122069.label: From summaries
122069.life_message: A gift everyone calls worthless can turn out to be the greatest; honest, patient work for the people around you, not the rank you were handed, decides a person's worth.

delivery.evidence: Those who scorn blacksmiths are proved wrong by results; the bishop explains the prejudice as distorted history (web novel ch. 60).
delivery.note: The underdog message is built into the premise rather than argued.

personified.ideology: Honest faith that protects the scorned

122069.dominant: Pragmatism, Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics (diligence and humility), Expressive individualism (defying an assigned role).

125624.heading: Even If You Slit My Mouth
125624.label: From summaries
125624.life_message: Love that is patient, honest and freely chosen can grow even between a feared monster and a human, and being truly seen and remembered by someone is what keeps a person alive.

content.framing: Neutral (the legend is recalled; scares played for comedy)
Neutral to affirming of a slow, chaste-seeming romance

delivery.evidence: Synopses show the message carried by the contract plot and the couple's banter (Mangapedia; MangaUpdates); no review opened discusses delivery.
delivery.note: The case for patient, chosen love rides on the running scare-or-love wager rather than on speeches.

125624.dominant: Pagan/occult (folk-belief spirits), Traditionalism, Duty ethics, Expressive individualism.

147863.heading: Even the Student Council Has Its Holes!
147863.label: From summaries
147863.life_message: A group of odd, flawed people can become a real family for one another; being accepted with your quirks matters more than being normal.

content.framing: Endorsed as comedy; harassment played for laughs

delivery.evidence: AnimeOshi calls it pure comedy with no deep arcs; Japanese Wikipedia cites a Da Vinci review noting serious backstory episodes placed between gags.
delivery.note: A gag comedy whose only message, friendship and belonging, is carried by situations, not statements.

105675.heading: Even Though We’re Adults
105675.label: From summaries
105675.life_message: Being honest about who you love matters, even when it comes late in life, but it costs the people around you real pain; adults keep growing up and must face what their choices do to others.

content.framing: Mixed: the affair that becomes a couple is sympathetic; Eri's affair is shown going badly

delivery.evidence: SOLRAD: no one in the comic stands for clear homophobia; Okazu: the characters are decent, flawed people and "no one is a terrible person"; Wataru's grief gets its own chapters (v7-8).
delivery.note: The story asks its moral question openly (v8 blurb: is it worth making everyone else miserable?) but answers it through quiet drama, not speeches.

personified.ideology: Honesty about who you love, late in life
Love outside a marriage (as the other woman)

105675.dominant: Expressive individualism (honesty about who you love), Progressivism (LGBTQ adults drawn with care), Duty ethics (honesty and promises in conflict), Traditionalism (critiqued: appearances and family pressure).

152235.heading: Everyone’s Darling Has a Secret
152235.label: From summaries
152235.life_message: Behind every public image is an ordinary person who needs someone to see and help them as they really are; honest effort and mutual help matter more than reputation.

delivery.evidence: The theme of image versus self is carried by the premise (a genius idol failing her exams) and by situations, not argument (Yen Press; Hakusensha blurbs).
delivery.note: A light romantic comedy; the message is gentle and implicit.

personified.ideology: The real person behind a perfect public image

152235.dominant: Expressive individualism (the real self behind the image), Classical virtue ethics (diligence), Confucian ethics (study and filial duty), Consumerism (idol culture) explored.

30043.heading: Eyeshield 21
30043.label: From summaries
30043.life_message: Courage is learned by running toward what scares you: a bullied boy becomes strong through effort, training and trust in teammates, and a team of misfits can beat the giants.

content.framing: Neutral (sports hits); comic gun-waving played for laughs; deliberate injury condemned

delivery.evidence: Courage and perseverance are shown through games and training rather than speeches; Murata points to Sena's rain practice as the clearest picture of perseverance (ANN, 2009); Hiruma's ruthlessness is treated as lovable.
delivery.note: The message is carried by matches, and rivals are usually given their own reasons and dignity.

personified.ideology: Ends-justify-means cunning in service of the team
Talent and contempt for the weak

30043.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (courage and perseverance), Communitarianism (the team), Pragmatism (Hiruma's methods), Might makes right (critiqued).

103845.heading: Failed Princesses
103845.label: From summaries
103845.life_message: People are worth something apart from their looks and popularity; real friends see that worth and say so, and love grows out of that honest acceptance.

delivery.evidence: The worth-beyond-looks message is shown through the makeover's mixed results and the clique's cruelty; the clique is thinly drawn (Okazu calls the cool kids boring), while Nanaki herself carries the opposing view and changes.
delivery.note: One "excellent conversation" per volume (Okazu) carries the theme, such as Kanade explaining why their lives cannot mix and the talk about LGBTQ people in vol. 4; there are no lectures.

personified.ideology: Popularity and image, giving way to sincerity
Insight and honesty about her own feelings

103845.dominant: Expressive individualism, Progressivism (a same-sex romance affirmed), Communitarianism (a welcoming friend group).

110989.heading: Failure Frame: I Became the Strongest and Annihilated Everything With Low-Level Spells
110989.label: From summaries
110989.life_message: Those who abuse and discard the weak deserve no mercy, and the discarded can become strong enough to protect each other; Touka answers cruelty with ruthless revenge while staying loyal to the few who are kind.

content.framing: Mixed: fan service; sexual predation condemned and punished

delivery.evidence: Villains are drawn as wholly cruel (ANN: one-dimensional villains and victim-focused framing), so each killing reads as deserved; Touka states his code of trampling the tramplers.
delivery.note: The message that cruelty deserves ruthless payback is carried by plot and by Touka's inner voice; Silverman notes the novels show his unease at enjoying it, which the manga trims.

personified.ideology: Contempt for the weak; divine tyranny
Honor, loyalty and seeing the best in people

110989.dominant: Might makes right (explored), Communitarianism (found family), Pagan/occult, Bushido / honor code (revenge on a false goddess; the discarded become strong).

103255.heading: Fairy Tail: 100 Years Quest
103255.label: From summaries
103255.life_message: Friends who stand together like family can take on any quest, even against gods, and an enemy can become a friend.

delivery.evidence: Characters speak about friendship and the guild in battle speeches (franchise convention); villains often get backstories and are forgiven (Faris, Selene).
delivery.note: The found-family theme is stated openly, as in the original Fairy Tail, but carried mostly by rescues and battles.

103255.dominant: Communitarianism (the guild as family, affirmed), Classical virtue ethics, Pagan/occult (magic and spirits, explored), Might makes right (critiqued in the Dragon Gods).

85319.heading: Fairy Tail Zerø
85319.label: From summaries
85319.life_message: Hope and kindness can outlast cruelty and loss, and friends who choose one another can become a family, and a home for others.

content.framing: Neutral (non-sexual bathing; level of nudity on the page not confirmed)
Shown with consequences; healing through friendship

delivery.evidence: Mavis states the founding vision (a guild that is a family, ch. 13), but the themes are mostly carried by events; Zeeself and Geoffrey are flat villains, while Precht's case for killing the possessed Yuri is given fair weight (ch. 9).
delivery.note: Hope and friendship are shown through Mavis's choices; Otaku USA found some dialogue sappy.

personified.ideology: Hard choices: sacrifice one to save many

85319.dominant: Communitarianism (the guild as family), Classical virtue ethics, Pagan/occult (magic world).

164263.heading: Fall in Love, You False Angels
164263.label: From summaries
164263.life_message: Being loved for your real self, not your public mask, is worth the risk of showing it; the person who sees through your act and likes what is underneath is a safe place.

delivery.evidence: The authenticity theme comes from the leads' secrets and rivalry (Kodansha copy; ANN). The teacher subplot sets self-protective masks against masks that hide harm (ANN).
delivery.note: The story does not demand that the leads drop their masks in public; it argues only for honesty with those close to you.

personified.ideology: being one's true, blunt self in private
a perfect public image hiding a darker private self

100456.heading: Farming Life in Another World
100456.label: From summaries
100456.life_message: Patient, honest work on the land and an open door to strangers can turn a wilderness into a peaceful, plentiful home; a life lost to overwork is answered by a slow, good life among family and neighbors.

content.framing: Endorsed (plural marriage and many children); pressure on Hiraku played as comedy

delivery.evidence: Episodic daily-life chapters; Anime UK News says each chapter reads like a diary entry with almost no conflict. Anime Feminist found the opening's apology from God heavy-handed.
delivery.note: The message rides on the slow growth of the village rather than on argument; no rival way of life is given a voice.

personified.ideology: Slow, honest work and an open door
Rumor and fear of the unknown

100456.dominant: Communitarianism (the village as family), Traditionalism (land, household, children), Hedonism (food, wine, comfort), Pacifism / nonviolence (conflicts ended by welcome).

86310.heading: Fire Force
86310.label: From summaries
86310.life_message: A good life is the hero's life: you keep hope against despair, protect people even when they call you a devil, and treat your team as a family. Faith is honored when it is sincere and serves people; institutions that use faith to control people are exposed.

content.framing: Endorsed as comedy; defended in ch. 280-282

delivery.evidence: Sincere believers, skeptics and fanatics each speak, and Ohkubo frames religion as a collective human creation (Anime Corner); the church's leaders and its fanatic officer are drawn as plain villains.
delivery.note: The message about hope and faith comes through battles and revelations rather than lectures, but the final arc states its view of gods and death directly.

personified.ideology: Hope and heroism; faith has worth whatever its object

86310.dominant: Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Nihilism (critiqued), Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Pantheist/New Age.

87170.heading: Fire Punch
87170.label: From summaries
87170.life_message: In a cruel world people survive by playing roles and believing stories, including gods they invent; revenge and false worship destroy, and what is left worth having is the plain choice to live and to love another person.

content.framing: Sexual violence condemned, but used as the backdrop of a cruel world

delivery.evidence: The story rarely states a moral; villains such as Doma and Judah are given reasons and inner lives, while Sulya and Jack are flatter.
delivery.note: Fujimoto changes genre almost every volume and undercuts each apparent message; readers have to draw their own conclusions.

personified.ideology: Revenge, then the will to live

87170.dominant: Existentialism, Nihilism, Postmodernism (film and fiction), critique of invented religion and authoritarian rule.

159142.heading: Firefly Wedding
159142.label: From summaries
159142.life_message: A short life is worth living by your own choice and for a love you choose, and even a violent, broken man can be changed by being accepted; but love that will not talk can cost a lifetime.

content.framing: Mixed: Shinpei's killing played as thrilling and romantic early on, then restrained; cruelty by others condemned
Assault condemned; brothel world shown with sympathy for the women; romance endorsed

delivery.evidence: The story shows rather than tells; Satoko voices objections to Shinpei's killing and he changes, but the narrative also enjoys his violence (But Why Tho; Aftermath).
delivery.note: Its view of love and freedom comes through Satoko's choices and the consequences of her family's schemes; it does not lecture.

personified.ideology: Violence and possessive love as devotion
Duty to family against self-chosen love
Patriarchal control of a daughter's future

159142.dominant: Expressive individualism (choosing her own love), Feminism and Traditionalism (a woman against the marriage system), Duty ethics (family duty weighed), Might makes right (explored through Shinpei).

31149.heading: Fist of the North Star
31149.label: From summaries
31149.life_message: Strength exists to protect the weak, and the deepest strength comes from love and the sorrow of loss, not from the wish to rule.

content.framing: Endorsed as just punishment; cruelty condemned

delivery.evidence: Heroes and villains state their creeds aloud before fighting; gang thugs are cartoon monsters (The Comics Journal), but major rivals (Raoh, Souther) get backstories and dignified deaths.
delivery.note: The protector's code is stated openly and proven in combat; the moral is plain, delivered through speeches at the moment of victory and through the deaths of friends.

personified.ideology: Strength to protect; sorrow as power
Love is pain; rule by fear

31149.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (courage and protection), Might makes right (critiqued in the tyrants), Bushido / honor code (warrior codes and honorable deaths), Stoicism (endurance of sorrow).

30646.heading: FLCL
30646.label: From summaries
30646.life_message: Growing up is a messy, painful collision with adults who use you and desires you do not understand; the story offers no clean lesson, only that you have to find your own way through it.

content.framing: Mixed: slapstick violence played for laughs; the father's death treated as tragedy (to verify)

delivery.evidence: Readers repeatedly call it one giant metaphor that must be reread (MangaUpdates comments); no character states a moral.
delivery.note: Meaning is carried by images and symbols, not statements; parents should expect to explain rather than find a lesson.

personified.ideology: Wants to be grown up and unaffected

30646.dominant: Absurdism, Existentialism (growing up without a script), Expressive individualism (against conformity), Postmodernism.

76258.heading: Flying Witch
76258.label: From summaries
76258.life_message: Magic is everywhere for those who slow down: daily life with family, nature and neighbors, human or spirit, is full of quiet wonder.
