Bitterness and control born of war, loss and envy

30655.dominant: Existentialism (choosing who you are against a remembered past), Buddhist ideas (rebirth, clinging and letting go), Environmentalism, Pantheist/New Age (past-life memory and ESP).

85939.heading: Plunderer
85939.label: From summaries
85939.life_message: A person's worth cannot be measured by a number, and a true hero refuses to keep killing even when he can; love and loyalty can pull even a broken man back from despair.

content.framing: Mixed: harassment played for comedy; sexual assault condemned

delivery.evidence: The count system and the Waste War's logic are argued by the villains (Schmerman's plan, Firenda's revenge) and answered by Licht's Non-Killing Army; ANN sees the non-killing ideal as the story's right step.
delivery.note: The anti-ranking and anti-war message is carried by reveals and battles; it is stated outright in climactic speeches (from general knowledge; to verify).

personified.ideology: Refusing to kill; worth beyond numbers
Planned war for the greater good
Revenge on a world that wronged her

85939.dominant: Utilitarianism (critiqued: the planned war), Pacifism / nonviolence (the Non-Killing Army), Critical theory (a society ranked by numbers and fed by stolen resources).

98175.heading: Plus-Sized Elf
98175.label: From summaries
98175.life_message: Health comes from steady habits and patient, non-judging help rather than shame or crash diets, and everyone backslides sometimes; the series tells this through comedy that keeps its camera on the characters' bodies.

content.framing: Endorsed as comedy (fan service); comic harassment unjudged
Played for comedy; drinking linked to weight gain

delivery.evidence: Diet and exercise advice is spelled out with instructions (ANN Fall 2018 guide); ANN's anime critics find the health message undercut by fan service.
delivery.note: The health lesson is stated outright in each chapter; the attitude to bodies is carried by the art.

personified.ideology: Patient, practical health help without shame
Family duty, then her own appetite

98175.dominant: Hedonism (explored), Pragmatism (practical health), Classical virtue ethics (temperance), Consumerism (junk food, critiqued).

30928.heading: Pokémon Adventures
30928.label: From summaries
30928.life_message: Courage, friendship and care for creatures, joined with growing up, let ordinary kids stand against people who treat living things as tools; even villains can be redeemed when they learn to love rather than use.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; cruelty to Pokémon condemned
Mixed: theft forgiven; danger as adventure

delivery.evidence: Villains are often given real motives (Pryce's grief, Giovanni's search for his son, Lance's and Team Plasma's claims about humans and Pokémon), and many are redeemed; the heroes' view still wins every arc.
delivery.note: Care for creatures and friendship are carried by the heroes' choices in battle rather than stated as lessons.

personified.ideology: Humans should be removed for Pokémon's sake

30928.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (courage, friendship, perseverance), Communitarianism (the Pokédex holders as one team), Environmentalism (care for creatures and land), Might makes right (critiqued in the villains).

139358.heading: PPPPPP
139358.label: From summaries
139358.life_message: Music made to bring other people joy, not to prove you are a genius, is what moves hearts; a parent who values children only for talent wounds the whole family, and love between brothers and sisters can outlast that wound even when the story does not end the way the hero hoped.

delivery.evidence: Gakuon's creed (the average make no music) is voiced by him and by Reijiro (ch. 5-6) and answered by Lucky's playing rather than by argument; the siblings who share their father's view are given sympathetic reasons.
delivery.note: The message lives in performances: each arc ends when Lucky's music shows someone what they truly want.

personified.ideology: Music as kindness; the worth of the average

139358.dominant: Might makes right (critiqued as talent-elitism), Expressive individualism, Classical virtue ethics, Confucian ethics (filial devotion explored).

47904.heading: Princess Jellyfish
47904.label: From summaries
47904.life_message: Everyone, however awkward or out of step, has worth and beauty, and a group of misfits who work together can protect their home and make something of their own.

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)

content.framing: Mixed: drugging condemned; drinking to cope shown with consequences

delivery.evidence: Polygon sums up the message as everyone being beautiful (Wikipedia); the anime's ending theme title asks readers to notice their own beauty. Inari is mostly a villain but gets some development (TV Tropes).
delivery.note: The message is carried by comedy and character growth, with occasional stated lines from Kuranosuke.

personified.ideology: Worth beyond appearance; devotion to what you love
Profit by any means, including sexual manipulation

87534.heading: Prison Lab
87534.label: From summaries
87534.life_message: Unlimited power over another person corrupts even someone who has been wronged; the bullied boy becomes a torturer, and the story traces both bullying and revenge to hidden wounds, though it ends by reuniting captor and captive as mutual crushes rather than with clear justice (ending as reported by reviewers; to verify).

content.framing: Mixed: torture is the engine of the plot; the captor's change is shown as corruption
Assault condemned as trauma, but used as a plot device; captor-captive romance not clearly judged

delivery.evidence: Both leads get backstories that explain their cruelty (Mangapedia; AniList user review); no one states a moral; reviewers disagree on whether the revenge theme is examined or dropped (Nontai; Idyvist).
delivery.note: The story shows revenge corrupting Aito but ends by reuniting the pair, which reviewers read as blurring its own warning.

personified.ideology: Power without law, sold as a game

87534.dominant: Might makes right (critiqued), Nihilism (explored), Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued: the hidden game-master).

67109.heading: Prophecy
67109.label: From summaries
67109.life_message: When work and society discard the people at the bottom, they may band together to strike back, but online mob justice is fickle and cruel; the deepest loyalty is a friend who keeps a promise to the dead and takes all the blame.

content.framing: Mixed: punishments shown as a dilemma, neither cheered nor simply condemned
Sexual violence used as punishment; shown as part of the vigilantes' cruelty

delivery.evidence: Both sides are given motives: The Fandom Post finds the vigilantes and police both sickening and justified; Comics Worth Reading finds some targets (the environmental group's leader) two-dimensional caricatures.
delivery.note: The social critique is voiced through Gates's videos and the men's histories, not narration; the ending explains rather than judges.

personified.ideology: Justice for the discarded, by any means
Control of the internet; manufactured consent

67109.dominant: Critical theory (labor critique), Duty ethics (a promise kept; the law kept), Communitarianism (a found family), Liberalism (speech and anonymity versus regulation).

33438.heading: Psyren
33438.label: From summaries
33438.life_message: The future is not fixed: ordinary people who refuse to give up, train hard and protect one another can change a doomed world, while those who would remake humanity by force or rule by lies bring ruin on themselves.

content.framing: Neutral (battle action); cruelty of W.I.S.E. and Usui condemned
Neutral (light comedy and a sincere romance)

delivery.evidence: Miroku's aims are explained and he is given a late turn (he is shown the truth and later dies saving the world in one timeline), while Usui and Mithra are drawn as plain villains.
delivery.note: The message of protecting friends and refusing a fixed fate is shown through action and spoken in shonen-style resolve rather than lectures.

personified.ideology: Protect your friends; refuse a fixed fate

33438.dominant: Communitarianism, Transhumanism (critiqued), Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Might makes right (critiqued).

85401.heading: PTSD Radio
85401.label: From summaries
85401.life_message: Wounds, broken promises and neglected obligations leave after-effects that spread and linger; the series offers no rescue, only unease about what lies under ordinary life.

delivery.evidence: Nakayama says he wanted readers to imagine everything and planned no "mythos" (ANN interview); stories stop at the revelation without comment (The Comics Journal).
delivery.note: Atmosphere is the message: the after-effects of harm, shown, never explained.

personified.character: The friend who broke his promise

85401.dominant: Pagan/occult (a malevolent local god and curse rites), Nihilism (explored), Traditionalism (neglected customs punished).

54457.heading: Puella Magi Madoka Magica
54457.label: From summaries
54457.life_message: Love that gives itself up completely for others is stronger than a bargain made for one's own wish, and hope can overturn a system built on using up young people's despair.

content.framing: Neutral (horror used to make the point)

delivery.evidence: Characters argue openly about why to fight (Mami's duty, Kyoko's self-interest, Sayaka's justice), and Kyubey states his case at length (ch. 9). Urobuchi said Kyubey is frightening because he lacks feelings, not because he is evil (Wikipedia).
delivery.note: The ideas are debated aloud, and Kyubey's logic is presented clearly before the story rejects it through Madoka's choice.

personified.ideology: devotion to one person at any cost

54457.dominant: Utilitarianism (critiqued), Existentialism, Duty ethics, Christian and Buddhist ideas (explored).

103082.heading: Pumpkin Night
103082.label: From summaries
103082.life_message: Cruelty, and the powerful who cover it up, breed their own destroyer: the bullies and the corrupt family who hid their crime are hunted down, but revenge also consumes the avenger and nearly everyone around her.

content.framing: Spectacle; the avenger is the protagonist, and her victims are drawn as deserving or as collateral
Mixed: the high-school advance is cut off by a killing; the central romance is tender
Shown with consequences, but madness is also played as power
Mixed: the bullying is condemned; the revenge is cheered; copycats are shown

delivery.evidence: The bullies and the Kuroki family are drawn as almost wholly cruel or selfish (Naruto kills his own friend to stay safe); Kazuya and Detective Matsui are the only figures with mixed views.
delivery.note: The message is carried by horror set pieces and dark humor (AniList: Surreal Comedy), not by speeches; Naoko's confrontations and Naruto's forced live-stream confession (ch. 14) state the moral case.

personified.ideology: Revenge on those who wronged her
Love and guilt; the bystander who failed to act
Institutional power protecting family and profit

103082.dominant: Might makes right (the powerful cover up; the avenger becomes the stronger), Nihilism, Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued corrupt power).

75613.heading: Pupa
75613.label: From summaries
75613.life_message: A brother's total devotion to his sister is shown both as love and as a chain of harm passed down through a violent family; in the end the two consume each other, and only their bond remains.

content.framing: Mixed: cruelty by the father and the researchers condemned; the siblings' violence shown as tragic love
Endorsed as "ultimate sibling love" (publisher tagline, Japanese Wikipedia); abuse condemned
Shown with consequences; the cycle of abuse condemned

delivery.evidence: The story states no lesson; its sympathy for the siblings and its condemnation of the abusive father and the researchers come through plot and backstory (Wikipedia; TV Tropes). The publisher markets it as "ultimate sibling love" (Japanese Wikipedia).
delivery.note: A shock-horror tragedy; any moral is left for the reader to draw.

personified.ideology: Pain as love; violence passed down

75613.dominant: Nihilism (suffering with no way out), Naturalism (instinct over will), with Utilitarianism critiqued in the researchers.

85303.heading: QQ Sweeper
85303.label: From summaries
85303.life_message: Dark feelings are real and can poison a person, but they can be cleansed with courage and care; a cheerful heart and a family that takes you in can help you face a past you cannot remember.

delivery.evidence: ANN found the supernatural story grounded in humanity rather than preachy; the moral (dark feelings must be cleansed, not fed) is built into the magic system.
delivery.note: The Bug Handlers are thin villains in this short series (Otaku USA on the sequel calls them stock characters); Manga Bookshelf hints they are less black-and-white later.

personified.ideology: Optimism and endurance; a power to master
Manipulating people through their negative emotions

85303.dominant: Communitarianism (found family), Pantheist/New Age (cleansing negative energy from souls, explored), Duty ethics (the Sweepers' calling).

81493.heading: Qualia the Purple
81493.label: From summaries
81493.life_message: People see the world in different ways, and loving someone means accepting them and the world as they are; trying to force every possible world to give you the one thing you want can turn love into something monstrous.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; the protagonist's killings are presented as her descent
Mixed: the central crush is chaste; a sexual relationship involving a child is part of the protagonist's dark path and is criticized by reviewers, not clearly by the story

delivery.evidence: Long narrated passages explain quantum mechanics and philosophy of mind (Okazu: most of the story is told in narration); the ending states its lesson about accepting reality through Yukari (AniList review).
delivery.note: Ideas are argued at length in narration rather than shown; the moral turns only at the end.

personified.ideology: Perception defines reality; accept the world

81493.dominant: Existentialism (meaning and choice across infinite worlds); Naturalism and philosophy of mind (persons as machines versus qualia); Transhumanism (a body rebuilt, a mind made god-like); critique of ends-justify-means reasoning.

86360.heading: Qualia Under the Snow
86360.label: From summaries
86360.life_message: Patient, non-transactional care can help a lonely person believe he is worth loving, and both people heal by letting someone in.

content.framing: Mixed: casual sex shown as a wound; committed same-sex love endorsed

delivery.evidence: Reviewers say meaning is carried by glances, weather and symbols (cats, flowers, child doubles) more than dialogue; one says the relationship is never directly declared (MyAnimeList reviews).
delivery.note: A quiet romance, not an argument; no character voices disapproval of same-sex love in sources opened.

personified.ideology: Sexual use followed by conventional marriage

86360.dominant: Love as healing; Expressive individualism (explored); Hedonism (critiqued).

86284.heading: Queen's Quality
86284.label: From summaries
86284.life_message: The darkness in a mind can be cleansed, not by destroying the parts of yourself you fear but by facing and accepting them, with people who love you at your side.

delivery.evidence: The message (accept, don't destroy, the dark self) is played out in Fumi's inner battles (v3-9) rather than stated as a lesson. Villains like Yanagi are flat, while Ataru, Tsubasa and Kaede get sympathetic backstories.
delivery.note: Fantasy action and romance carry the themes.

personified.ideology: Domination of minds; family as tools

86284.dominant: Pagan/occult (spiritual cleansing as healing), Communitarianism (found family), Pantheist/New Age (minds linked through the Void; negative energy).

99065.heading: Ragna Crimson
99065.label: From summaries
99065.life_message: A future that seems fixed can be changed by someone who refuses to give up on the people he loves, but power pursued by any means corrupts; how you fight matters as much as whether you win.

content.framing: Mixed: killing dragons endorsed; cruelty and mass killing condemned; Crimson's ruthless tactics often rewarded
Mixed: crushes played for comedy; early age-gap closeness flagged by a critic

delivery.evidence: Villains get human backstories (Olto Zora, Taratectra, Ultimatia, Woltekamui), and Ragna and Crimson argue over means and ends; the dragons' cruelty is never presented as right.
delivery.note: The moral debate (ends versus means, mercy versus murder) runs through dialogue between Ragna and Crimson rather than through narration.

personified.ideology: Protect the beloved; refuse cruelty as a method
Duty of a ruler to her people

99065.dominant: Might makes right (critiqued), Utilitarianism (ends versus means, explored), Classical virtue ethics and Communitarianism (affirmed in the Argentum Corps).

69291.heading: Rainbow Days
69291.label: From summaries
69291.life_message: Real friends tell you the truth, stand by you and help you grow up; sincere, patient love beats playing games with people's hearts.

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)
content.framing: Mixed: sincere love endorsed; sadism jokes played as comedy
Played as comedy; the playboy changes

delivery.evidence: The lessons come through comic episodes and friends' blunt advice (v1 warning about Natsuki's girlfriend; the v15 intervention); the playboy and the man-hating girl both change, and rivals are drawn fairly (The Outerhaven).
delivery.note: Its outlook on friendship and sincere love is carried by ensemble comedy rather than stated lessons; the sadism jokes are never questioned by the story.

personified.ideology: Love as a game, later faithful love
Playful sadism; fear of growing up
Distrust of others after being hurt

100801.heading: Rainbows After Storms
100801.label: From summaries
100801.life_message: Love grows in small, ordinary days: kindness, loyalty and patience between two girls carry them through school and toward a shared future.

delivery.evidence: The Outer Haven notes no overarching plot and little drama; Okazu does not expect a coming-out drama (vol. 9).
delivery.note: The message is carried entirely by everyday scenes; no one argues against the relationship in sources opened.

100801.dominant: Expressive individualism, Communitarianism (friends), Progressivism (same-sex love as ordinary).

104233.heading: Rainy Day Serenade
104233.label: From summaries
104233.life_message: True love seeks the other's good even when it means letting go, and each person deserves to choose her own path rather than have family, rank or fortune choose it for her.

content.framing: Mixed: the central love endorsed; exploitation condemned

delivery.evidence: The values come through choices and consequences in a romantic mystery: Hinako's rescue, the exposure of the fathers' crimes, Hina's sacrifice. The obstructing parents are drawn as hard, but the troupe leader's grievance is given a real history (vol. 10).
delivery.note: Sources describe no lecturing; the story asks its questions about duty and choice through the double heroines.

personified.ideology: Love that is willing to let go
Duty as heir weighed against truth and love
A daughter's right to choose and to learn
Patriarchal authority over a daughter's marriage
Revenge for wrongs done by the rich

104233.dominant: Expressive individualism (choosing one's own love and path); Traditionalism explored (Meiji family duty and arranged betrothal); Feminism (a daughter's wish to study and to speak for herself).

52986.heading: Ran and the Gray World
52986.label: From summaries
52986.life_message: Growing up cannot be rushed: a child who borrows an adult's body before she has an adult's heart is hurt, and she grows up through loss, family love and her own choices, in her own time.

content.framing: Mixed: framed as a child growing up too fast, but harassment is often played as comedy (reviewers)

delivery.evidence: The lesson is shown through Ran's misadventures and grief, and stated by Irie in VIZ's vol. 7 post; reviewers do not report lecturing.
delivery.note: The view that growing up cannot be rushed is carried by plot consequences (sleep, loss, grief) more than by any speech; Otaro's conduct is treated inconsistently, sometimes as comedy.

52986.dominant: Communitarianism (family), Pagan/occult (a family of sorcerers), Expressive individualism (a child's push to be grown, tempered).

101265.heading: Ran the Peerless Beauty
101265.label: From summaries
101265.life_message: Love grows when someone sees the real person behind the image and you find the courage to let yourself be known, past and all; patient care, like tending flowers, helps people bloom.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (healed through honesty and love)

delivery.evidence: The theme of image versus self is built into the title and premise; the father's objection is a real obstacle, presented with some sympathy (Mechacomic readers call him a doting dad).
delivery.note: A gentle romance that carries its message through character growth rather than speeches.

101265.dominant: Expressive individualism (being known as one really is), Classical virtue ethics (kindness, honesty, courage), Communitarianism (family business and club), Confucian ethics (a father's authority and family duty, explored).

114388.heading: Ranking of Kings
114388.label: From summaries
114388.life_message: Real strength is kindness, courage and friendship, not size or power; people who are mocked as weak can grow into true leaders, and even those who did great wrong can be understood and given a second chance.

delivery.evidence: Power-worship is carried by sympathetic, remorseful characters (Bosse, Domas, Hiling) rather than cartoon villains; ANN's finale discussion: one host says everyone in this world can do both good and evil.
delivery.note: The kindness-and-forgiveness message is earnest and shown through action; the story asks a lot of readers in forgiving Miranjo.

personified.ideology: Kindness and perseverance as true strength
Becoming strongest is worth any price
Only the physically capable should rule

114388.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Strength rules (critiqued), Pacifism / nonviolence (Bojji's non-lethal sword), Communitarianism (found family).

30023.heading: Ranma ½
30023.label: From summaries
30023.life_message: Pride and stubbornness keep people from saying what they feel, but loyalty, courage and care for the people you love count for more than winning every fight, whatever body you are in.

content.framing: Mixed: harassment and nudity played as comedy; Ranma and the victims object, the lecher is beaten but never stops
Mixed: some played as harmless gags

delivery.evidence: Takahashi said she was after a light, fun premise with no social agenda (Animerica, 1993, via Wikipedia); no character argues a worldview at length.
delivery.note: The message about pride and hidden love comes through the bickering couple and the endless rescues, never through speeches.

30023.dominant: Expressive individualism (gender play), Traditionalism (arranged marriage and family honor, mocked), Bushido / honor code (as farce), Might makes right (the Anything-Goes school).

87471.heading: Rascal Does Not Dream of Bunny Girl Senpai
87471.label: From summaries
87471.life_message: Being truly seen by someone who cares, and refusing to go along with a crowd that erases people, is what keeps a person from disappearing; love takes the courage to say it out loud.

content.framing: Mixed: teasing played as comedy; a child actress's exploitation criticized
Shown as an act of care, not endorsed as a practice

delivery.evidence: Sakuta states his view of "the atmosphere" openly, but the story makes its case through Mai's fading rather than lectures.
delivery.note: The message about being seen is carried by the supernatural premise and the romance.

personified.ideology: Ignore rumor; act for the people you love
Success and image over a child's wishes

87471.dominant: Expressive individualism, Existentialism, Communitarianism (friends who see you).

30014.heading: Rave Master
30014.label: From summaries
30014.life_message: Courage, friendship and mercy, carried on from those who sacrificed before you, can overcome a darkness that wants to dominate or destroy the world; even enemies can be turned.

content.framing: Endorsed as heroic defense; cruelty and conquest condemned

delivery.evidence: The message is carried by quest, battles and sacrifices; Haru states his reasons in key duels (v29); villains are given backstories (King, v9; Doryu, v17; Hardner, v28; Lucia's family curse) per Mashima's stated aim.
delivery.note: Villains are understood but never vindicated; the story clearly sides with Haru's band, and several villains change sides rather than win the argument.

personified.ideology: destroying a world he sees as cursed
revenge on those who drove out his people

30014.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (courage, loyalty, mercy), Communitarianism (found family), Might makes right (critiqued).

104277.heading: RaW Hero
104277.label: From summaries
104277.life_message: A good life means doing honest work to keep your family fed, holding on to your sense of right even when "heroes" and "villains" both turn out to be compromised, and refusing to give up on the people you love.

content.framing: Neutral; shown with consequences in the finale
Endorsed as comedy; coercion shown with some consequences (it wrecks Chiaki's romance)

delivery.evidence: Reviewers describe random, "nonsensical" plotting and absurd comedy, not lectures (MAL reviews); the good-versus-evil question surfaces in Chiaki's doubts (Kodansha vol. 3).
delivery.note: The series raises who is truly just through situations and reversals rather than speeches, and treats both sides as comic and compromised.

personified.ideology: Sincere justice in service of family
Violence in the name of justice

85495.heading: Re:Monster
85495.label: From summaries
85495.life_message: In a world where the strong eat the weak, the one who keeps growing stronger, plans well and stays loyal to his own pack comes out on top.

content.framing: Mixed: captivity and attempted rape condemned; sex with captives turned wives, group sex and harem endorsed

delivery.evidence: Rou narrates his creed of eating and growing stronger; his enemies (raiding goblins, cruel humans, a noble coup) are drawn as plainly worse, so his methods are never seriously questioned.
delivery.note: The power-fantasy message is carried openly by the hero's evolution and victories rather than by argument.

personified.ideology: Strength, appetite and loyalty to his pack

85495.dominant: Might makes right (affirmed), Naturalism (survival of the fittest), Hedonism (eating and sex as reward), Pragmatism (results first).

85736.heading: Re:ZERO -Starting Life in Another World- Chapter 1: A Day in the Capital (manga)
85736.label: From summaries
85736.life_message: Repaying kindness is worth great cost, and learning from each failure can change a terrible outcome.

delivery.evidence: Reviews describe humor, restarts and trope play; no lectures are noted (No Flying No Tights); the message is carried by the plot's outcome.
delivery.note: The villain is simply menacing in this short arc; no rival worldview is argued.

85736.dominant: Existentialism (facing death and choosing again), Pragmatism (learning by trial and error), Classical virtue ethics (gratitude and courage), Pagan/occult (spirits and spirit arts).

85814.heading: Re:ZERO -Starting Life in Another World- Chapter 2: A Week at the Mansion (manga)
85814.label: From summaries
85814.life_message: Keep trying to earn the trust of people who misjudge you, ask for help instead of carrying everything alone, and protect people even after they have hurt you.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; Rem's attacks framed as a tragic mistake; the witchbeasts and Witch Cult condemned
Mixed: framed as despair and as a strategy only his power allows

delivery.evidence: Rem's suspicion is given a reason (the witch's scent, her village's destruction) and her backstory is told with sympathy (The Outerhaven, vol. 4); the lesson comes through outcomes, not lectures.
delivery.note: Subaru states his feelings in big emotional scenes (the lap pillow, ch. 12-13), but the moral is carried by the plot.

personified.ideology: protective loyalty that turns to suspicion

85814.dominant: Existentialism (facing death and choosing again), Pragmatism (solving the curse by trial and error), Classical virtue ethics (courage, forgiveness), Pagan/occult (curses, witch lore, oni).

85250.heading: Real Account
85250.label: From summaries
85250.life_message: Follower counts are a hollow measure of friendship; the people who stand by you in real life, especially family, are the ones worth protecting.

content.framing: Mixed: nudity played for shock and fan service; the sibling relationship treated as tragic rather than condemned

delivery.evidence: ANN's vol. 1 review calls the commentary heavy-handed and unsubtle, at times like a rant; the ending restates the internet's dark side (Wikipedia).
delivery.note: Yuuma's closing view that the internet can do good softens an otherwise one-sided critique.

personified.ideology: Online "friendship" as a game of numbers
Real bonds and wit over follower counts

85250.dominant: Transhumanism (clones and copied minds), Postmodernism (what is real online), Communitarianism (real bonds), Critical theory (platform critique).

80767.heading: Real Girl
80767.label: From summaries
80767.life_message: Love asks you to stop judging people by labels and risk being hurt; real people, flawed and present, are worth more than safe fantasies, and faithful love can outlast illness, distance and lost memory.

content.framing: Mixed: teen dating affirmed; sexual reputation shown as unfair gossip

delivery.evidence: Hikari's distrust of "3D girls" is voiced through his monologue and his imaginary Ezomichi, then worn down by Iroha's sincerity; gossiping classmates are shown as wrong, and Mitsuya is given a reason for his pride and a chance to change.
delivery.note: The lesson is carried by events and Hikari's inner voice rather than by lectures.

personified.ideology: Distrust of real people; otaku isolation

80767.dominant: Expressive individualism, Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism.

116551.heading: Reborn as a Space Mercenary: I Woke Up Piloting the Strongest Starship!
116551.label: From summaries
116551.life_message: With skill, nerve and a little luck you can live freely on your own terms, protect the people who depend on you, and build a comfortable home life with those you choose.

content.framing: Endorsed: the harem and sexual relationships are presented as rewards; the thugs' assault is condemned

delivery.evidence: Hiro's choices are always vindicated; the military life Serena offers is turned down and the story agrees (anime ep. 5-6); villains are pirates and schemers without inner lives.
delivery.note: The message (freedom, competence and comfort are the good life) is carried by wish-fulfillment rather than argument.

personified.ideology: Free agent; earn your own way

116551.dominant: Hedonism (comfort, food and sex as rewards), Libertarianism (freedom from imperial service), Consumerism (ships, gear and a dream house), Strength rules.

182970.heading: Reborn as an Aristocratic Scoundrel, I Broke the Game and Mastered Magic Beyond Limits!
182970.label: From summaries
182970.life_message: Your past and your reputation do not have to be your fate: owning up to wrongs and working hard every day can change who you are and how people see you.

content.framing: Past abuse condemned and repented; fan service played as comedy

delivery.evidence: The change is shown through actions (freeing slaves, apologizing, training) rather than lectures (novel ep. 3, 10); the old Weiss is drawn as wholly vile, a figure to reject.
delivery.note: A redemption-by-effort message carried by comedy and power fantasy.

182970.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Might makes right (explored), Pragmatism.

30047.heading: Reborn!
30047.label: From summaries
30047.life_message: Courage is fighting for the people you love, not for power; a weak boy grows strong through loyal friends, and he can refuse the sins he was born into and choose a better way to lead.

content.framing: Mixed: slapstick at first, then heroic battle; cruelty by villains condemned
Played for comedy; harassment shown as a joke and sometimes stopped
Neutral (shown as part of a cool image)

delivery.evidence: Tsuna states his reasons for fighting in key battles (Byakuran, Bermuda), but most of the series is comedy and action; villains get tragic backstories (Mukuro, Daemon Spade, Bermuda) while some are cartoon tyrants (Xanxus).
delivery.note: The message is carried by Tsuna's choices rather than lectures; the gag chapters carry no message beyond friendship.

personified.ideology: Fight only to protect friends; lead by serving
Revenge on the Mafia; the world is to be cleansed

30047.dominant: Communitarianism (the family of friends), Classical virtue ethics (courage and growth), Might makes right (critiqued: power-seekers lose).

111212.heading: Rebuild World
111212.label: From summaries
111212.life_message: In a world that throws the poor away, you survive by your own strength, wits and the help you can trust, and the debts you repay and promises you keep are what stop you from becoming just another killer.

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)
content.framing: Mixed: fan service presented as comedy; the slums' sexual exploitation shown as part of a cruel world

delivery.evidence: The survival ethic is carried by Akira's choices in a dystopia; reviewers describe a personal moral code rather than a stated lesson (Operation Rainfall; The OASG).
delivery.note: Self-reliance and the cost of trust are shown through plot, not lectures; Katsuya acts as a foil whose different ideal is shown failing.

personified.ideology: Instrumental reason; guidance with hidden aims

111212.dominant: Strength rules (survival by force in a lawless world), Pragmatism, Libertarianism (corporate city-states, self-reliance), Transhumanism (AI, nanotech, augmented reality).

107098.heading: Record of Ragnarok
107098.label: From summaries
107098.life_message: Human beings have worth the gods cannot take away: ordinary and flawed people prove it by refusing to bow, fighting to the end for those they love, and earning even their enemies' respect.

delivery.evidence: Brunhilde and the commentators state the theme (humanity's worth) outright; many gods are arrogant or petty, but Heracles, Zerofuku and Buddha are given full, sympathetic reasons.
delivery.note: Each fight is an argument by flashback: why this person fights and what they love. The message is spoken openly but carried by spectacle.

personified.ideology: Humanity deserves to live; defy unjust gods
A father's love for all his descendants
Choose your own side, freely and with compassion

107098.dominant: Secular humanism (human worth against the gods), Might makes right (explored), Classical virtue ethics, Pagan/occult (polytheistic setting), Buddhist ideas (explored).

98822.heading: Record of Wortenia War
98822.label: From summaries
98822.life_message: In a cruel world that rewards killing, a strong and calculating man survives by meeting force with greater force, trusting only those bound to him, and building his own power instead of serving any ruler.

content.framing: Endorsed (killing makes the hero stronger and is rarely questioned)

delivery.evidence: Ryoma's reasoning about survival and power drives the narration; rulers and nobles who oppose him are cruel or foolish and underestimate him (J-Novel Club, vols. 1, 6, 11).
delivery.note: The worldview is shown through Ryoma's calculated choices rather than speeches; the opposing view (mercy, restraint) is rarely voiced.

personified.ideology: Strength and calculation; trust no ruler
Rule by fear of the strong
Loyalty unto death to a master

98822.dominant: Might makes right, Pragmatism, a critique of authoritarian empire.

30079.heading: Red River
30079.label: From summaries
30079.life_message: Courage, compassion and honesty can turn a frightened outsider into a leader people follow freely; a ruler earns loyalty by caring for the people and seeking peace, and love is worth giving up an old life for.

content.framing: Mixed: assaults by villains condemned; the hero's coercion often framed as passion; later consensual romance and marriage

delivery.evidence: Nakia is "cartoonishly evil" (ANN), but rivals Mattiwaza and Ramses are given reasons and redeemed; the values of mercy and just rule are shown through Yuri's choices rather than speeches.
delivery.note: A sweeping historical romance; the moral line is clear (mercy beats scheming), but it is carried by plot and character, not lectures.

30079.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Feminism (a heroine who leads), Patriotism / nationalism (devotion to the Hittite nation), Pagan/occult (explored).

101468.heading: Reincarnated as a Dragon Hatchling
101468.label: From summaries
101468.life_message: What makes a monster or a hero is how you treat others, not how you look; strength gained alone does not cure loneliness, and even a guiding voice should be questioned.

content.framing: Neutral (survival combat); cruelty by humans condemned

delivery.evidence: Marielle's fear of monsters is given real reasons (warding stones, past attacks; anime ep. 3), and Gregory's hostility turns to trust; only the slime and the Hero are flat villains.
delivery.note: The message is carried by the dragon's actions and inner monologue; no character lectures.

personified.ideology: Protect others whatever they think of you
Power for its own ends; obedience
Status and cruelty behind a holy office

101468.dominant: Strength rules (explored), Classical virtue ethics, Naturalism, Existentialism.

98014.heading: Reincarnated as a Sword
98014.label: From summaries
98014.life_message: A protector's patient love and a young person's own hard work can lift someone out of slavery and contempt; strength is for protecting your own and proving your people's worth.

content.framing: Mixed: monster-slaying as game action; killing slavers and persecutors endorsed
Fan service around a 12-year-old in bath and outfit scenes; no romance
Shown with consequences; healing through care
Endorsed: retaliation and summary killing of villains by a child

delivery.evidence: Slavers and racists (August, Gyuran) are drawn as gloating villains with no inner life; the overtaxed pirates are the rare opponents given a fair hearing (likely ch. 44-45).
delivery.note: The message is carried by action and by Teacher's inner voice rather than by speeches; the moral lines are drawn sharply.

personified.ideology: Prove your people's worth by growing strong
Rank and charm used to oppress commoners

98014.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (courage and perseverance), Communitarianism (found family), Pragmatism (game-system problem solving), Might makes right (explored: strength earns respect).

107980.heading: Reincarnated as the Daughter of the Legendary Hero and the Queen of Spirits
107980.label: From summaries
107980.life_message: Family love, honest marriage and knowledge used to heal can protect people, but an old wrong is forgiven only when those who did it truly repent.

content.framing: Condemned (the spirits' torture); rescue fighting shown as just
Fidelity upheld; lust and adultery condemned

delivery.evidence: Ellen states her view that the royals must earn forgiveness (ep. 3, 11); Ravisel is drawn as cunning and competent, but Agielle is a cartoon villain.
delivery.note: The rule that coercing spirits is a crime, and that ritual without repentance is empty, is carried by the curse plot and by Ellen's short speeches rather than long lectures.

personified.ideology: Knowledge and love protect family; justice before forgiveness
Royal power and use of others for the crown
Sincere repentance for an ancestor's crime

107980.dominant: Pagan/occult (a real goddess pantheon and spirit contracts), Communitarianism (family and land), Traditionalism, Pragmatism.

33992.heading: Remina
33992.label: From summaries
33992.life_message: When fear spreads, crowds look for someone to blame and an innocent girl pays the price; a few people protect her, but the story offers no larger rescue.

content.framing: Condemned (mob and cult violence); Neutral (the planet)

delivery.evidence: The anti-mob message is carried by plot and images, not speeches; ANN's Rebecca Silverman found it "too on the nose with its imagery" (via Wikipedia). The mob's fear is shown as understandable but its answer as monstrous.
delivery.note: Scapegoating and the fragility of fame are shown through the hunt for Remina; the cosmic ending denies any lesson a happy resolution.

personified.ideology: Innocent scapegoat; a person turned into a symbol
Decency toward a stranger under persecution

33992.dominant: Nihilism (cosmic indifference), Critical theory (scapegoating, class and celebrity), Christian imagery (scapegoat and crucifixion).

119767.heading: Rent-A-(Really Shy!)-Girlfriend
119767.label: From summaries
119767.life_message: Small brave steps count: shyness can be faced a little at a time, with patience from others and from yourself.

delivery.evidence: The message comes through Sumi's inner monologue and small wins; there is no antagonist, and the ethics of rental dating are not debated.
delivery.note: A gentle slice-of-life spin-off; its premise is accepted rather than argued.

119767.dominant: Expressive individualism (becoming who she wants to be), Classical virtue ethics (courage built by practice), Consumerism (companionship as a rated product, explored).

85296.heading: Requiem of the Rose King
85296.label: From summaries
85296.life_message: Hatred, revenge and the hunger for a crown destroy everyone they touch, yet even a person told from birth that he is a monster can love, be loved and choose to protect others to the end.

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)
content.framing: Mixed: love between Richard and Henry, and later Buckingham, shown sympathetically; abuse and assault condemned

delivery.evidence: No narrator states a lesson; the tragedy shows the cost of each choice. Henry and Cecily give two sides of religion; Buckingham and Catesby two kinds of loyalty; villains such as Richmond are drawn flatly (the fan wiki calls him psychopathic).
delivery.note: Kanno's gothic melodrama asks whether Richard is fated or chooses his path, and lets the reader decide (VIZ blurb, vol. 1 catalog copy on AniList).

personified.ideology: The outcast who accepts the label of devil to seize power
Christian meekness and refusal of war
Religious fanaticism and rejection of difference

85296.dominant: Might makes right (critiqued), Christian (explored), Existentialism, Progressivism (intersex and bisexual lead).

85475.heading: Rikudo
85475.label: From summaries
85475.life_message: A child broken by abuse is not doomed to become what was done to him: through discipline, mentors who do not give up on him and the people who love him, he can turn his fists from a killer's weapon into a craft, and choose who he becomes.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; sport violence admired, criminal violence condemned
Condemned (sexual violence and exploitation); romance chaste and slow

delivery.evidence: Rival boxers each get backstories and reasons to fight (Tsuwabuki's debts, Kaede's abusive father, Fukuro's love of the sport, Mizuki's belief that some wins cannot be bought; Japanese Wikipedia).
delivery.note: The message is carried by fights and by what each fighter is fighting for; there are few speeches, and the vol. 23 reviewer says the real subject is Riku and the society that rejects him.

personified.ideology: Strength to remake yourself, without cruelty
Win at any cost to the body
Pain as joy; living to die smiling

33586.heading: River's Edge
33586.label: From summaries
33586.life_message: Honest friendship between hurt people is worth more than the cruel games of popularity and sex around them, even when the world stays bleak and adults are absent.

delivery.evidence: ANN finds the ending inconclusive and says the book never glosses over hurt; TCJ (Nicholson) ends by leaving open what the real tragedy is.
delivery.note: The story observes rather than argues; even the bully Kannonzaki is shown with moments of vulnerability (From Cover To Cover).

personified.ideology: Dominance and status through sex and violence
Self-worth through consumer goods and men
Hidden identity; finding life in death

49423.heading: Rohan at the Louvre
49423.label: From summaries
49423.life_message: The past lives on in our blood and memories: hatred can reach across centuries and destroy those who come near it, and it is love and the willingness to let go, not curiosity, that finally lays it to rest.

content.framing: Neutral (a first crush; nothing sexual reported)

delivery.evidence: Rohan narrates a ghost story and draws no moral; ANN calls the plot flimsy and CBR says the ending explains too quickly. The meaning (love frees, hatred binds) is left in the final pages.
delivery.note: A mood piece told for its art and atmosphere; the moral about memory and love is implied, not argued.

personified.ideology: Love that sacrifices to free another

49423.dominant: Pagan/occult (explored), Expressive individualism (affirmed), Confucian ethics (ancestors and bloodline).

98382.heading: Rokudo's Bad Girls
98382.label: From summaries
98382.life_message: Real strength is refusing to run and standing by your friends; even the "worst" people can change, and love only counts when it is freely chosen.

content.framing: Mixed: brawls as heroism, bullying and cruelty condemned
Mixed: compelled affection questioned, then resolved by free choice
Mixed: delinquency shown as fun, reform rewarded

delivery.evidence: Rokudou states his resolve to be strong and to keep his word in speeches and tearful declarations (Japanese Wikipedia, Onishima arc); villains like the Sakura Finance executives are cartoonish, but most rivals get sympathetic backstories and reform.
delivery.note: The otokogi code is preached by the characters themselves; the story undercuts the spell's control by having Rokudou refuse to exploit it and by ending it.

personified.ideology: Courage of the weak; keeping your word
Raw violence seeking a place to belong

98382.dominant: Bushido / honor code (otokogi), Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics; Might makes right explored and tamed.

124895.heading: Ron Kamonohashi: Deranged Detective
124895.label: From summaries
124895.life_message: Truth should serve justice, not vengeance: a brilliant mind needs a good-hearted friend to keep it humane, and even murderers must be taken alive to face the law.

content.framing: Condemned; crimes solved and culprits exposed
Shown as a dangerous disorder that must be stopped

delivery.evidence: Each case ends with the culprit's motive explained and Ron's trance stopped; the moral (keep them alive, let the law judge) is built into the premise rather than stated in speeches (ANN; Wikipedia).
delivery.note: Values are carried by the case formula and the buddy comedy; the Moriarty family is drawn as cold villains, while culprits' motives are often given a hearing (to verify).

personified.ideology: Brilliant reason with a troubled, dangerous mind

124895.dominant: Duty ethics (culprits must live and face the law), Classical virtue ethics, Secular humanism (reason and evidence).

127554.heading: Rooster Fighter
127554.label: From summaries
127554.life_message: Real strength protects the weak, even monsters may once have been suffering people who can be saved, and a hero has to let go of hatred to become truly strong.

content.framing: Endorsed (heroic fighting); demons often freed back to human form

delivery.evidence: ANN says the series takes itself seriously in the best way while mocking its premise; values come through Keiji's code and each rescue (ch. 1-5), and later through the Righteous Master's teaching (vols. 9-11).
delivery.note: The anti-hatred theme becomes more explicit in the training arc (vol. 11); demons' human origins give villains a sympathetic side.

personified.ideology: Lone warrior's code; protection and revenge
Discipline and mastery of the inner self

127554.dominant: Bushido / honor code, Classical virtue ethics, Absurdism (played straight).

33403.heading: Rosario+Vampire: Season II
33403.label: From summaries
33403.life_message: Friendship and love can bridge peoples who fear each other; strength is for protecting others, and coexistence is worth fighting for even when hatred runs deep on both sides.

content.framing: Fan service endorsed as comedy; molestation condemned

delivery.evidence: Coexistence is stated often by Tsukune and the Headmaster, but villains get backstories (Aqua's murdered sister, Gyokuro's longing for her husband's love, fan wiki) and humans are shown as capable of hatred too.
delivery.note: Message carried by action and speeches at climaxes; ANN calls the emotional moments contrived (vol. 6).

33403.dominant: Communitarianism (coexistence), Pagan/occult (a world of monsters, witches and seals), Might makes right (critiqued in Fairy Tale).

30894.heading: Rosario+Vampire
30894.label: From summaries
30894.life_message: Friendship and kindness can bridge peoples who fear each other: an ordinary person who refuses to hate can win over enemies, and strength is for protecting friends, not ruling others.

content.framing: Fan service endorsed as comedy; predatory acts condemned

delivery.evidence: Moka states the hope that meeting others changes the world after Witch's Knoll (fan wiki); villains get backstories (Ruby's parents killed by a drunk driver, Hokuto's life between worlds), but Kuyo and Ishigami are drawn flat.
delivery.note: Coexistence is spoken at the end of each arc and carried by Tsukune's kindness; ANN calls the friendship resolutions convenient (vol. 9).

personified.ideology: Coexistence; kindness even to enemies; protect your friends
Rule by force; extortion dressed as order
Hatred of humans after harm to her land
Tear down the order; a human who belonged nowhere

30894.dominant: Communitarianism, Might makes right (critiqued), Pagan/occult, Liberalism (free press).

125528.heading: Rosen Garten Saga
125528.label: From summaries
125528.life_message: The story celebrates shameless appetite and loyalty among misfits: nothing is too taboo to laugh at, the strong and the "degenerate" are accepted as they are, and a sincere love (Lynn's for Brünhild) and a party of friends carry the hero through a tournament of legends.

content.framing: Endorsed as comedy; sexual violence played for laughs

125528.dominant: Hedonism, Expressive individualism, Postmodernism (parody), Might makes right. "Postmodernism" and "Might makes right" here are my own framing, not a source's.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers call it a parody that "doesn't take these concepts very seriously" and "will joke about everything"; none calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its values come through the jokes and the cast's acceptance of one another rather than through any stated message.

personified.ideology: Sincere love and wanting to be worthy

114003.heading: Run Away With Me, Girl
114003.label: From summaries
114003.life_message: A love you were told to grow out of can be the truest one; leaving an abusive partner and choosing an honest life takes courage, and help comes when you ask for it.

delivery.evidence: ANN: events explain why characters act as they do "without excusing any of it"; the story gives Tazune his own point-of-view chapter (ANN) and a backstory, though critics found him unsympathetic.
delivery.note: The message is carried by the relationships, with alternating viewpoints (Maki, Midori, Tazune) rather than speeches.

114003.dominant: Expressive individualism, Feminism and Progressivism (critique of heteronormativity), set against a critique of traditional expectations.

30022.heading: Rurouni Kenshin
30022.label: From summaries
30022.life_message: A person who has done great wrong can make amends by living to protect others, without taking life again; revenge and the belief that the strong should rule only destroy, and a sword should serve life.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; killing condemned, nonlethal defense endorsed

delivery.evidence: Kenshin states his vow and its reasons often, but Saito's and Shishio's creeds are given strong voices and are never simply mocked; Saito is left standing (Beneath the Tangles, 2015; fan wiki).
delivery.note: The anti-killing, anti-revenge message is carried by plot tests and speeches in the duels; Watsuki said redemption came from the shojo manga he grew up on (Wikipedia).

personified.ideology: Atonement through protecting others, never killing
The strong should rule the weak
Swift death to evil (Aku Soku Zan)

30022.dominant: Pacifism / nonviolence (the no-kill vow), Classical virtue ethics (atonement), Might makes right critiqued (Shishio), Communitarianism (the dojo family).

86560.heading: RWBY
86560.label: From summaries
86560.life_message: Real heroes are made by choosing to protect others and by working as a team, not by where you come from or what your family wants for you.

delivery.evidence: Values are shown through each girl's backstory chapter rather than speeches (Otaku USA; fan wiki); Adam is given a cause, not just villainy (ch. 5-6).
delivery.note: The book is mostly action; its values come through character choices.

86560.dominant: Communitarianism (teamwork), Classical virtue ethics (courage), Expressive individualism (Weiss), Pacifism / nonviolence (Blake, explored).

31271.heading: S.A: Special A
31271.label: From summaries
31271.life_message: Work hard, compete fairly and never accept a win you did not earn; friends who push you make you better, and love grows from respect.

content.framing: Endorsed (teen romance aimed at marriage); jealousy shown as romantic

delivery.evidence: Hikari's code (no cheating, no thrown matches) is shown in contests rather than lectures (fan wiki; Gaffney, vol. 17); rivals and villains (Yahiro, the grandfather) are given reasons and redemption.
delivery.note: A comedy that teaches through contests and friendships; romance carries most of the message.

31271.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (effort and fair play), Communitarianism (the S.A as family), Traditionalism (family duty and marriage), with Feminism contested.

87384.heading: Sacrificial Princess and the King of Beasts
87384.label: From summaries
87384.life_message: Kindness that is not afraid can see past appearances and prejudice, heal a wounded ruler who hates half of himself, and bring enemies and peoples together.

content.framing: Condemned (cruelty and war); protective force endorsed
Mixed: chaste romance endorsed; critics question the age gap and early dominance
Shown with care; answered by love

delivery.evidence: The anti-prejudice message is spoken at arc climaxes and lived through Sariphi's acts; opponents like Anubis, Galois and Fenrir get backstories and change, while Set and Vivian are flat villains (Wikipedia; fan wiki). ANN's McNulty praised it for having no clear villain early on.
delivery.note: A fairy-tale romance whose politics of prejudice grow more explicit in the last arcs.

personified.ideology: A ruler who hides his true self to keep order
Order and the king's image above all
Strength and revenge as the right to rule

87384.dominant: Communitarianism (a found family of outcasts), Classical virtue ethics (kindness, courage, mercy), Progressivism (prejudice overcome).

30773.heading: Saikano: The Last Love Song on This Little Planet
30773.label: From summaries
30773.life_message: Love is what keeps us human, even at the end of the world; war and the people who run it turn the young into weapons and destroy everything ordinary and dear.

content.framing: Mixed: teen sex presented as love's fulfillment; adult pursuit and forcing shown as wrong or troubling

delivery.evidence: ANN (vol. 6) calls the message heavy-handed and says characters at times become vessels for the author's voice; MadInkBeard finds the closing sins-of-the-world imagery over-the-top; whole pages of text-only narration carry the characters' thoughts (MadInkBeard).
delivery.note: The anti-war and love themes are stated openly by characters and narration; no character argues for the war, which stays faceless and unexplained.

personified.ideology: Love keeps you human; the weapon is not who I am
Faithful love grown out of guilt and confusion
State necessity: it could not be helped

30773.dominant: Pacifism / nonviolence (anti-war lament), Existentialism, Nihilism (explored), Transhumanism (critiqued).

30092.heading: Sailor Moon
30092.label: From summaries
30092.life_message: Love, loyal friendship and the courage of an ordinary, flawed girl are the strongest powers in the universe; a destined love and a chosen life are worth protecting even at the cost of your own.

delivery.evidence: The power of love and friendship is carried by battles in which villains are often purified; Jason Thompson describes the fights as a clash of wills (via Wikipedia); the outer Guardians' hard-headed view is given real weight before it is overruled.
delivery.note: Love and friendship are named as the source of power in battle after battle, but the story does not lecture.

personified.ideology: Love and hope can save even enemies

30092.dominant: Feminism, Communitarianism, Pagan/occult, Traditionalism (destined marriage and monarchy).

38947.heading: Saint Young Men
38947.label: From summaries
38947.life_message: Kindness, patience and good-humored friendship across differences make ordinary life good; even the holiest figures are at their best in small acts of gentleness toward neighbors.

delivery.evidence: Both founders are drawn warmly and neither is shown to be right; The Guardian notes little overt commentary on religion (via Wikipedia).
delivery.note: The kindness comes through daily gags, not lessons; the creator says she aimed for simple jokes anyone could get (Global Voices).

38947.dominant: Christian and Buddhist ideas (as comedy), Communitarianism, Consumerism (gently mocked).

125828.heading: Sakamoto Days
125828.label: From summaries
125828.life_message: A good life is a peaceful, ordinary family life. Even a killer can start over, and he makes up for the lives he took by protecting and helping others, never by taking more.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (killing condemned; non-lethal force endorsed)

delivery.evidence: Common Sense Media lists the message that it is never too late to change; no review opened calls it preachy; reviewers focus on comedy and action. In ch. 282 Boiled and Seba argue against sparing Uzuki and the story lets them speak.
delivery.note: The no-kill message is carried by a household rule and by action choices more than by speeches; the final fight states it most openly, as Sakamoto rejects his old "prime" self (ch. 281).

personified.ideology: Strength restrained for family; no killing
Sanctity of life; atonement by service
Violent revenge on an abusive system

125828.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism (family-first), Pacifism / nonviolence (no-kill form), Secular humanism, Traditionalism.

113801.heading: Sakurai-san Wants to Be Noticed
113801.label: From summaries
113801.life_message: Love grows when two people stop hiding behind hints and jokes and say plainly what they feel.

content.framing: Neutral (fan service as comedy); romance endorsed

delivery.evidence: Episodic teasing comedy (AniList: Episodic); the message about honesty is carried only by the final confession (vol. 4 blurb).
delivery.note: There is no lesson stated; honesty wins simply because the story ends when both speak plainly.

113801.dominant: Expressive individualism (say what you feel), with light Hedonism in the fan service.

106654.heading: Samurai 8: The Tale of Hachimaru
106654.label: From summaries
106654.life_message: Strength is not something you have but something you choose to try for: a weak boy becomes a samurai by finding people to protect and a calling worth living for.

content.framing: Endorsed (heroic sword combat); villains' cruelty condemned
Mixed: self-sacrifice presented as heroic; a child's failed seppuku shown as tragedy

delivery.evidence: Daruma delivers long lectures on the samurai Trinity, calling and fate (ch. 6-7, 15, 35-36), a running joke since Hachimaru itches through them (ch. 7); SLJ and ANN both note heavy exposition. Villains state their creeds (Ata's godhood, Benkei's 'loyalty' by killing his master, ch. 29) and are defeated.
delivery.note: The message (try to be strong for others; find your calling) is spoken outright by Daruma and by Hachimaru's vows, and acted out in battles.

106654.dominant: Bushido / honor code, Buddhist ideas, Classical virtue ethics, Transhumanism (explored).

31461.heading: Sanctuary
31461.label: From summaries
31461.life_message: Two loyal friends who refuse to accept a corrupt, stagnant order can remake their country, and the story treats crime, violence and manipulation as acceptable tools for that end.

content.framing: Mixed: the heroes' violence endorsed; rivals' violence condemned
Mixed: the heroes' conquests endorsed; Tokai's assaults shown casually

delivery.evidence: Thompson: the heroes win over enemies with speeches and face consequences only when no one cares about the victim; villains are mostly foreigners or ugly old men. The leads state their goals openly and often.
delivery.note: The political message is argued in speeches and rallies; the story rarely lets the opposing side make a fair case, apart from Isaoka.

personified.ideology: Any means to remake a stagnant nation
The status quo of seniority and money

31461.dominant: Utilitarianism (utopia justifies the means), Patriotism / nationalism, Might makes right, Pragmatism, Bushido / honor code (yakuza loyalty).

136680.heading: SANDA
136680.label: From summaries
136680.life_message: Growing up cannot and should not be frozen: children deserve the freedom to change and become adults, and a true adult uses strength to protect children, not to control them.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; violence against children condemned

delivery.evidence: The critique of controlling adults is plain in the setting and in Oshibu, but Tetsudome and Yagiuda give adults real reasons, and Oshibu later allies with Sanda (ciatr).
delivery.note: Its themes of puberty and control come through absurd comedy and action; reviewers praise it as thought-provoking rather than preachy (UK Anime Network; Real Sound).

personified.ideology: Youth worship and control of children
Acceptance of aging and moral compromise

48597.heading: Sankarea: Undying Love
48597.label: From summaries
48597.life_message: Real love accepts a person whole, even as their body fails, and a person has the right to choose their own life apart from a parent who treats them as a possession.

content.framing: Mixed: the father's behavior condemned; fan service neutral to endorsed as comedy

delivery.evidence: Rea states that her body and soul do not belong to her father (fan wiki, vol. 1); the father is a near-villain but is given grief as a motive and partial redemption (Wikipedia).
delivery.note: The message comes through melodrama and comedy, not lectures.

personified.ideology: A father's ownership of a daughter
The dead as objects of study and desire

48597.dominant: Expressive individualism (a girl claims her own life), Transhumanism (overcoming death by science, explored), Feminism (escape from a controlling father, explored).

98370.heading: Sasaki and Miyano
98370.label: From summaries
98370.life_message: Love that is honest, patient and respectful of the other person's pace lets both people understand themselves; what you love, shared without shame, is a good way to know someone.

delivery.evidence: No character argues against the relationship; doubts are Miyano's own and Ogasawara's brief skepticism (v2, v7). Harusono says each chapter is built around an interaction between the two (ANN interview).
delivery.note: Patient, consensual love is shown in small scenes rather than stated as a lesson; the meta jokes about BL tropes carry the commentary.

98370.dominant: Expressive individualism, Progressivism, Postmodernism (the BL-genre lens on real life).

101715.heading: Saving 80,000 Gold in Another World for My Retirement
101715.label: From summaries
101715.life_message: Secure your own future with your wits, then use your advantages to protect the friends and the place you come to love; money buys safety and freedom, and cleverness beats force.

delivery.evidence: Mitsuha explains her economic reasoning to the reader at length (AniList Economics tag at 93%), but the moral is carried by results: greedy or aggressive opponents are flat and quickly beaten (Wikipedia episode summaries).
delivery.note: Explanatory rather than preachy; opponents exist to be outsmarted.

personified.ideology: Self-reliance and profit, joined to loyalty

101715.dominant: Pragmatism, Consumerism, Libertarianism (self-reliance and trade), Might makes right (explored).

41767.heading: Say "I Love You".
41767.label: From summaries
41767.life_message: Risking trust and letting others in, even after being hurt, is how people grow; being seen and accepted as you are lets you become who you are meant to be.

content.framing: Mixed: casual sex shown as empty; sex within a loving relationship accepted

delivery.evidence: Rivals and schemers (Aiko, Megumi, Kakeru) are given backstories and redemption rather than flattened; Mei's inner voice states lessons about trust at turning points.
delivery.note: The message is carried by Mei's inner monologue and by each side character's arc.

41767.dominant: Expressive individualism (be accepted as you are), Communitarianism (friendship as healing), Classical virtue ethics (kindness and courage).

30661.heading: Sayonara, Zetsubou-Sensei
30661.label: From summaries
30661.life_message: Laughing hard at the absurd and painful sides of modern life is one way of surviving them; and beneath the despair jokes, the story ends by showing a teacher quietly keeping fragile young people alive.

content.framing: Played for laughs; fan service of high-school characters recurring
Black comedy; reframed by the ending

delivery.evidence: Nozomu states each chapter's complaint outright and lists examples; Kafuka's optimism is mocked as hard as his pessimism; Maria often gives the closing moral (Wikipedia).
delivery.note: The message is satirical rather than preachy: the rant is the joke, and no single view is endorsed until the finale.

46922.heading: School Babysitters
46922.label: From summaries
46922.life_message: Those we lose do not come back, but no one has to be left alone: love grows by caring for others, and a family can be built from people who choose to look after each other.

delivery.evidence: The Comikey blurb leads with the message that the lost don't return but we are not left alone; chapters end in small lessons (keeping promises, vol. 14) shown through the children rather than stated.
delivery.note: Warm and sometimes sentimental; the lessons are carried by the children's behavior and by Ryuichi's example.

46922.dominant: Communitarianism, with Confucian ethics, Classical virtue ethics and Duty ethics (deontology).

85235.heading: School-Live!
85235.label: From summaries
85235.life_message: When everything has collapsed, hope is something people choose and keep for one another: kindness, routine and friendship let the girls survive, grow up and, in the end, save others.

content.framing: Survival violence shown as tragic; human cruelty condemned

delivery.evidence: The Militants' harsh logic is given real reasons (scarce food, infection risk) before it fails; Miki's objection to playing along with Yuki is treated as fair (ANN vol. 3). The final message is spoken in Yuki's speech, but earned over twelve volumes.
delivery.note: Hope is shown more than stated: routines, club activities and small kindnesses carry it until the closing speech.

personified.ideology: Strict survival rules; expel the weak
A teacher's duty to the end

85235.dominant: Communitarianism (affirmed), Existentialism (chosen hope), Might makes right and Utilitarianism (critiqued in the Militants and Randall).

30160.heading: School Rumble
30160.label: From summaries
30160.life_message: Loving someone sincerely, even when it is not returned, makes a person braver and kinder; real love wants the other's good more than its own way.

content.framing: Mixed: sincere romance endorsed; lechery played for laughs and punished with beatings

delivery.evidence: Kobayashi built arcs on misunderstandings he then resolves (Wikipedia); values come through gags and a few serious chapters, never lectures.
delivery.note: A gag-romance; the message is carried by the characters' constancy, not argued.

personified.ideology: Love shown in deeds, not words

30160.dominant: Absurdism (surreal gags), Classical virtue ethics (constancy and reform), Communitarianism (class 2-C).

120537.heading: School Zone Girls
120537.label: From summaries
120537.life_message: Ordinary school days are worth living because of the friends who share them; the people closest to you may care more than they can say, and finding the courage to say it is part of growing up.

content.framing: Endorsed (same-sex crushes treated warmly); gags unjudged

delivery.evidence: Reviewers describe episodic, low-stakes comedy with occasional bittersweet flashbacks and no lectures (Okazu; ANN).
delivery.note: The romance is shown, not argued; nobody in the story objects to the girls' crushes.

120537.dominant: Communitarianism (the friend group), Absurdism (comedy of boredom), Expressive individualism (finding and saying who you are).

87377.heading: Science Fell in Love, So I Tried to Prove It
87377.label: From summaries
87377.life_message: You can measure love, but you prove it by choosing it: reason and feeling are partners, not rivals, and people are fine just as they are.

content.framing: Mixed: teasing romance between adults endorsed; harassment and assault condemned
Mixed: played as comedy, sometimes rebuked in-story

delivery.evidence: Science lessons are spelled out in panels and, in the anime, by the mascot Rikekuma (ANN preview: Silverman found the notes heavy-handed); Kanade's common sense and the ending's turn to feeling push back on pure measurement.
delivery.note: The educational content is overt and the message is said aloud (season 2 finale title: proving that you are fine just as you are), but it is wrapped in rom-com gags.

personified.ideology: Ordinary common sense; the wish to be normal

87377.dominant: Naturalism (tested), Secular humanism, Expressive individualism, Communitarianism.

74929.heading: Scum's Wish
74929.label: From summaries
74929.life_message: Using other people's bodies to fill loneliness leaves everyone emptier; real love starts with honesty about yourself and letting go of what you cannot have.

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)
content.framing: Shown with consequences (hollow, damaging); assault and adult-student relationships not clearly condemned; some scenes staged for titillation (Anime Feminist)
Shown with consequences, but adult misconduct unpunished

delivery.evidence: Anime Feminist: the story refuses to moralize ("not ... moralised as yet," premiere review) and lets characters rationalize; inner monologue, not lectures, carries the meaning.
delivery.note: The message emerges from consequences and inner monologue; the author does not state a moral, and some abusive behavior is left unjudged.

74929.dominant: Hedonism (critiqued), Existentialism (loneliness and authentic choice), Expressive individualism (explored)

85617.heading: Seaside Stranger: Harukaze no Étranger
85617.label: From summaries
85617.life_message: Love is not a single confession but years of choosing each other: a family can learn to accept a gay son slowly and imperfectly, and a couple has to keep working at honesty after the happy ending.

content.framing: Endorsed: a consensual adult same-sex relationship

delivery.evidence: ANN reads the father as uncomfortable rather than hateful, and Fumi's confusion as a child's; a MyAnimeList reviewer says the characters are flawed but not villainous.
delivery.note: The message of acceptance is carried by everyday family life and the couple's talks, not by speeches; those who disapprove are given room and motives.

personified.ideology: Internalized shame learning self-acceptance and duty
Traditional family expectations; discomfort with homosexuality

85617.dominant: Communitarianism (family reconciliation), Expressive individualism (self-acceptance), Progressivism (affirming same-sex love).

85616.heading: Seaside Stranger: Umibe no Étranger
85616.label: From summaries
85616.life_message: Accepting who you are, and letting yourself be loved, is the way out of shame and loneliness; and real love sends you home to mend family ties rather than away from them.

content.framing: Endorsed: a consensual adult same-sex romance

delivery.evidence: ANN's Silverman says it shows rather than tells; Shun's parents' rejection is seen through his memories, and the sequel gives his father's struggle more room.
delivery.note: The message of self-acceptance is carried by Shun's choices and Mio's patience, not by speeches; the rejecting family is not drawn as cartoon villains.

85616.dominant: Expressive individualism (self-acceptance), Progressivism (affirming same-sex love), Communitarianism (found family and reconciliation).

99587.heading: Seirei Gensouki: Spirit Chronicles
99587.label: From summaries
99587.life_message: A person split by grief and two lives can become whole by finding his roots and protecting the people he loves; rank and birth do not decide a person's worth, and the story keeps asking whether a life aimed at revenge can also hold happiness.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; cruelty condemned; revenge pursued
Mostly chaste harem-style admiration; one comic nudity scene
Mixed: revenge pursued and questioned; rescue endorsed

delivery.evidence: Villainous nobles are cartoonishly cruel (knights torturing a child; a noble forcing a marriage), while the spirit folk's prejudice is corrected through apology and friendship (anime ep. 1, 5; J-Novel Club).
delivery.note: The values (protect the weak, judge no one by birth) are carried by plot and rescue, not by speeches; Rio's inner debate about revenge is the main explicit thread.

personified.ideology: Protection, roots and a questioned revenge
Learning and kindness across class lines

99587.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (protecting the weak), Communitarianism (found family and the spirit village), Pagan/occult (a world of spirits), Strength rules (critiqued in corrupt nobles).

30873.heading: Sekirei
30873.label: From summaries
30873.life_message: Bonds that are freely chosen and faithfully kept are stronger than any game the powerful set up; a timid young man finds courage by protecting the people who chose him.

content.framing: Mixed: fights as spectacle; cruelty by MBI, Higa and Karasuba condemned
Mixed: fan service endorsed as the draw; forced bonding and assault condemned

delivery.evidence: Minaka is a cartoonish game master and Higa a cold manipulator, but Mikogami and several rival Ashikabi are given motives (Wikipedia, characters).
delivery.note: The message about bonds and consent comes through action and comedy rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Protect without forcing; bonds freely chosen
Life as a game: fight until one is left

30873.dominant: Communitarianism, Might makes right (critiqued), Liberalism (consent), Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Hedonism.

38070.heading: Sengoku Youko
38070.label: From summaries
38070.life_message: Humans and spirits share the same kind of soul, so peace across the divide is possible; true strength protects others, and each person can choose what they become rather than be ruled by hatred.

content.framing: Neutral (battle action); cruelty by warlords and monks condemned
Mixed: chaste romances endorsed; lechery played as a gag

delivery.evidence: Jinka's hatred has a real cause (humans killed his friend), Yazen's crimes are rooted in love for a fox spirit, and the monks fear real man-eating spirits (Japanese Wikipedia; ANN ep. 2).
delivery.note: The peace message is spoken by Tama and lived by Shinsuke and Senya, but the story lets the misanthrope and the villains state their case.

personified.ideology: Misanthropy; power as escape from being human
Scientific power over people and spirits

38070.dominant: Pagan/occult (a Japanese folk-spirit world), Classical virtue ethics (courage from cowardice), Strength rules (critiqued), Pacifism / nonviolence (Senya), Communitarianism.

118570.heading: Senpai is an Otokonoko
118570.label: From summaries
118570.life_message: Love and friendship should accept people as they are, and being honest about yourself, with friends and with family, takes courage that is worth it; families can change when they listen.

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)

delivery.evidence: ANN calls the book increasingly thoughtful; Pom says she wrote about how a person works through a problem, not to combat prejudice as such (Japanese Wikipedia); Da Vinci singles out a ch. 31 line asking whether one must choose one or the other.
delivery.note: The disapproving mother is given a backstory and a change of heart, though the story clearly sides with Makoto.

118570.dominant: Expressive individualism, Progressivism, Traditionalism (critiqued, then reconciled), Communitarianism.

35461.heading: Serial Experiments Lain: The Nightmare of Fabrication
35461.label: From summaries
35461.life_message: Who we are rests on memory and on real relationships; trying to replace people with made-to-order copies, or to rewrite memory to escape pain, deepens loneliness and loosens the hold on what is real.

delivery.evidence: The story stages one argument (Eiri's case that memory can be rewritten) and lets its effect on Lain answer it, without commentary.
delivery.note: Entirely implicit: images and Lain's inner monologue; no character states a moral.

personified.ideology: Reality as editable memory; a self-proclaimed higher being

35461.dominant: Postmodernism (reality as memory), Transhumanism (critiqued), Existentialism, Nihilism.

59887.heading: Servamp
59887.label: From summaries
59887.life_message: No one, human or monster, should be left alone with their pain; reaching out and taking responsibility can turn enemies into family.

content.framing: Mixed: fights for others endorsed; Tsubaki's and Lawless's killings condemned

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)
