delivery.evidence: ANN's Silverman says groups and characters are shaded in gray and that backstories make the darkness feel earned; Mahiru's motto is repeated but carried by action.
delivery.note: Comedy on the surface, with the message carried by backstories and reconciliations.

personified.ideology: Melancholy, revenge and loyalty to his own
Human control and extermination of vampires

59887.dominant: Communitarianism (found family), Classical virtue ethics (sins and virtues personified), Existentialism (immortal guilt and purpose).

39296.heading: Seven Days
39296.label: From summaries
39296.life_message: Love becomes real when you stop keeping it at arm's length: honesty and the risk of being hurt turn a game into a relationship.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers describe a character-driven romance with no lectures (Anime UK News; AVO Magazine); the message is carried by the seven-day structure.
delivery.note: The case for commitment is made by Seryou's choice, not by any speech; the story never argues about same-sex love at all.

personified.ideology: Love on a timer: kind but noncommittal

39296.dominant: Expressive individualism (love whom you love), Progressivism (an unremarked same-sex romance), Classical virtue ethics (honesty and constancy).

104063.heading: Shadows House
104063.label: From summaries
104063.life_message: Every person has a face and a name of their own; truth, friendship and courage can free people from a system that treats them as tools, and real loyalty is to people, not to the house that uses them.

content.framing: Condemned (abuse by masters); defensive fighting by the rebels

delivery.evidence: The message comes through mystery reveals (the coffee, unification) rather than speeches; the house's own Teachings are shown as propaganda.
delivery.note: Villains like Sarah are flat, but Edward, Barbara and Anthony are given motives and histories, so the system is criticized more than individuals.

personified.ideology: Free inquiry and loyalty to persons
Ambition and obedience to the system
Absolute rule through control of minds

104063.dominant: Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Expressive individualism (identity), Critical theory (indoctrination), Duty ethics (persons not tools).

30050.heading: Shaman King
30050.label: From summaries
30050.life_message: Strength of soul, friendship across every people and forgiveness, not the destruction of one's enemies, are what can save the world; Takei says his final message is that fighting is no good.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; killing condemned by the hero

delivery.evidence: Takei states the message outright (Wikipedia); the X-Laws and the Tao father are drawn with real backstories, and Hao is given grief and loneliness rather than pure malice.
delivery.note: The anti-violence message is carried by Yoh's choices and Hao's arc rather than speeches, inside a story that is still mostly fights.

personified.ideology: easygoing gentleness; fighting is no good
wiping out ordinary humans for a world of shamans
eradicating evil by force; zealous justice
raising an heir by cruelty to rule

30050.dominant: Pantheist/New Age (the Great Spirit), Pagan/occult (shamanism and mediumship), Pacifism / nonviolence (Takei's message), Buddhist ideas.

122063.heading: Shangri-La Frontier
122063.label: From summaries
122063.life_message: Play is worth doing well: mastering a hard challenge for the joy of it, alongside friends and rivals, is its own reward, and an opponent's story deserves respect as much as your victory does.

delivery.evidence: The series asks each lead "what do you game for?" and lets them answer differently (ch. 1, 97-98): fun, profession, or the thrill of beating people; none is mocked.
delivery.note: The message rides on action and comedy; it is never lectured.

personified.ideology: Play for the joy of mastery
Exploit the system for safe gain

122063.dominant: Pragmatism, Classical virtue ethics, Expressive individualism, Bushido / honor code (the Wethermon arc).

96791.heading: She and Her Cat
96791.label: From summaries
96791.life_message: Adult life can be lonely and uncertain, but steady companionship (a cat's quiet devotion, a friend, a mother) and the courage to take one more step and ask for help can carry a person through.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; asking for help affirmed

delivery.evidence: Told from a cat's limited view, using smells to show feeling (AniList review); the ending leaves the lesson to the reader.
delivery.note: The message is implied by mood and seasons, not stated.

96791.dominant: Existentialism (the freedom and loneliness of adult life), Communitarianism (companionship and asking for help).

142320.heading: She Loves to Cook, and She Loves to Eat
142320.label: From summaries
142320.life_message: Food shared freely is a picture of love: people deserve to be fed, valued and loved as they are, not ranked by gender or pressed into someone else's idea of normal.

content.framing: Endorsed (a slow romance between two adult women)
Shown with care: therapy and support

delivery.evidence: Sexism is shown through everyday incidents and explained in conversations (Yako's advice), and Farris (via Wikipedia) says it still reads as comfort food. Kasuga's father is shown only as a source of harm, and no character speaks for traditional family roles sympathetically in sources opened.
delivery.note: The social message is clear and sometimes explained outright, but carried by warm daily scenes rather than lectures.

personified.ideology: Self-respect; freedom from a male-first family
A traditional household where men come first

142320.dominant: Feminism, Progressivism, Expressive individualism; Traditionalism critiqued.

97529.heading: She Professed Herself Pupil of the Wise Man
97529.label: From summaries
97529.life_message: Loyalty to old friends and the duty to protect others matter more than how you look, and real ability shows through any disguise.

delivery.evidence: A low-stakes adventure (ANN); values of loyalty and service are implied by the quest, never argued.
delivery.note: Little message beyond friendship and competence; the comedy carries the book.

97529.dominant: Communitarianism (reuniting old comrades), Pragmatism (game knowledge as power), Pagan/occult (summoning and spirits, explored), Patriotism / nationalism (defending the kingdom).

101756.heading: She's Adopted a High School Boy!
101756.label: From summaries
101756.life_message: Unconditional care from an unexpected benefactor can rescue someone his own family abandoned; the series turns that care into a romance between the adult woman and the high school boy she supports, and presents it as a happy ending.

delivery.evidence: Volume blurbs and reader reviews describe comedy and romance with no character questioning the arrangement; cousin Hana's claim that family should care for him is framed as rivalry (vol. 7).
delivery.note: The series makes no argument; its assumptions (that the arrangement is sweet) are built into the premise.

101756.dominant: Hedonism (comic indulgence), Expressive individualism (love over convention), Consumerism (money as care).

100444.heading: Shigahime
100444.label: From summaries
100444.life_message: The story offers no good life to imitate. It shows a boy trying to keep his humanity and his love after being made a monster, in a world where the powerful treat others as food and toys, and it ends without a way out.

content.framing: Endorsed as fan service; villain seduction condemned by framing (to verify)

100444.dominant: Nihilism, Might makes right, Existentialism, Hedonism.

delivery.evidence: Reviews discuss pacing, art and bleakness; none mentions a stated message or calls it preachy (DTF; MAL).
delivery.note: The story presents cruelty and despair as atmosphere rather than arguing a thesis.

personified.ideology: Cruelty as pleasure; power over the weak
Belonging bought by serving a predator

33486.heading: Shiki
33486.label: From summaries
33486.life_message: When fear takes over, ordinary people can become as monstrous as the monsters they hunt; neither the predators nor the frightened village is innocent.

content.framing: Mixed: shiki predation condemned; the villagers' massacre shown as atrocity

delivery.evidence: Both sides get point-of-view chapters (Natsuno, Toshio, Sunako and Seishin arcs; Wikipedia chapter titles); reviewers note the question of who is right is left to the reader (MyAnimeList).
delivery.note: The message is argued through events and paired arcs rather than speeches; Seishin's Cain-and-Abel novel is the one explicit statement.

personified.ideology: Rational extermination to protect the community
Compassion for the outcast; religious doubt
The right of predators to live

33486.dominant: Existentialism, Nihilism (explored), Utilitarianism (critiqued in practice), Christian themes (Cain and Abel, God's abandonment).

79017.heading: Shino Can't Say Her Name
79017.label: From summaries
79017.life_message: You do not have to be "fixed" to belong: a friend who makes room for the way you speak, and the courage to keep reaching out, matter more than sounding normal.

content.framing: Neutral (shown from Shino's point of view)
Shown with consequences; resolved by friendship

delivery.evidence: Oshimi avoided the word "stutter" so the book would not read as a lesson about one condition (HuffPost Japan); reviewers note the lessons come through Shino's point of view and the other characters' actions (Outer Haven).
delivery.note: The book is told from inside Shino's head; Oshimi said he drew only what she could see (HuffPost Japan), so no character lectures the reader.

personified.ideology: The anxious self who wants to be heard
Careless talk that hurts; clumsy apology

79017.dominant: Expressive individualism (finding one's voice), Communitarianism (friendship as belonging), Secular humanism.

180881.heading: Shinobi Undercover
180881.label: From summaries
180881.life_message: Bonds with other people are strength, not dead weight: a lonely, anxious boy grows stronger by letting friends in and by protecting someone out of love rather than orders.

content.framing: Neutral (shonen action); protection endorsed, cruelty condemned

delivery.evidence: scrmbl says ch. 11 states its friendship thesis with no subtlety at all, as Yodaka beats a villain who calls attachments dead weight.
delivery.note: Shonen Jump style: the theme is spoken in fights and comedy; later arcs give villains (Kasasagi, Kawasemi, Yoichi) more depth.

personified.ideology: Bonds are strength; protect out of love
The strong owe nothing to the weak
Discipline and putting the mission first
Protecting Aoi by force, loving the fight

180881.dominant: Communitarianism (bonds as strength), Duty ethics (orders versus heart), Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued agency and clans).

100758.heading: Shiver: Junji Ito Selected Stories
100758.label: From summaries
100758.life_message: No model of a good life is offered: in a cold, uncaring universe, obsession, vanity, envy and fear consume ordinary people, and the stories warn against fixation without offering a way out.

content.framing: Neutral (horror); murder shown as horror, never as triumph

content.frequency: Central in one story, recurring obsession
content.framing: Shown as horror; no safe-messaging frame

delivery.evidence: Foreword Reviews says Ito aims at scares and discomfort more than messages; McNulty (ANN) calls the stories sometimes frustratingly enigmatic; Loveridge (ANN) says the underlying messages are easy to find. Ito's notes discuss how each story was made, not what it means (TCJ).
delivery.note: The anthology offers mood and images rather than an argued worldview; any message is in the shape of each punishment.

personified.ideology: Beauty as monstrous power; revenge on disrespect
Beauty that drives men to obsession and violence
The family line comes before the person
Greed and cruelty within the family

86645.heading: Shortcake Cake
86645.label: From summaries
86645.life_message: Home and love are built by people who stay, speak honestly and wait patiently for one another; family is the people who choose you and whom you choose.

delivery.evidence: Reviews praise quiet, silent moments and emotional nuance (Manga Bookshelf, vols. 4, 9-10); no lecturing reported.
delivery.note: Lessons about honesty and family come through character choices rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Hidden pain; fear of being unwanted

30101.heading: Shugo Chara!
30101.label: From summaries
30101.life_message: Everyone carries the seed of who they could become; finding it takes courage, giving up on it hurts, and the best way to grow is to protect other people's dreams, even an enemy's.

content.framing: Neutral (magical-girl battles; enemies are purified, not hurt)
Mixed: chaste crushes treated warmly; the age-gap romance is endorsed as the main pairing

content.frequency: Outside the book; Recurring in the story (critiqued)

delivery.evidence: The premise is a stated wish to be one's "would-be" self, each Guardian Character names a trait, and reviewers say it centers on self-esteem (Jason Thompson via Wikipedia) and on supporting friends' dreams (Peach-Pit article). Easter's agents get sympathetic motives (Ikuto, Utau, Nikaidou), but the company itself is a villain.
delivery.note: The message is spoken in the transformations and in Amu's inner voice, but carried by comedy and character growth; Carlo Santos (ANN) praises how it handles self-doubt while finding it light on substance in places.

personified.ideology: courage to be one's true self
dreams as resources to extract for profit
freedom from control; love for Amu
an adult who abandoned his childhood dream

30101.dominant: Expressive individualism (be your "would-be" self), Classical virtue ethics (traits practiced into character), Communitarianism (the Guardians), Consumerism (critiqued: the idol company).

171758.heading: Shut Up, Takamori!
171758.label: From summaries
171758.life_message: Being truly known is frightening but good: love grows from kindness shown even in private, and a relationship becomes real when both people are honest about who they are.

delivery.evidence: The publisher's volume 5 tagline says what is in the heart is the same whether or not it can be heard (BOOK☆WALKER); the message comes through the comedy premise.
delivery.note: A light romantic comedy; values are shown by Takamori's private kindness and Minamikawa's final honesty, not stated in lectures.

personified.ideology: Sincere love shown in private and public alike
Fear of being seen, growing into honesty

171758.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (kindness and honesty), Duty ethics (telling the truth), Expressive individualism (being accepted as you are).

110909.heading: Shy
110909.label: From summaries
110909.life_message: Real heroism means reaching for the hurting hearts of others, even your enemies', and you can do it while still afraid; no one can save everyone, but the bonds you make live on.

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)

content.framing: Mixed: played partly for comedy, tied to grief

delivery.evidence: The grandfather, Spirit and Teru state the message directly (fan wiki); ANN notes the anime spends long stretches repeating its point; villains receive full, sympathetic backstories (Wikipedia).
delivery.note: The theme is spoken aloud often, but nearly every villain gets an inner life, which keeps it from feeling one-sided.

personified.ideology: Heroism as reaching out to hurting hearts
Set hearts free by their darkest feelings; a world without adults

110909.dominant: Communitarianism, Pacifism / nonviolence (limited form), Secular humanism, Existentialism.

55096.heading: Silver Spoon
55096.label: From summaries
55096.life_message: You do not need a dream to begin: by working hard beside others, facing hard truths about life, death and money, and helping your friends reach their goals, you find your own path, and failing or running away does not have to be the end.

content.frequency: Outside the book; some in story

delivery.evidence: Aki, Tamako and Komaba each argue a different way of farming (family, industrial, debt-ridden), and Hachiken's father is given his reasons; Arakawa says she was telling a growth story, not promoting a cause (Wikipedia).
delivery.note: Lessons come through chores, failures and food rather than speeches; the comedy keeps it light.

personified.ideology: Work hard, help others, find your path by doing
Duty to the family farm versus her own dream

55096.dominant: Communitarianism, Pragmatism, Classical virtue ethics, Expressive individualism (finding one's own path).

31155.heading: Sing "Yesterday" for Me
31155.label: From summaries
31155.life_message: You cannot live in yesterday: grief and old loves should be honored and then let go, and a vocation and a love are found by small, awkward steps forward rather than by waiting for life to start.

delivery.evidence: MyAnimeList reviewers describe a realistic, novel-like story without lessons stated; ANN's Farris found the anime a rewarding slow burn; no reviewer calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Each character's way of living (drifting, grieving, waiting, striving) is given a fair hearing; the story moves them forward without condemning anyone.

31155.dominant: Existentialism (choosing a path after drift), Expressive individualism (living one's own way), Communitarianism (friends who help each other move on).

98900.heading: Skeleton Knight in Another World
98900.label: From summaries
98900.life_message: Strength is for protecting the powerless: whatever you look like underneath, your worth shows in freeing captives and standing against people who treat others as property.

content.framing: Endorsed (killing slavers and bandits as justice)
Condemned (sexual violence is the villains'); fan service light

delivery.evidence: Slavers and nobles are drawn as leering, cruel caricatures (the Marquis, ch. 8; the slaver who stabs children, ch. 5); Common Sense Media says justice and oppression are not explored in depth.
delivery.note: The anti-slavery message is carried by rescue action rather than argument; villains have no sympathetic case.

personified.ideology: Strength used to protect the weak

98900.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (protective chivalry), Critical theory (systemic slavery and supremacy), Might makes right (explored).

31414.heading: SKET DANCE
31414.label: From summaries
31414.life_message: Helping others with whatever they need, for nothing in return, is how you carry the love of those who came before you; friends pull each other out of grief and isolation, and no one should be left alone.

content.frequency: Occasional, heavy in the drama arcs
content.framing: Shown with consequences; healing through friendship

delivery.evidence: Serious arcs end with clear lessons about friendship and responsibility, and ANN calls the drama obvious sentimentality; rivals (the student council, Momoka) are given their own dignity and become allies.
delivery.note: Mostly episodic comedy; the message lands hardest in the backstory arcs.

personified.ideology: Help others for its own sake

31414.dominant: Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics (kindness, loyalty, courage), Postmodernism (parody and fourth-wall comedy).

30610.heading: Skip Beat!
30610.label: From summaries
30610.life_message: Real self-worth comes from building your own craft and character, not from living for someone else; hurt can be turned into growth instead of revenge.

content.framing: Mixed: slapstick; Ren's fighting shown as part of his dark past
Mixed: forced kisses resented; the central romance romanticized and slow

delivery.evidence: Kyoko's growth is shown role by role; Sho's view of her is shown as wrong but he is given depth; Lory states the theme that an actor needs love.
delivery.note: Comedy, inner monologue and acting jobs carry the message; the president and Ren sometimes spell out lessons.

personified.ideology: Self-worth through work instead of living for someone else
Discipline and professionalism masking a dark past
Love as the root of all acting

30610.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (diligence and professionalism), Expressive individualism (a self of her own), Feminism (not living for a man), with Confucian senpai-kouhai respect.

30051.heading: Slam Dunk
30051.label: From summaries
30051.life_message: Anyone can change: a hot-tempered delinquent and a bitter dropout find themselves through hard practice, humble basics and a team that takes them back. Talent matters only when it serves the team, and you are not finished until you give up.

content.framing: Played for comedy early; fighting shown with consequences in the Mitsui arc

content.frequency: Pervasive outside the book; rare inside

delivery.evidence: Carlo Santos (ANN, via Wikipedia) says the off-court stories are its "heart and soul"; Common Sense Media stresses teamwork and humility.
delivery.note: Lessons arrive through games and character turns, and rival teams' approaches are treated with respect.

personified.ideology: Bitterness and gang life, then repentance
Patient faith in players; never give up

30051.dominant: Communitarianism (the team), Classical virtue ethics (perseverance, humility), Pragmatism and Confucian ethics; Strength rules and Nihilism critiqued.

87510.heading: Sleepy Princess in the Demon Castle
87510.label: From summaries
87510.life_message: Rest and comfort are worth pursuing, and even captors and "enemies" can become a household that cares for you.

content.framing: Endorsed as comedy; often punished with chores

delivery.evidence: Episodic gag comedy with no stated message (Wikipedia episode list; reviews call it one joke done well: ICv2, Otaku USA).
delivery.note: Demons who want order are comic victims, yet they are drawn with affection, and the household they form is the warmest thing in the story.

87510.dominant: Hedonism (comfort-seeking), Absurdism, Expressive individualism, Communitarianism (the demon household).

99757.heading: Smile Down the Runway
99757.label: From summaries
99757.life_message: A dream other people call impossible can be reached through relentless work, real skill and people who believe in you, and the point of making things is to make people smile.

content.framing: Mixed: dedication praised; some critics see overwork glamorized

delivery.evidence: Doubters have reasons: Chiyuki's father is harsh out of love and Igarashi acts from her own insecurity (Japanese Wikipedia; anime ep. 7); speeches about dreams recur at key moments.
delivery.note: The message comes through contests and shows in a sports-manga structure rather than lectures; the author built it around human drama for non-fashion readers (Japanese Wikipedia).

personified.ideology: Craft, humility and duty to family
Talent should go where it pays

99757.dominant: Expressive individualism (a dream against doubters), Communitarianism (family and team), Classical virtue ethics (diligence and craft).

34571.heading: Snow White with the Red Hair
34571.label: From summaries
34571.life_message: A good life is one you choose and earn yourself: honest, skilled work for the good of others, and love between equals that respects each person's path.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; villains arrested more often than killed

delivery.evidence: Themes come through Shirayuki's choices (refusing Zen's help with the exam) rather than speeches (ANN Spring 2019 Manga Guide); the opponents of the match (Haruka, Izana) are given reasons and some come round.
delivery.note: The message is carried by everyday work and loyal friendships; villains are thin, but the main opposing voices are treated fairly.

34571.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (diligence, honesty, loyalty), Feminism (a working woman's agency), Communitarianism (Zen's circle as found family).

107265.heading: Soloist in a Cage
107265.label: From summaries
107265.life_message: Love for family is worth any danger: a promise to protect someone is kept even when it costs you your innocence, and hope can survive in the cruelest place.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (killing haunts the heroine)

delivery.evidence: No review describes lectures; the message rides on Chloe's mission. Reviewers note there is no fully developed antagonist, and the cult leader's introduction felt rushed (MyAnimeList).
delivery.note: Family devotion is carried by action and by Chloe's guilt rather than stated as a lesson.

personified.ideology: Love for family at any cost
Power through a claim to be God

107265.dominant: Communitarianism (family and the children's band), Classical virtue ethics (courage and fidelity), Might makes right and Collectivism/authoritarianism (both critiqued in the prison city and the cult).

86788.heading: Somali and the Forest Spirit
86788.label: From summaries
86788.life_message: A parent's love can grow where no one expects it, and seeing past fear and prejudice to the person in front of you is how old wounds between peoples begin to heal.

delivery.evidence: The prejudice theme is carried by encounters on the journey with kind and hostile non-humans alike; the hostile ones are given reasons (Rosa's village, Uzoi's love, the war's history), and humans are shown as having started the hatred (fan wiki; Wikipedia episode summaries).
delivery.note: No review opened discusses delivery (to verify); the summaries suggest the message is shown through events rather than stated.

113076.heading: Sometimes Even Reality Is a Lie!
113076.label: From summaries
113076.life_message: The masks we hide behind can protect us for a while, but friendship and love only grow when people find the courage to step outside and tell the truth to the people who care about them.

delivery.evidence: The honesty theme is raised by characters (Kaoru's father, ch. 112; Shōko, ch. 134-136) inside slice-of-life comedy; the overprotective father's view is treated with sympathy, not mocked.
delivery.note: The message that the truth must eventually be told is carried by the plot and the title rather than lectures.

personified.ideology: Kindness first, even through a disguise

113076.dominant: Communitarianism (friends and family heal Nanami), Expressive individualism (stepping out of hiding to be oneself), Classical virtue ethics (kindness and courage), Duty ethics (the truth must be told to parents).

33042.heading: SoreMachi: And Yet the Town Moves
33042.label: From summaries
33042.life_message: Everyday life among neighbors, family and friends, met with curiosity and goodwill, is worth paying attention to; an ordinary town turns out to be full of wonder.

content.framing: Played for comedy, often with consequences

delivery.evidence: Episodic comedy with no stated thesis; Ishiguro's afterword hopes it can be a "textbook of communication" (Japanese Wikipedia); the Japan Media Arts jury noted the lack of trauma or melodrama (English Wikipedia).
delivery.note: Values are implied by daily life rather than argued; no character stands for a worldview the story attacks.

33042.dominant: Communitarianism (the shopping street as a community); Expressive individualism (quirks accepted); Confucian ethics and Traditionalism (elders and continuity); Absurdism (surreal comedy).

53661.heading: Soul Eater Not!
53661.label: From summaries
53661.life_message: Ordinary people find courage through friendship: you do not have to be the strongest to protect the people you love, and you may not have to choose between them.

delivery.evidence: Shaula states the counter-view (friends are a weakness) and Meme refutes it in the climax (ch. 42); otherwise values come through daily-life comedy.
delivery.note: The message is carried by the friendship plot and stated briefly at the end, not lectured.

53661.dominant: Communitarianism (the trio and the dorm), Classical virtue ethics (courage, loyalty), Expressive individualism (Tsugumi finding her own goal).

30908.heading: Soul Eater
30908.label: From summaries
30908.life_message: A good life faces fear with courage, trusts the partners beside you, and keeps soul, mind and body in balance; neither rigid order nor madness is the answer, but courage and human bonds are.

delivery.evidence: Asura's view that Death's order is arbitrary gets a hearing, and Kid fears his own order could be madness (vol. 25 summary, fan wiki); villains like Medusa are drawn without much depth. No review opened calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its message about courage over fear is stated in key moments (ch. 112-113) but mostly carried by fights and gags.

personified.ideology: Fear and madness; order is arbitrary
Blind faith in whichever god is strongest

30908.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (courage), Pagan/occult (as setting), Communitarianism, Existentialism, Bushido / honor code (explored).

44483.heading: Space Brothers
44483.label: From summaries
44483.life_message: It is never too late to chase the dream you promised yourself: ordinary people who keep going after failure, lean on family, friends and mentors, and stay true to who they are can reach extraordinary places.

content.frequency: Occasional, heavy in the final arc

delivery.evidence: The message is carried by Mutta's choices and setbacks; mentors state lessons (Sharon, Brian), and ANN's Kimlinger finds it over-explains and can be heavy-handed in emotional moments.
delivery.note: Lessons about dreams and courage are spoken aloud by mentors, but the story mostly shows them through work, failure and rescue.

personified.ideology: Ordinary perseverance; it is never too late
Talent and courage that must face fear

44483.dominant: Secular humanism, Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Pragmatism.

33299.heading: Spice & Wolf
33299.label: From summaries
33299.life_message: A life worth living is a journey shared: honest wits, trust and love outlast loneliness and change, and even a forgotten goddess can find a home.

content.framing: Mixed: nudity shown as a goddess's ease with her body; flirtation; ends in marriage
Mixed: cunning endorsed; fraud and violence condemned

delivery.evidence: The themes come through trades and conversations; Hasekura says he did not set out to make a statement (B&N, 2017); the Church is shown as overbearing, but Elsa gives faith a sympathetic face (v7-8).
delivery.note: Ideas about money, faith and change are argued through deals and banter between the two leads, not lectures.

personified.ideology: Profit at any cost after loss

33299.dominant: Pragmatism (economics and wit), Pagan/occult (an old goddess), Christian (a Church critiqued), Libertarianism (free trade).

68071.heading: Spirit Circle
68071.label: From summaries
68071.life_message: Grudges carried from the past only end when people understand and forgive each other and themselves; however hard life gets, it is worth living, because something good will happen.

content.framing: Condemned; shown as the engine of the cycle
Mostly chaste; fan service as comedy

delivery.evidence: Kouko's grievance is treated as real (her past selves were truly wronged), and the message comes through each life's outcome and Rune's stated hope that something good will happen (Wrong Every Time).
delivery.note: The theme is stated at key moments but carried mostly by the structure: each past life is a case study in how cruelty starts and how it might end.

personified.ideology: Understanding and forgiveness end the cycle
Justice as revenge for past wrongs
Mastery over life, death and the universe
Simple hope: something good will happen

68071.dominant: Buddhist ideas (rebirth and letting go), Pacifism / nonviolence (breaking the cycle of revenge), Existentialism, Classical virtue ethics.

108556.heading: SPY x FAMILY
108556.label: From summaries
108556.life_message: A good life is building a family, even an imperfect or "fake" one, and protecting the peace that lets children grow up without war.

content.frequency: Occasional; heavy in a few arcs
content.framing: Shown with consequences (Yor's work) / Neutral (spy action, comic)

delivery.evidence: Plugged In calls it fun and thought-provoking about family; Common Sense Media says all the Forgers are lying to each other; neither calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its anti-war and family themes mostly sit under comedy, with occasional direct flashbacks such as Loid's childhood (v10) and Martha's story (v15).

personified.ideology: Trade one's own life for peace

108556.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Secular humanism, Communitarianism, Patriotism / nationalism (explored), Traditionalism (family form), Utilitarianism (explored).

163923.heading: ST☆R: Strike it Rich
163923.label: From summaries
163923.life_message: Friends who hit rock bottom can build something of their own; skill and nerve can beat raw power, and women can win a place in a man's sport, though the shortcuts the story treats as normal (gambling, a corrupt cop, yakuza money) carry real costs.

content.framing: Neutral (spectacle); killers and schemers shown as dangerous

delivery.evidence: No character lectures; the dirty cop and the yakuza heir are heroes, while the rival boss and the cult are drawn as schemers and fanatics.
delivery.note: An action comedy with little explicit moralizing; its values show in who it roots for.

personified.ideology: Skill and business sense over raw power
Fighting for joy; strength without limits
Bending the law for friends and goals

163923.dominant: Might makes right (explored), Feminism (explored), Pragmatism, Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued).

51467.heading: Stargazing Dog
51467.label: From summaries
51467.life_message: Even when a person has lost everything the world counts, love and loyalty (here between a man and his dog) give that life its worth, and the forgotten people around us deserve to be seen.

delivery.evidence: Publishers Weekly (via Wikipedia) calls the dog's name heavy-handed; The Comics Reporter finds the sorrow laid on very thickly; Okutsu states the parable at the end of Story 2 (Wikipedia).
delivery.note: The meaning is carried by the dog's narration and the man's choices; only Okutsu's closing reflection spells it out.

personified.ideology: Loyal love with nothing left to give but presence
Duty that learns compassion from another life

51467.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (loyalty and self-sacrifice), Existentialism (meaning in an overlooked life), Secular humanism.

97764.heading: Starving Anonymous
97764.label: From summaries
97764.life_message: People are not livestock: even when the powerful treat human beings as food, refusing to abandon a friend and giving oneself for others are what keep people human.

content.framing: Condemned (the facility and the creatures); the heroes' fight endorsed

delivery.evidence: The Manga Critic says any point about factory farming is pushed aside for an escape plot; the facility and the creatures are drawn as pure horror; the creatures' own reasoning (coexistence through managed farming) appears only in the reveal (vol. 6, ciatr).
delivery.note: Its condemnation of treating people as livestock is carried entirely by horror and action; the villains are not given a real case.

97764.dominant: Might makes right (critiqued), Utilitarianism (critiqued), Naturalism (explored), Transhumanism (explored).

47517.heading: Steins;Gate
47517.label: From summaries
47517.life_message: Every choice changes the world for someone: a person must take responsibility for the power he uses, and real love pays a heavy price, and refuses to give up, to protect the people entrusted to him.
47517.dominant: Existentialism, Utilitarianism (explored and rejected), Communitarianism, Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued).

delivery.evidence: The moral emerges from cause and effect rather than speeches; Udon's vol. 3 description says repairing the timeline will require sacrifices; the game's makers aimed for hard-science plausibility (Wikipedia).
delivery.note: The message is carried by the puzzle of the timelines and by Okabe's choices; even the villains' motives (jealousy, control) are shown rather than argued.

personified.ideology: Self-made rebel persona giving way to responsible love
Control of technology and the future

106232.heading: Still Sick
106232.label: From summaries
106232.life_message: Being honest about who you are and what you love, and believing in someone else's gift, can heal old wounds and open the way to love.

delivery.evidence: Okazu and WWAC describe a character-driven romance; no lectures are reported. The only hostile view (childhood bullying) appears in backstory.
delivery.note: Acceptance is carried by the two women's relationship and by Makoto's fear and relief, not argued.

personified.ideology: Living openly with what you love

106232.dominant: Expressive individualism, Progressivism (queer acceptance), Secular humanism.

30045.heading: Strawberry 100%
30045.label: From summaries
30045.life_message: Growing up means following your dream and finally being honest about whom you love; indecision hurts everyone, and a first love can shape you even when it does not last.

content.framing: Mixed: fan service and desire played as comedy; commitment and honesty rewarded at the end

delivery.evidence: No lecturing reported; the moral lands at the end, when Junpei names his own immaturity and Yui scolds him for hurting both girls (vol. 19).
delivery.note: Romantic comedy first; the message about honesty and dreams is carried by consequences in the last volumes rather than speeches.

30045.dominant: Expressive individualism (dreams pursued), Hedonism (desire as comedy), Communitarianism (the film club).

37378.heading: Strobe Edge
37378.label: From summaries
37378.life_message: First love asks for honesty and courage: be true to what you feel instead of hiding it out of pity or fear, keep faith with the people you care about, and treat other people's hearts gently even when love is not returned.

content.framing: Neutral (chaste romance; a stolen kiss shown as hurtful)

delivery.evidence: Rivals and exes (Mayuka, Ando, Mao) are given sympathetic reasons (Wikipedia; ANN vol. 10).
delivery.note: Lessons about honesty and rejection come through inner monologue and small moments, not speeches.

37378.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (honesty and restraint), Expressive individualism (follow your heart), Duty ethics (keeping a promise).

138847.heading: Studio Cabana
138847.label: From summaries
138847.life_message: Honest, steady care can reach someone who has been hurt and is hiding, and love that treats a person as a whole human being is worth more than a relationship built on looks or on the body alone.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (a body-only relationship presented as empty and unhealthy)

delivery.evidence: The critique of unhealthy relationships is carried by character and backstory (MyAnimeList reviewers; Julsa), not stated as a lesson.
delivery.note: A shoujo drama: the message comes through Yukari's choices and Yusuke's pain.

personified.ideology: Hiding hurt behind a delinquent image

138847.dominant: Expressive individualism (music and being seen), Classical virtue ethics (Yukari's honesty), Hedonism (critiqued: a body-only relationship).

41434.heading: Suicide Island
41434.label: From summaries
41434.life_message: Even people who have tried to die can choose life again: meaning grows from hard work with your own hands, from caring for others and letting them care for you, and from passing life on to the next generation, while despair, domination and the voice that says death is a relief all destroy.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; the story concludes suicide is wrong

delivery.evidence: The choice to live is made in the plot from the first chapter, and Sei states his conclusion near the end; Kai's nihilism is given a voice and an explanation, Sawada less so (Japanese Wikipedia).
delivery.note: The message is carried by survival work and relationships; Mori said he wanted it to be entertaining as well as helpful (Da Vinci News).

personified.ideology: If we cannot die, we must learn to live
Humans have no worth; dying is a relief

41434.dominant: Existentialism (choosing to live), Communitarianism, Nihilism (critiqued in Kai), Might makes right (critiqued in Sawada).

102989.heading: Summertime Rendering
102989.label: From summaries
102989.life_message: Grief and fear can be faced with a clear head and loyal friends; love and sacrifice, not a hidden god, are what save the people you care about, and the dead you lost may be restored.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (deaths undone by the loops)
Shown with consequences (as a desperate tactic)

delivery.evidence: Themes carried by the mystery and the loops; ANN (vol. 3) notes the Shadows' motives stay unclear, so the villains are mainly monsters.
delivery.note: No speeches; love and sacrifice are shown through choices in each loop.

personified.ideology: Think clearly; never give up on anyone
Destroy the world with the god's power
Reason and justice for the dead

102989.dominant: Pagan/occult (a worshipped god exposed, critiqued), Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Existentialism.

53571.heading: Sunny
53571.label: From summaries
53571.life_message: Children who have been left behind still deserve wonder, belonging and adults who stay; imagination and friendship help them bear it, but cannot replace a family.

delivery.evidence: Rebecca Silverman notes the story shows rather than tells (Sei imagining driving home); AnimeClick praises its restraint and lack of melodrama.
delivery.note: Vignettes carry the feeling without lessons; the reader is left to draw conclusions.

personified.ideology: Defiance as a shield for longing

53571.dominant: Communitarianism (the home as found family), Existentialism, Secular humanism.

123747.heading: Survival in Another World with My Mistress!
123747.label: From summaries
123747.life_message: Practical skill and hard work earn an outsider a place, love and influence among refugees fighting a racist empire; the story offers this as a wish-fulfilment fantasy in which several women share one man, with ownership and submission played as romance.

delivery.evidence: The Holy Kingdom and its church are drawn as racists with no sympathetic voice except the reformers who agree with the heroes (TV Tropes).
delivery.note: A power fantasy: little argument, much wish-fulfilment.

personified.ideology: Hard work and skill; enjoys submission
Duty to her people; possessive love

30430.heading: Suzuka
30430.label: From summaries
30430.life_message: Love takes honesty, patience and persistence, and growing up means taking responsibility for the people you love and the choices you make together.

content.framing: Mixed: pressure condemned; premarital sex accepted, with consequences faced

delivery.evidence: The last volume lets both choices (abortion and university, or the child and work) be argued by the couple and their families before they decide (Wikipedia, characters).
delivery.note: Romance and sport carry the themes; the story rarely lectures.

30430.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (perseverance), Traditionalism (the ending), Expressive individualism.

105332.heading: Sweat and Soap
105332.label: From summaries
105332.life_message: Your body is nothing to be ashamed of: the right person loves you as you are, and love lasts when two people talk honestly through each step toward a shared life.

content.framing: Endorsed (loving adult couple); groping by a stranger condemned

delivery.evidence: No lectures; each volume poses a relationship problem (secrecy, jealousy, moving in, meeting parents) and resolves it through conversation; the rival and the protective family are shown fairly.
delivery.note: The message is carried by everyday scenes rather than statements; the bully is the only character drawn without sympathy.

105332.dominant: Pragmatism (communication solves problems), Traditionalism (marriage and family as the goal), Expressive individualism (self-acceptance).

31363.heading: Sweet Blue Flowers
31363.label: From summaries
31363.life_message: Love is truest between equals who are honest with each other; being true to whom you love, and giving the people you love time to understand themselves, matters more than fitting what family or society expects.

content.framing: Endorsed (same-sex romance); the cousin's relationship with a young Fumi shown as painful and regretted, not named as abuse

delivery.evidence: Characters with traditional expectations (Kyōko's mother, Chizu's family) are drawn with sympathy; Friedman finds no melodrama or parody.
delivery.note: The message comes through small scenes and inner monologue; ANN (via Wikipedia) found the plot so calm it is easy to gloss over.

personified.ideology: Friendship first; love in its own time
Conformity to marriage and family expectation

86044.heading: Sweetness and Lightning
86044.label: From summaries
86044.life_message: Cooking and eating together at a shared table heals grief, and a parent's patient attention turns lonely people into a family.

content.framing: Restrained: a student's feelings for her teacher, not acted on while she is his student; an adult relationship implied after a time skip
Shown with consequences; handled with care
Shown with consequences; adult supervision modeled

delivery.evidence: No reviewer calls it preachy; Creamer (ANN) describes a gentle episodic formula without major conflict; family lessons are tied to each recipe.
delivery.note: The message is carried by meals and small domestic scenes; there are no antagonists whose views are set against it.

86044.dominant: Communitarianism, Traditionalism, Classical virtue ethics, Confucian ethics.

82277.heading: Sword Art Online Progressive
82277.label: From summaries
82277.life_message: Even trapped in a deadly world, you can choose to live and not just survive, and you grow strongest by learning to trust and work with others.

content.framing: Neutral (game combat); real deaths taken seriously

delivery.evidence: Asuna's change is shown through events; ANN praises how her work ethic and Kirito's influence make her growth believable.
delivery.note: A coming-of-age message told through game mechanics and partnership rather than speeches.

82277.dominant: Transhumanism (virtual worlds and AI personhood), Existentialism (choosing to live in a trap), Communitarianism (parties and guilds).

106890.heading: Tadokoro-san
106890.label: From summaries
106890.life_message: Being truly seen and loved, for what you make and who you are, heals the hurt of being mocked; the story celebrates the two girls' love, including its physical side.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; healed by love and friendship

delivery.evidence: Short episodic chapters of romance and comedy; the message lives in the couple's growing adoration (AniList review).
delivery.note: Opponents are bullies, mostly male and crude (AniList review); no serious objection to the relationship is voiced in sources opened.

106890.dominant: Expressive individualism (being loved for who you are), Hedonism (desire celebrated), Progressivism (same-sex romance as ordinary).

96754.heading: Taisho Girl Fairy Tale
96754.label: From summaries
96754.life_message: A person's worth does not depend on being useful: patient, cheerful love and a caring community can heal someone the world has written off, and a family built on kindness is better than one built on money and pride.

content.framing: Endorsed as chaste, devoted love; fan service mostly neutral

delivery.evidence: Moore (ANN): kindness resolves problems neatly and Yuzuki lacks interiority; the father and Tamayo are given little sympathy, while Tamao and Tamako are redeemed (Wikipedia).
delivery.note: The message comes through Yuzuki's example and Tamahiko's narration of his change rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: family honor and money over a disabled son

96754.dominant: Communitarianism (healing community), Traditionalism (Taisho family order, explored), Classical virtue ethics, Expressive individualism (leaving the family house).

86734.heading: Takane & Hana
86734.label: From summaries
86734.life_message: Real love sees past money, looks and pride: two stubborn people grow up by learning to be honest with each other, and the one who seems more powerful has as much to learn as the one who seems weaker.

content.framing: Mixed: the romance is endorsed and ends in marriage; the age gap is acknowledged as a problem by the characters
Mixed: Takane's arrogance mocked; the courtship endorsed

delivery.evidence: The romance and its problems (age, class, power) are raised by the characters themselves (ANN); the money-cannot-buy-love theme is played through gags rather than speeches.
delivery.note: The values ride on comedy and character growth; the story never lectures, which some critics read as too light a touch on the age gap.

86734.dominant: Consumerism (critiqued), Classical virtue ethics (pride to humility), Traditionalism (arranged marriage), Expressive individualism.

45306.heading: Takemitsu Zamurai
45306.label: From summaries
45306.life_message: A man can choose, day after day, to lay down the violence in him, and ordinary neighbors, children and small pleasures help him do it; but a sword not truly given up keeps calling, and peace may cost the life he built.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (the creators deliberately limit killing so it carries weight)
Neutral (part of Edo street life; nothing explicit documented)

delivery.evidence: The creators deliberately avoided glorifying death and made the hero a psychologically complex man rather than a conventional hero (Wikipedia; du9); the killer and the plotter are given motives (poverty, a domain's survival).
delivery.note: The message is shown through daily life, the bamboo sword and the sword-ghost's pull, not stated; the ending is quiet and open.

personified.ideology: restraint over the love of combat
the sword as identity and trade
the pull of the sword itself

45306.dominant: Bushido / honor code (explored and questioned), Pacifism / nonviolence (the bamboo sword), Communitarianism (the tenement), Buddhist ideas (attachment and letting go).

99536.heading: Talentless Nana
99536.label: From summaries
99536.life_message: A person trained to see others as monsters can still choose to see them as people and to make amends; the real danger is those who manufacture fear of a group and use children to act on it.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; the early killings are framed as suspense
Shown with consequences (late); clever in the early arcs

delivery.evidence: ANN anime review (eps 1-3, Steve Jones) finds information delivered unobtrusively but calls the officials almost cartoonishly evil; the fan wiki describes Tsuruoka as proudly evil.
delivery.note: The questioning of state-ordered killing comes through Nana's missions, doubts and confession; the people who order the killings are drawn as plain villains, so the government's case is never given a fair hearing.

personified.ideology: The state's claim that the Talented are enemies of humanity, later rejected
Manipulation and killing for power, dressed as protecting humanity

99536.dominant: Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Utilitarianism (critiqued kill-count logic), Liberalism (rights of a persecuted group).

85310.heading: Tales of Wedding Rings
85310.label: From summaries
85310.life_message: True love means staying faithful, honest and brave for the people who depend on you; power, even heroic power, corrupts unless it is shared in trust and finally given up.

content.framing: Endorsed (sex within plural royal marriage); coercion questioned

delivery.evidence: The warnings about power (the first Ring King, the Emperor's realism) are given their due; the case for plural marriage is assumed by the plot rather than argued.
delivery.note: Its view of faithful love and of power is carried by plot turns (the Spire, the library, the final battle) rather than speeches.

85310.dominant: Hedonism within marriage, Might makes right (critiqued: power corrupts), Classical virtue ethics (courage, fidelity, mercy), Traditionalism (royal marriage and duty).

140495.heading: Tamon's B-Side
140495.label: From summaries
140495.life_message: The real person behind any public image deserves care: loving someone means supporting who they actually are, not only the role they play, and being supported can help a struggling person grow.

content.framing: Played for comedy; family violence in backstory condemned
Neutral (an adult's hidden vices, played for comedy)
Shown with care, often through comedy
Mixed: obsessive fandom and possessiveness played as comedy and romance

delivery.evidence: Every member's gap between image and self is explained with a sympathetic backstory (Keito's family, Ouri's parents, Natsuki's guilt), so the "money-minded" and "arrogant" positions are given real reasons.
delivery.note: The message rides on gag comedy (mushrooms, broken glasses, dropped fans) and is rarely stated outright.

personified.ideology: Supporting the real person; a fan's code of distance

140495.dominant: Expressive individualism (the real self behind a persona), Consumerism (fandom and the idol industry, explored), Communitarianism (a band that becomes a family).

85898.heading: Tanaka-kun is Always Listless
85898.label: From summaries
85898.life_message: A slow, easygoing life lived among loyal friends has its own quiet worth, and being seen for who you really are matters more than keeping up an image.

delivery.evidence: Episodic 4-koma comedy; reviewers note the slow pace and a hero who is more thoughtful than he looks (ANN, ep. 1-5); no lectures.
delivery.note: Tanaka's philosophy is both admired and teased: his idleness causes small troubles (ep. 6, 8), but the story never asks him to change.

85898.dominant: Communitarianism (friendship), Classical virtue ethics (kindness and loyalty), Hedonism (the joy of rest), Expressive individualism (being seen as you are).

139855.heading: Tatsuki Fujimoto Before Chainsaw Man: 17-21
139855.label: From summaries
139855.life_message: Wholehearted devotion, to a dream, a teacher, a confession or one lonely person, is the best answer to sudden violence and despair, even when it cannot save the world.

content.framing: Mixed: alien slaughter and the hostage-taking condemned; Shikaku's killing played as black comedy
Mixed: the sexual demand condemned; teen and vampire romances sympathetic
Shown with consequences; despair turned toward life

delivery.evidence: The stories carry their meaning through absurd escalation and sudden violence; Real Sound reads repeated patterns (a weak, resentful young man; a disaster-like intruder) rather than stated morals.
delivery.note: Fujimoto states no moral; "Sasaki" comes closest, with its speech about believing in the impossible (ANN anime review).

141157.heading: Tatsuki Fujimoto Before Chainsaw Man: 22-26
141157.label: From summaries
141157.life_message: Love means staying close to people the world fears or mocks, a mermaid, a changed friend, a "monster" sister, a rival sibling, and facing your own fear and envy instead of turning away.

content.framing: Mixed: nudity framed as art and humiliation; sexual pressure in "Woke-Up" passes without judgment

delivery.evidence: The stories carry their meaning through plot and image; Real Sound's critic finds the same structure repeated (one who accepts versus a society that fears) without stated morals.
delivery.note: Fujimoto rarely explains; two endings are left open, and some troubling moments (Rie's pressure) pass without comment.

141157.dominant: Existentialism, Expressive individualism, Progressivism (gender identity), Absurdism.

31709.heading: Tegami Bachi
31709.label: From summaries
31709.life_message: Every person's heart, their memories and love, is worth carrying through any darkness; a world that feeds on people's hearts must be changed, and the way to light is to give your own heart for others.

content.framing: Neutral (monster battles); cruelty by the state condemned

delivery.evidence: ANN (vol. 14) faults dialogue that keeps returning to heart and protecting others; the government and Reverse are both shown with faults (TV Tropes).
delivery.note: The message is carried by deliveries and memory flashbacks rather than lectures, though the later volumes state the theme of heart often.

personified.ideology: Every heart can be saved; no one should be sacrificed
Destroy the artificial sun by stealing hearts
Revolution against a government that experimented on him

31709.dominant: Communitarianism, Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Duty ethics, Classical virtue ethics.

30442.heading: Tekkonkinkreet: Black & White
30442.label: From summaries
30442.life_message: No one is whole alone: tough Black and innocent White each hold what the other lacks, and love, not violence, keeps a person, and a place, from falling apart.

content.framing: Shown with consequences: violence ruins Kimura and nearly destroys Black
Mixed: shown as survival, with costs

delivery.evidence: The message is carried by images and by the boys' relationship, not speeches; Arias says the manga asks questions rather than answering them. Snake is a near-faceless villain, but Suzuki and Kimura are drawn with sympathy.
delivery.note: The film is more explicit about "purity" and innocence (THEM calls it moralizing); the manga leaves more open.

personified.ideology: Old yakuza honor and love of place
Violence and despair as Black's inner darkness

30442.dominant: Existentialism, Taoist ideas (yin-yang balance), Communitarianism; Might makes right critiqued.

30073.heading: Tenjo Tenge
30073.label: From summaries
30073.life_message: Strength is worth having only when it serves something beyond itself, such as protecting the people you love and breaking cycles of hatred handed down by your elders; strength sought for its own sake destroys the one who seeks it.

content.framing: Endorsed as spectacle; cruelty and torture condemned
Mixed: fan service and sex endorsed as appeal; sexual violence condemned within the story but drawn in a way a critic calls exploitative

delivery.evidence: Characters regularly stop fights to debate the meaning of strength (Wikipedia, Reception); villains such as Ryuuzaki are drawn without depth, while Mitsuomi and Dōgen get reasons.
delivery.note: The message is spoken aloud in long exchanges between fights; Santos (ANN) finds the dialogue heavy and the pacing awkward.

personified.ideology: Strength for the people you love
Power to end the cycle, whatever it costs

30073.dominant: Might makes right (explored and finally questioned), Hedonism, Pagan/occult, Bushido / honor code, Taoist ideas (ki cultivation and immortality).

137158.heading: Tenkaichi: The Greatest Warrior Under the Rising Sun
137158.label: From summaries
137158.life_message: Under a tyrant who turns succession into a blood sport, strength is tested to the death, but the story honors most those who fight for someone or something beyond themselves.

content.framing: Mixed: duels to the death shown as glorious; the tyrant's and Yagyu's cruelty shown as cruelty

delivery.evidence: Values are shown in how fighters die and what they fight for (Honda, Kamiizumi); the one character who objects to the tournament is killed in ch. 1.
delivery.note: The story does not argue against the tournament; it lets the tyrant's madness and the fighters' nobility speak.

personified.ideology: power as entertainment; might as right
loyalty to one's lord unto death

137158.dominant: Bushido / honor code (explored), Strength rules (explored), Authoritarianism (critiqued).

109122.heading: TenPuru -No One Can Live on Loneliness-
109122.label: From summaries
109122.life_message: No one can live alone: desire is part of being human, and what matters is honesty, self-control and caring for the people who become your family.

delivery.evidence: The motto is stated in the title and dramatized in ep. 12; monastic renunciation is given a hearing through Yuzuki and Kiki, but mostly as a setup for jokes.
delivery.note: Its view that desire is human and that people need each other is carried by comedy and a few sincere episodes rather than by argument.

personified.ideology: Womanizing; no one can live alone, as an excuse

109122.dominant: Hedonism (desire as human, played for comedy), Buddhist ideas (temple setting and renunciation, explored), Communitarianism (no one can live alone).

41366.heading: Teppu
41366.label: From summaries
41366.life_message: Talent without effort, and without other people, is empty; a worthy rival, hard training and honest struggle give life meaning, even when you lose.

content.framing: Neutral (sport); Natsuo's cruelty shown as a flaw

delivery.evidence: Natsuo's arrogance is shown with its costs and Yuzuko's tenacity with its rewards, without speeches; rivals such as Sanae are given their own pasts (Wikipedia; TV Tropes).
delivery.note: A sports drama that lets the fights carry the message.

personified.ideology: Talent and contempt seeking a worthy challenge

41366.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (affirmed), Existentialism (explored), Might makes right (critiqued).

67563.heading: Terra Formars
67563.label: From summaries
67563.life_message: In a universe where evolution rewards only strength, people prove what humanity is worth by loyalty and self-sacrifice for their comrades, while the powerful who treat people as tools are the real danger.

content.framing: Mixed: killing Terraformars celebrated as heroic; betrayal and human experiments condemned

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)
content.framing: Mixed: sexual abuse and forced breeding condemned; some fan service played straight
Neutral (the drug is the power source); overdoses fatal

delivery.evidence: The refrain "Don't underestimate humanity" and Bible verses at last stands state the theme (TV Tropes); villains such as Victoria and Joseph receive backstories (poverty and genital cutting; a loveless contract birth) that explain without excusing (fan wiki).
delivery.note: The message is carried by battles and deaths rather than speeches; national politics are shown through cut-aways to Earth (vol. 7 synopsis).

personified.ideology: Eugenic elitism; love is an illusion

67563.dominant: Transhumanism (explored), Naturalism, Patriotism / nationalism (explored), Might makes right (explored), Communitarianism.

110393.heading: That's My Atypical Girl
110393.label: From summaries
110393.life_message: Two people who find life painful can keep living one day at a time by holding on to each other; being understood, and learning to understand, is what makes a place to belong.

content.framing: Abuse condemned; Saito's outbursts shown as symptoms

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)

delivery.evidence: Much of the story is explained through dialogue: one MyAnimeList reviewer says the characters become mouthpieces and the later chapters grow preachy; another notes the author's afterwords explain his approach. ANN notes the condition itself is never named in vol. 1; it is shown through behavior and others' reactions.
delivery.note: The message about acceptance and mutual support is stated often by the leads, set against realistic setbacks rather than easy fixes.

personified.ideology: A different way of perceiving, seeking a place to belong
A loner who learns to care for and understand another
Abuse and control in the family

110393.dominant: Secular humanism (human care as the way through), Existentialism, Communitarianism, Progressivism (disability inclusion).

85632.heading: That Wolf-Boy Is Mine!
85632.label: From summaries
85632.life_message: Trust grows when you keep someone's secret and accept them as they are, and the fear of being left can be overcome by choosing to love anyway.

content.framing: Mixed: memory erasure shown as hurtful and undone

delivery.evidence: Themes of trust and acceptance come through the romance; reviewers note the story favors heart over melodrama (ANN, vol. 4).
delivery.note: A light romance; its message about trust and accepting others is never stated as a lesson in sources opened.

personified.ideology: Keep faith with others; be yourself
Fear of being left; learning to love

85632.dominant: Communitarianism (belonging and trust), Expressive individualism (accepted as you are), Pagan/occult (folklore spirits, explored).

85435.heading: The Ancient Magus' Bride
85435.label: From summaries
85435.life_message: Even a person everyone has thrown away has worth; healing comes from being cared for and learning to care for yourself, and love has to be learned, by people and monsters alike.

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)
content.framing: Mixed: the purchase and power imbalance questioned inside the story; romance tender, not sexual

delivery.evidence: Characters inside the story (Angelica, Renfred, Alice, Titania) challenge Elias's purchase and his control; villains like Cartaphilus are given sympathetic motives (fan wiki; AniFem).
delivery.note: The message of worth and healing is shown through Chise's choices and the care she receives, not lectured; Elias's flaws are named by other characters.

personified.ideology: Ending one's own suffering at others' cost
Suspicion of magi; protection of the young

85435.dominant: Pagan/occult (folk magic and fae, affirmed), Communitarianism (found family), Classical virtue ethics (compassion), Christian (church and legend, explored).

126722.heading: The Anemone Feels the Heat
126722.label: From summaries
126722.life_message: Choosing warmth over resentment can turn a loss into love: kindness given and returned helps two girls grow, take care of themselves and build a life together.

delivery.evidence: The romance is shown as natural and good without argument (Okazu; AniList); no character opposes same-sex love in sources opened.
delivery.note: A gentle school romance; the message of kindness over resentment is stated in Nagisa's resolve, the romance is simply assumed.

personified.ideology: Choosing to like instead of resent
Experienced romantic advice; love that cannot be returned

126722.dominant: Expressive individualism, Progressivism (same-sex love as normal), Classical virtue ethics (kindness over resentment).

122337.heading: The Angel Next Door Spoils Me Rotten
122337.label: From summaries
122337.life_message: Small, steady acts of care, given without strings and received with gratitude, can heal loneliness and old hurts and let two guarded people show their true selves and grow into love.

delivery.evidence: No antagonist argues another view; the message is carried by meals, small favors and the slow reveal of the leads' pasts (Penguin Random House synopses).
delivery.note: Care healing loneliness is shown in daily acts, never stated as a lesson.

personified.ideology: Care freely given; the true self behind a public mask
Reserve and self-doubt learning to give back

122337.dominant: Communitarianism (found family), Classical virtue ethics (gratitude and care), Expressive individualism (the true self behind the "angel").

171024.heading: The Babe at My Back Has Her Eye on Me. I'm Done For.
171024.label: From summaries
171024.life_message: Simple kindness given with no agenda can open a lonely life, and love grows when two people look past labels like "loner" and "popular girl" to who the other really is.

content.framing: Endorsed (romance); fan service treated as comedy

delivery.evidence: A sweet romantic comedy; the kindness theme is shown in the first chapter and not argued.
delivery.note: Little that could be called a message is stated; the story is about the relationship.

171024.dominant: Romance and kindness; Expressive individualism (looking past labels).

128319.heading: The Barbarian’s Bride
128319.label: From summaries
128319.life_message: Prejudice falls away when you live among the people you were taught to fear; honest strength, respect and patient love can turn enemies into family, and duty and happiness need not be opposites.

content.framing: Mixed: nudity matter-of-fact and comic; consent handled partly

delivery.evidence: Serafina states her change of heart aloud (anime ep. 4); the Western view is voiced by Malcius and the king, the first given sympathy and a second chance, the second drawn as unhinged (anime eps. 5-7, 12).
delivery.note: The anti-prejudice message is carried by culture-shock comedy and by Serafina's own admissions rather than by lectures.

personified.ideology: Knightly duty; the West's view of the East
Fanatical devotion to the Western church
Pragmatic freedom from codes and churches

128319.dominant: Communitarianism (the tribes as family), Pagan/occult (the land's will and its rites), Environmentalism (magic that drains the land), with Bushido / honor code, Duty ethics and Patriotism explored and softened.

87220.heading: The Black Healer
87220.label: From summaries
87220.life_message: Knowledge used with compassion makes a person valuable wherever they are; a healer earns trust and a place to belong by caring for others.

delivery.evidence: Reader comments note long explanations of the world's lore; villains are mostly flat (MangaUpdates comments).
delivery.note: The value of knowledge and care is shown through healing scenes, not stated as a moral.

87220.dominant: Pragmatism, Classical virtue ethics (compassion), Pagan/occult (fantasy magic).

153007.heading: The Bugle Call: Song of War
153007.label: From summaries
153007.life_message: Even a child pulled into war can keep his conscience and his dream; power that uses people, however kindly it speaks, must be questioned, and comrades must be treated as people, not weapons.

delivery.evidence: Luca's confrontations with the Pontiff carry the critique (fan wiki); Walt's Comic Shop notes an abrupt shift from war drama to mystical fantasy; the Pontiff is drawn as polite and reasonable, not a cartoon (fan wiki, Personality).
delivery.note: The message lives in Luca's choices and the revelations about the Pontiff rather than speeches; enemies like the Doppelganger and the Garland are given sympathetic sides.

personified.ideology: Faith and kindness used to exploit child soldiers
Devotion to a ruler who gave him a miracle

129694.heading: The Café Terrace and Its Goddesses
129694.label: From summaries
129694.life_message: Family is the people who keep faith with one another: honoring the grandmother who raised you means keeping her home and her people together, and a found family is worth more than a planned career.

delivery.evidence: The family message comes through each woman's arc and Hayato's regret; ANN's Dupree found the family drama clashing with the fan service.
delivery.note: The found-family message is carried by events and character arcs; there is no argument against it, and the fan service runs alongside without comment.

personified.ideology: Following your own dream against family expectations

146181.heading: The Classroom of a Black Cat and a Witch
146181.label: From summaries
146181.life_message: Effort, imagination and friends can carry someone with little talent past the prodigies, and a teacher who believes in misfits can turn them into a team.

delivery.evidence: The underdog message is stated through Claude's lessons and Spica's victories (e.g. Claude says she won because past failures taught her to manage her magic; anime ep. 23 summary). Rivals like Aria and Chiron are given their own reasons and redeemed.
delivery.note: A school-battle comedy whose lessons about effort and teamwork come through events and a few mentor speeches.

personified.ideology: A teacher who believes in misfits
A cult that claims divine choice

146181.dominant: Communitarianism (the misfit class as found family), Expressive individualism (following your own dream), Pagan/occult (witches and zodiac magic as setting).

37375.heading: The Climber
37375.label: From summaries
37375.life_message: A life is worth living when you give all your strength to something, but no one can live entirely alone. The rope that ties climbers together, and in the end a family, is what brings a person back down the mountain.

delivery.evidence: Aftermath: the art "illustrates its point far more effectively than dialogue"; Animechu notes long stretches with little dialogue. No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The message comes through visual metaphor, interior monologue and consequences rather than speeches.

37375.dominant: Existentialism, Expressive individualism (critiqued), Stoicism, Classical virtue ethics.

145531.heading: The Color of the End: Mission in the Apocalypse
145531.label: From summaries
145531.life_message: Even after the end of the world, keeping faith with your task, caring for what others left behind and mourning the dead give a life meaning, and finding even one other person is worth the long search.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers describe an episodic structure in which each robot's story carries the theme without comment (Goodreads; MyAnimeList); James Nicoll calls vol. 1 skillfully executed and familiar.
delivery.note: The message is shown through encounters and silences, not stated.

personified.ideology: Faithful to a mission; searching for others

145531.dominant: Existentialism (meaning after the end), Transhumanism (an engineered heroine and faithful machines), Duty ethics (orders and promises kept for the dead).

117675.heading: The Coppersmith's Bride
117675.label: From summaries
117675.life_message: Love grows through patient work and honest words, and a family craft lives on when the young learn it, respect it and make it their own.

delivery.evidence: Values come through daily scenes and craft work; the OASG review and the MAL user review describe a slice-of-life story without a lesson-driven plot; educational info pages are set apart from the story (Wikipedia).
delivery.note: A gentle romance with craft education; no antagonist voices a rival worldview in sources opened.

personified.ideology: Love that learns and adapts while staying itself
The family name and its standards
Claiming a tradition as a new heir

117675.dominant: Traditionalism (a family craft carried forward), Communitarianism and Classical virtue ethics (skill and character built by practice).

137614.heading: The Credits Roll into the Sea
137614.label: From summaries
137614.life_message: Discovering what you are meant to make, and making it with others, gives life new direction at any age; grief, doubt and illness are part of the voyage, not the end of it.

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)

delivery.evidence: The message comes through Umiko's projects and setbacks, not speeches; Sora, the voice of doubt, is drawn as perceptive and given his own arc; the creator says she avoids defining Kai from outside.
delivery.note: Kai states the opening challenge directly (ch. 1), but later volumes show rather than tell, through critiques, failures and festivals.

personified.ideology: A calling can be found late; observation is a gift
Make what you must; ignore the norms
Ambition and blunt critique; fame as a tool

137614.dominant: Existentialism, Expressive individualism, Secular humanism; Communitarianism (the film crew) and a quiet Feminism (an older woman claiming her calling).

56144.heading: The Daily Lives of High School Boys
56144.label: From summaries
56144.life_message: Being young and foolish with good friends is worth treasuring; the boys' overblown dramas are part of growing up, and the story laughs with them more than at them.

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)
content.framing: Played for embarrassment; peeking framed as guilty

delivery.evidence: Episodic gag sketches with no stated lesson (MangaUpdates Episodic; reviews).
delivery.note: Any message, that friendship and foolishness are part of growing up, comes only from the tone.

111764.heading: The Daughter of the Demon Lord Is Too Kind!
111764.label: From summaries
111764.life_message: Kindness is stronger than fear: a gentle heart can soften the cruelest people around it, and those who love a child should support who she truly is.

delivery.evidence: Each chapter repeats one joke: a cruel plan becomes an act of kindness. Jahi states the lesson outright at the end (ep. 12); the case for cruelty is only ever played for laughs.
delivery.note: The message is obvious and repeated, carried by gentle comedy rather than lectures.

personified.ideology: Duty to demon tradition and discipline
Power and conquest, softened by love

111764.dominant: Pacifism / nonviolence (kindness disarms every foe), Communitarianism (family and friends), Might makes right (critiqued).

103203.heading: The Death Mage
103203.label: From summaries
103203.life_message: An outcast wronged in three lives can build a home and a people of his own by his own power, protecting those the powerful call monsters and repaying cruelty in full.

content.framing: Endorsed when aimed at persecutors; cruelty by others condemned
Mixed: sexual violence condemned; fan service played straight

delivery.evidence: Persecutors are drawn as fanatics and sadists (Gordan, the researchers, the vampire lords who enjoy breaking people, ch. 34); Heinz is the main exception, shown as a would-be hero who did wrong.
delivery.note: The story tells the reader whom to hate through its opening atrocities, then lets the revenge play as payoff.

personified.ideology: A god's order without care for persons

103203.dominant: Pagan/occult (necromancy and rival gods), Communitarianism (found family and refuge), Might makes right, Patriotism / nationalism (founding a refuge nation).

147468.heading: The Delinquent and the Transfer Student
147468.label: From summaries
147468.life_message: Looking past a frightening reputation, and being gently honest about your feelings, opens the way to real affection.

delivery.evidence: No character argues against the romance in sources opened; the second-in-command's objection is about time, not the relationship (Okazu). Yattatachi notes there is no identity crisis.
delivery.note: The romance is shown as ordinary rather than argued for; comedy carries the story.

147468.dominant: Expressive individualism (being yourself in love), Progressivism (a same-sex romance treated as ordinary), Classical virtue ethics (kindness, loyalty).

180547.heading: The Delinquent Girl Beside Me Suddenly Dyed Her Hair Black
180547.label: From summaries
180547.life_message: People are more than their reputations: small, steady acts of care, and noticing the person beside you, build real affection.

delivery.evidence: A light romantic comedy with no ideological opponents; the stereotype of the delinquent is undercut through comedy (The Outerhaven).
delivery.note: No message is stated outright in sources opened.

personified.ideology: Effort in love; reputation versus true self

180547.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (kindness and effort), Communitarianism (sisters and club), Traditionalism (explored: the ideal of the poised, black-haired girl).

107462.heading: The Demon Girl Next Door
107462.label: From summaries
107462.life_message: Enemies by birth can choose friendship; kindness, honesty and stubborn effort count for more than power, and light and dark can share a town.
