delivery.evidence: Sumika states the plea not to judge (ANN, omni. 1); homophobic classmates and the smear campaign are minor, unsympathetic figures; family pressure is treated with more sympathy and eases (ANN; Okazu).
delivery.note: The message is mostly carried by the friendship and its slow change, with a few open statements about prejudice.

personified.ideology: Hide love to protect a friendship; then honesty
Open about liking girls, afraid of real love
Love between girls should be pure and hidden

101762.heading: Why Does Nobody Remember Me in This World?
101762.label: From summaries
101762.life_message: Hatred is the true enemy: the hero who accepts those everyone else rejects can end a war between peoples, even if the world never remembers what he did.

content.framing: Played for comedy and harem rivalry

101762.dominant: Patriotism / nationalism (critiqued as hatred between peoples), Might makes right (critiqued), Existentialism (identity when forgotten), Liberalism (a pact of coexistence).

delivery.evidence: ANN says Kai's lack of hatred for other races, unlike the war-scarred humans, makes him the peacemaker; supremacy is voiced by Alfreya and shown as madness (ep. 6-8).
delivery.note: The anti-hatred message is stated near the end (the world was reset because of hatred, ep. 8; Last Riser as hatred embodied, ep. 11) but mostly carried by action and alliances.

personified.ideology: Acceptance of all races; loyalty to truth
Hatred of a world that rejected her kind

167022.heading: Wild Strawberry
167022.label: From summaries
167022.life_message: Family is the people you refuse to abandon: a boy keeps faith with the sister he grew up with even when the system says she must be burned, and mercy for the infected is shown as right.
167022.dominant: Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Critical theory (class access to the vaccine), Communitarianism.

delivery.evidence: The class critique is built into the setting (VIZ series blurb) rather than argued in speeches; the Force has sympathetic members (the 7th Squad, Akira) beside its harsh rules. No reviewer calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The message lives in the premise and in Kingo's choices; the state is both villain and the place where his allies are.

personified.ideology: Burn the infected and those who shelter them
Reform from within; no needless deaths

98671.heading: Will It Be the World or Her?
98671.label: From summaries
98671.life_message: You should not have to trade the person you love for the world, or the world for her: the story rewards refusing that false choice, and its god-girl learns that love means giving herself so the people she loves can live.

content.framing: Mixed: slapstick played for comedy; the organization's violence condemned
Played for comedy; the hero mostly resists; later reframed as real feelings
Shown with sympathy; healed through love

delivery.evidence: The dilemma is put to the reader directly (the title; ch. 40 is titled "The Ultimate Choice") and, per a reviewer, the whole school is asked to make Kouki's choice and none can (MyAnimeList); the organization's case for taking Ayumi's power is given voice through Aiko (ch. 29, 33) but loses.
delivery.note: The message is carried by comedy for most of the run and by melodrama at the end; there are no lectures in sources opened.

personified.ideology: Refuse to choose between love and the world
Protect the world by any means; later, self-giving love
Take Ayumi's power for the world's sake

98671.dominant: Utilitarianism (critiqued), Duty ethics (deontology), Expressive individualism; a love story about refusing a false choice.

135083.heading: WIND BREAKER
135083.label: From summaries
135083.life_message: Strength is for protecting others, not for standing above them: a loner becomes stronger when he lets a community accept him and fights for the people who need him.

content.framing: Mixed: fighting to protect the town endorsed; fighting to dominate condemned

delivery.evidence: Bofurin's creed is stated by Kotoha (ch. 1), Umemiya and the recited motto (fan wiki); Natori is drawn as a sadist with no sympathetic side, while Shishitoren, GRAVEL and Noroshi get backstories (fan wiki).
delivery.note: The message is spoken openly by mentors and acted out in fights; Nii says the aim is entertainment with "cool" characters (K MANGA interview).

personified.ideology: Protect the town; fights as conversation

135083.dominant: Communitarianism (protect the town), Classical virtue ethics (Tsugeura's question about virtues; Sakura's growth), Might makes right (critiqued in KEEL and Noroshi), and an honor code of fair fights and loyalty.

125116.heading: Wistoria: Wand and Sword
125116.label: From summaries
125116.life_message: Keeping your word through relentless effort can overcome a world that says you lack the gift; worth is not set by talent, and those who look down on others are proved wrong.

delivery.evidence: ANN 2024 critics call the bullies' hostility excessive and cartoonish and compare Edward to Snape; the message is carried by Will's victories and the promise flashbacks rather than speeches.
delivery.note: The anti-elitism and perseverance themes come through plot (each test Will passes) and through repeated flashbacks to the childhood promise.

personified.ideology: Effort and fidelity over innate gifts
Magic supremacy; prejudice against non-mages and dwarves
Talent gives the right to sneer
Revenge on a society that scorned them

125116.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (courage and perseverance), Duty ethics (the promise), Critical theory (prejudice of a magical elite).

98263.heading: Witch Hat Atelier
98263.label: From summaries
98263.life_message: A good life uses one's skills carefully and creatively to help others. Power must come with responsibility, mistakes must be owned, and no one should be shut out of learning because of their birth or body.

delivery.evidence: CSM lists strong positive messages; the Brimmed Caps' case for free healing magic gets a real hearing through Custas and Ininia; Shirahama says readers should question what seems like common sense (ANN, 2024).
delivery.note: Themes come through character choices and the magic system rather than lectures; both sides of the Pact debate are given sympathetic voices.

personified.ideology: Knowledge for all, used carefully to help
Care for students mixed with secret revenge
Order through secrecy and memory erasure

98263.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (prudence and responsibility), Pragmatism (magic as craft), Critical theory (access and gatekeeping), Communitarianism, Progressivism.

128896.heading: WITCH WATCH
128896.label: From summaries
128896.life_message: Friends who protect and accept each other's strangeness become a family, and power is meant for helping others, not for revenge.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; fights defend others

delivery.evidence: The warlocks are given real grievances (a witch burned by inquisitors, ch. 255-256; Kokuryo's despair) and several are redeemed; the witches' oath to help people is stated early (ch. 1) and carried by plot.
delivery.note: Comedy chapters carry the found-family theme; battle arcs carry the case against revenge, with villains shown sympathetically before they are stopped.

personified.ideology: Revenge for persecution; love that will not let go

128896.dominant: Communitarianism (found family), Pagan/occult (witchcraft as a calling), with duty ethics and a rejection of revenge.

49896.heading: Witchcraft Works
49896.label: From summaries
49896.life_message: Devoted love that protects, and a kindness that will not give up on anyone, can redeem even a destroyer; a bond of mutual sacrifice is worth more than power.

content.framing: Mixed: fantasy battles endorsed; torture and bullying played as comedy; child abuse condemned
Neutral (comic fan service and teasing); romance endorsed

delivery.evidence: The moral comes through action: Honoka's mercy (Rinon), the KMM Gang taken in, Evermillion changed by kindness (Wikipedia). Villains get backstories and many become allies.
delivery.note: A comedy-action series that rarely lectures; its values show in how enemies are treated after they lose.

personified.ideology: Protect the one you love at any cost

49896.dominant: Pagan/occult (witches and a demon as a fantasy power system), Feminism (role reversal), Communitarianism (enemies taken into the household), Pacifism / nonviolence (mercy toward beaten foes).

199999.heading: WITCHRIV
199999.label: From summaries
199999.life_message: Hunting people for what they are is wrong, and the answer to it is to protect and free one another rather than to take revenge.

content.framing: State violence condemned; the heroes' violence shown as escape and defense
Framed as escape from unjust imprisonment

delivery.evidence: AniTrendz: the persecution theme is presented bluntly and the Bureau's hypocrisy makes it unequivocally villainous in ch. 1-2; later chapters add Belator, a Bureau veteran whose family a mage killed (fan wiki), and Da Vinci Web stresses that good intentions can cause tragedy.
delivery.note: The anti-persecution message is stated early through events and Nona's anger; later arcs appear to complicate the human side (to verify past ch. 4).

personified.ideology: Resistance to persecution without revenge; loyalty
Submission as survival, turning to resolve
Grief and fear of mages, later doubt

199999.dominant: Authoritarianism (critiqued), Liberalism (rights and consent), Critical theory (persecution of a minority).

148305.heading: Within the Villainess
148305.label: From summaries
148305.life_message: A person who was never loved can be remade by one person's kindness, and lies that destroy the innocent deserve to be exposed and repaid in full.

delivery.evidence: The revenge is carried by schemes and plot rather than speeches (Abrams; MyAnimeList reviews). Readers say the villain is given little depth (MyAnimeList; MangaUpdates).
delivery.note: Whether Rina is given any sympathetic motive could not be confirmed; reviews call her bratty to the end.

148305.dominant: Might makes right (explored), Utilitarianism (ends justify means), Communitarianism (found family), Pagan/occult (gods, souls and demons).

70761.heading: Wolf Children: Ame & Yuki
70761.label: From summaries
70761.life_message: Loving your children means giving everything to raise them and then letting them choose who they will be, even when that means letting them go.

delivery.evidence: Long wordless montages carry the story (Wrong Every Time); Hana states her promise to let the children choose (Plugged In). Yuki's and Ame's opposite choices are both treated with respect, and their fight over them is shown (Wikipedia).
delivery.note: The message is shown, not preached; the two children embody two fair answers to the same question.

58825.heading: Wolf Girl and Black Prince
58825.label: From summaries
58825.life_message: Real love grows when two flawed people stop pretending, learn to understand each other and change for each other's sake; a cold heart can be softened by steady, loyal affection.

content.framing: Mixed: a slap condemned; Kyoya's punches framed as protective
Endorsed (romance); teen sex treated as a natural step
Mixed: lying shown with consequences; controlling behavior softened and partly romanticized

delivery.evidence: The romance carries the message; Kasai and Kusakabe voice doubts about how Kyoya treats Erika, and the story answers them through his growth rather than dismissing them (Wikipedia).
delivery.note: There are no lectures; the story sides with the couple but lets critics inside the story speak.

personified.ideology: Devotion and the wish to belong

58825.dominant: Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Expressive individualism, Traditionalism.

101072.heading: Wonder Cat Kyuu-chan
101072.label: From summaries
101072.life_message: Taking in someone who was abandoned and caring for each other day by day makes an ordinary life warm, and that love can give you the courage to follow your heart.

delivery.evidence: Seven Seas blurbs describe gags and daily moments; the only stated lesson, following your heart, comes in the final volume (v8).
delivery.note: Values are shown by small acts of care rather than stated.

101072.dominant: Communitarianism (found family), Expressive individualism (follow your heart, v8).

130965.heading: Working for God in a Godless World
130965.label: From summaries
130965.life_message: Belief gives real power to whoever gathers it, so what matters is how it is used; manipulating people the way Yukito's father did turns Yukito into his father, and people caring for each other may matter more than any god.

content.framing: Neutral (action and dark comedy); state killings condemned
Played as comedy; sexual assault rarely condemned
Played as comedy; Yukito later sees the cost

delivery.evidence: The premise states its theme openly (a cult heir who wished for a world without religion must found one); Yukito's moment of self-recognition (ep. 11) and his ep. 12 reflection are the clearest statements. ANN finds no sincere engagement with belief.
delivery.note: The message comes through satire and shock comedy; the Empire is a near-pure strawman, while rival gods get sympathetic backstories.

personified.ideology: Faith as a tool; distrust of religion
Cult power through force and fear

85467.heading: World Customize Creator
85467.label: From summaries
85467.life_message: Power is best used to build, protect friends and break down unfair prejudice; a person is not what a prophecy, a caste or the color of their hair says they are.

content.framing: Romance and polyamory normalized; assault attempts condemned and stopped

delivery.evidence: A Japanese reader praises a serious drama about tradition, discrimination and a modern person's sense of equality (Mechacomic); villains are mostly drawn as murderous (TV Tropes), while ordinary people's prejudice is shown as learned and changeable.
delivery.note: The anti-prejudice message is carried by plot and politics rather than speeches; the fictional religion is treated mainly as a political tool.

personified.ideology: Theocratic rule by invented faith and caste

87260.heading: World's End Harem
87260.label: From summaries
87260.life_message: Its hero holds that love, fidelity and consent matter more than the pleasure and power a society offers him, though the story itself dwells on that pleasure and lets other men profit from coercion.

content.framing: Mixed: Reito's refusal and fidelity endorsed; coercion often staged as titillation; Shōta's predation rewarded
Mixed: coercion condemned in Reito's story, endorsed as fantasy in Shōta's and Hino's

delivery.evidence: Reito states his refusal outright; Erisa argues the genetic case for many partners (TV Tropes); ANN's Martin says the monogamy question is raised but not explored deeply; the council and Sages are drawn as cartoonish man-haters (TV Tropes).
delivery.note: Reito's stance is spoken plainly, but the book's weight falls on the sexual scenes around him, which works against the stated message.

personified.ideology: Female rule; ending the Y chromosome

87260.dominant: Hedonism (as spectacle), Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Liberalism (consent and bodily autonomy, carried by the hero), Utilitarianism (the species versus the person).

78151.heading: World Trigger
78151.label: From summaries
78151.life_message: Do what you believe you should, even when you are weak, and do it with a team that plans and trusts each other; enemies are people too, and many of them can become allies.

content.framing: Action and tactics; real death treated seriously

delivery.evidence: Kido's hardline and Miwa's hatred are given causes (lost family, Yūma's father's death) rather than mocked; Aftokrator's commander has reasons tied to his own world's survival; a captured enemy becomes a teammate (Wikipedia; fan wiki).
delivery.note: Values come through decisions in battle and post-battle analysis rather than speeches; ANN's Silverman praises how it shares information through story rather than info-dumps.

personified.ideology: Imperial taking of people as resources

78151.dominant: Pragmatism, Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Duty ethics.

86717.heading: Wotakoi: Love Is Hard for Otaku
86717.label: From summaries
86717.life_message: A good life is shared with people who accept the whole of you, hobbies included; you need not hide what you love, and those who love you should let you open up at your own pace.

content.framing: Neutral to Endorsed (social drinking as normal adult life)

delivery.evidence: Fujita rates the mix as comedy 8, romance 1.5 and seriousness 0.5 out of 10 (Anime Corner); critics call it relatable and grounded.
delivery.note: Its anti-stigma theme emerges through gags and small arcs, and the non-otaku Naoya is drawn as kindly as the otaku.

personified.ideology: Hiding one's hobbies to fit social norms
Enjoying things in moderation; a respectable image

86717.dominant: Expressive individualism (gently), Communitarianism (the friend group), Consumerism (fandom as joy), Secular humanism (implicit).

30027.heading: X (X/1999)
30027.label: From summaries
30027.life_message: The future is not fixed: each person chooses, by what they most truly wish, whether to protect or destroy, and love for particular people is the reason to save the world, even when it costs everything.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (tragedy); cruelty by the Dragons of Earth condemned
Mixed: committed love treated tenderly; sex work and affairs shown without judgment

delivery.evidence: Each Dragon of Earth has a stated reason (Kusanagi's love of nature, Satsuki's rationalism, Kakyo's fatalism); Wikipedia notes the social themes go unspoken rather than lectured.
delivery.note: The theme of choice is stated by Tokiko, Hinoto and Subaru, but the moral weight is carried by tragedy and loss rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Free choice to protect loved ones
Fate; granting wishes; the planet over people

30010.heading: xxxHOLiC
30010.label: From summaries
30010.life_message: Every wish has a price and every choice shapes what becomes inevitable; you cannot buy happiness by throwing yourself away, because your life is bound up with the people who care about you.

delivery.evidence: Yuko states the lesson of many chapters directly to customers and to Watanuki (Wikipedia, Themes: Clamp stresses the weight of words); customers voice their own reasons before facing consequences.
delivery.note: Each episode is a moral fable delivered through Yuko's speeches and a twist; the long arc carries quieter themes of identity, grief and choice.

30010.dominant: Pagan/occult (spirits, witchcraft, wishes), Buddhist ideas (cause and effect, craving), Existentialism (identity and choice).

99897.heading: Yakuza Fiancé: Raise wa Tanin ga Ii
99897.label: From summaries
99897.life_message: It holds up meeting a dangerous world on your own nerve and on your own terms; love appears as a contest of wills between two damaged teenagers, and the story enjoys their cruelty more than it judges it.

content.framing: Neutral; played as thrill and character
Neutral; casual sex and sexual coercion talk unjudged; the predator Ozu condemned

delivery.evidence: ANN (episodes 1-2) says it is free of conventional morality and offers no moral lessons; CSM finds no positive messages; Yoshino's objections to Kirishima's crimes are voiced (anime ep. 3) but not borne out by consequences.
delivery.note: The story does not argue for a message; its view of love as a contest of wills is carried by the leads' bargains and power games.

personified.ideology: Self-respect and nerve in a dangerous world
Obsessive, violent devotion; nothing matters but her

99897.dominant: Might makes right (explored), Hedonism (explored), Expressive individualism (Yoshino), Traditionalism (clan and arranged marriage).

113624.heading: Yakuza Reincarnation
113624.label: From summaries
113624.life_message: Real strength is a code kept in any body and any world: protect ordinary people, keep faith with those who trust you, and never profit from their ruin.

content.framing: Drugs condemned; drinking played for comedy

delivery.evidence: Ryu lectures thugs on right and wrong (MyAnimeList review); Ryumatsu's code is stated through his contempt for drugs (TV Tropes). The brother is given a traumatic backstory, but dealers and crooked knights are flat.
delivery.note: The code is stated openly in lectures and played out in fights; comedy (the gender switch, the drinking) carries most scenes.

personified.ideology: Ninkyō: protect the neighborhood, keep faith, never profit from ruin
Power and control, born of trauma

personified.character: Tashtria's corrupt knights and drug dealers

113624.dominant: Bushido / honor code (ninkyō), Communitarianism, Traditionalism, Classical virtue ethics.

116822.heading: Yankee JK Kuzuhana-chan
116822.label: From summaries
116822.life_message: Kindness and honest skill can win a place where you do not fit, and a feared loner opens up when someone sees who she really is.

content.framing: Bullying and extortion condemned; Hanako's fighting endorsed as protection
Fan service endorsed as comedy; the attempted assault condemned

delivery.evidence: The kindness theme is carried by situations (rescues, mending clothes, apologies) rather than speeches; bullies are drawn as comic and most are redeemed rather than strawmen.
delivery.note: Message is light and mostly implicit; the publisher's marketing leads with the harem and fan service.

116822.dominant: Harem comedy; kindness that sees past a tough image; fan service.

147997.heading: You and I Are Polar Opposites
147997.label: From summaries
147997.life_message: Being honest about who you are, and learning to respect people who are not like you, makes better love and better friendship than trying to fit in.

delivery.evidence: The theme comes through small daily scenes and the characters' inner thoughts; Taira's cynical view gets a sympathetic hearing before he outgrows it (Wikipedia episode summaries).
delivery.note: An ensemble romance with no villain; its point about honesty and difference is shown through choices, not stated as a lesson.

147997.dominant: Expressive individualism (honesty over conformity), Communitarianism (the friend group), Classical virtue ethics.

146858.heading: You Can’t Be In a Rom-Com with Your Childhood Friends!
146858.label: From summaries
146858.life_message: Fear of losing a friendship can keep people from being honest about love, and in the end you have to say what you feel and choose, even if it changes things.

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)

delivery.evidence: The hero's argument against romance with friends is the comedy's premise and is slowly taken apart by events; ANN's season review notes it works best as parody and stumbles when it plays tropes straight.
delivery.note: The honesty theme is carried by comic situations and the volume-by-volume confessions, not by speeches.

personified.ideology: Make life a rom-com; say what you feel

146858.dominant: Communitarianism (the circle of friends), Hedonism (desire as comedy), Postmodernism (rom-com parody), Expressive individualism (say what you feel).

99640.heading: You Got Me, Sempai!
99640.label: From summaries
99640.life_message: Honest, kind communication and trust make a relationship last, even between two awkward teenagers under pressure.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers describe a relationship shown through small moments, apologies and dates rather than lessons (ANN); the publisher's descriptions frame each step as a happy milestone (Kodansha).
delivery.note: No character argues against teen sexual relationships or for a different path; the values (honesty, patience, consent) are modeled rather than stated.

personified.ideology: Quiet sincerity; respect for a partner's pace
Charm and persistence toward someone else's girlfriend

99640.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (relationship virtues), Expressive individualism, Feminism (light).

124676.heading: You Like Me, Not My Daughter?!
124676.label: From summaries
124676.life_message: A woman who gave her twenties to raising an orphaned child is free to be loved for herself: love that is patient, sincere and respectful can cross an age gap, and a parent's love and a romantic love need not compete.

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)
content.framing: Endorsed: committed adult romance; fan service played for comedy

delivery.evidence: Ayako voices the case against the relationship (age, motherhood, what people think) at length in vols. 1-5 before being won over; Takumi's respect for her decisions carries the counter-case (Otaku USA).
delivery.note: The message is delivered through romantic comedy rather than argument; objections are treated as fears to be overcome rather than as wisdom.

personified.ideology: Parental duty first; fear of the age gap
A child's blessing on her parent's happiness

124676.dominant: Expressive individualism (follow your heart across the age gap), Communitarianism (family first), Traditionalism (motherhood honored).

120977.heading: You're My Cutie!!
120977.label: From summaries
120977.life_message: People deserve to be seen as persons, not admired or used as objects for their looks; love grows from respecting someone's boundaries, and honesty and effort keep it alive.

content.framing: Shown with sympathy; healed through trust
Mixed: harassment condemned; teen romance endorsed

delivery.evidence: The point about objectification is made through the harassment episode and Shikura's reactions; ANN notes the story gives a classmate room to apologize rather than casting all the girls as villains (vol. 2).
delivery.note: The message is shown in Madoka's actions; the story becomes mostly romantic comedy after vol. 2.

120977.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Feminism (objectification with the genders reversed).

30392.heading: You're My Pet
30392.label: From summaries
30392.life_message: Real love lets you be yourself: a partner who accepts you matters more than one who looks perfect on paper, though finding that out takes honesty, growing up and a long, messy road.

content.framing: Mixed: slaps and fights played as relationship drama; harassment answered with a punch
Neutral to endorsed (adult relationships); predation condemned

delivery.evidence: Hasumi, the rival, is drawn sympathetically and given a happy ending (v14); Wikipedia's reception notes the story's contrast of the "three highs" ideal with a compatible partner without mocking either man.
delivery.note: The message comes through comedy and romance; chapter titles framed as pet-care "Rules" carry the irony.

personified.ideology: Status, pride and career, learning acceptance
Conventional success and the ideal match

30392.dominant: Expressive individualism (love that lets you be yourself), Feminism (a career woman, harassment answered), Traditionalism (critiqued: status ideals of marriage), Communitarianism (friends and sisters).

144718.heading: You Were Experienced, I Was Not: Our Dating Story
144718.label: From summaries
144718.life_message: A person's past does not decide their worth; real love means accepting your partner as they are and waiting until both of you truly want the next step, rather than treating intimacy as a duty.

content.framing: Explored; pressure rejected; non-judgment of a partner's past endorsed

delivery.evidence: The theme is spoken aloud in the opening, where Ryuto says he wants to wait until Runa wants it too (Anime Corner; Anime Feminist); A Case Suitable for Treatment says the light novel sticks to its anti-shaming theme; Moore finds the leads too bland to carry it.
delivery.note: The message is stated in Ryuto's inner monologue and the couple's talks; rumor-mongers and past boyfriends stay offstage, so the opposing view is mostly implied.

personified.ideology: A girl's past should not define her
Wait for mutual desire; listen first
Jealousy and judgment of a sister

144718.dominant: Feminism (no shaming of a girl's sexual past), Classical virtue ethics (patience and restraint), Expressive individualism (each sets their own pace).

114646.heading: Young Ladies Don't Play Fighting Games
114646.label: From summaries
114646.life_message: A passion you are told to hide, pursued honestly and competed in fairly, can show who you really are and turn rivals into the closest of friends.
114646.dominant: Expressive individualism, Classical virtue ethics (excellence through practice), Traditionalism (gently critiqued).

delivery.evidence: The theme comes through comedy and matches, not speeches (ANN; Okazu). The rule-keepers are not villains: Tamaki and Yuu are enforcers who secretly play, and the school later allows a club (vol. 9).
delivery.note: Authority is teased rather than attacked; the story's argument is that passion and propriety can coexist.

67707.heading: Your Lie in April
67707.label: From summaries
67707.life_message: Grief and fear need not silence you: pour yourself into your art and into the people you love while you have time, and they stay with you after they are gone.

content.framing: Abuse condemned; comic hitting played for laughs

delivery.evidence: The message about living and playing freely is spoken by Kaori and enacted in performances; the opposing view (perfection, playing to the score) is given to Saki and the judges, and Saki's reasons are explained (Wikipedia; fan wiki).
delivery.note: Inner monologue during performances carries much of the theme; the final letter states it directly.

personified.ideology: Live and play freely while you can
From fear and grief to expression

67707.dominant: Existentialism and Expressive individualism (affirmed through Kaori), Classical virtue ethics (perseverance and courage), Communitarianism (friends as family).

97337.heading: your name.
97337.label: From summaries
97337.life_message: People are bound together across distance and time; hold on to those connections, act to save others even when it costs you, and keep searching for what you have lost.

content.framing: Played for comedy; the romance itself is chaste

delivery.evidence: The meaning of musubi is stated once by Hitoha (Wikipedia); otherwise the theme of connection is carried by images (threads, the braid, the comet) and action. The mayor's resistance is shown as human, not cartoonish.
delivery.note: The story shows rather than argues; its spirituality is presented as quietly true.

97337.dominant: Pantheist/New Age (musubi, the binding of people and time), Communitarianism (saving the town), Traditionalism (the shrine's ways prove true).

30054.heading: Yu-Gi-Oh!
30054.label: From summaries
30054.life_message: Everyone has a hidden strength that comes out when they believe in themselves and their friends; play fair, because those who cheat or prey on others are undone by their own darkness; and love lets go of the dead.

content.framing: Mixed: punishment of villains endorsed in early chapters; killing by villains condemned
Mixed: lecherous gags as comedy; assault punished

delivery.evidence: Speeches about the "Heart of the Cards" and friendship are frequent; Takahashi states the message directly (Wikipedia, Development). Early villains are cartoon wrongdoers; later ones (Pegasus, Marik, Bakura) get tragic backstories.
delivery.note: Friendship and fair play are said aloud often, but the darker material carries its own weight.

30054.dominant: Pagan/occult (Egyptian myth), Communitarianism (friendship), Duty ethics (fair play), Consumerism.

30053.heading: Yu Yu Hakusho
30053.label: From summaries
30053.life_message: A good heart can be hidden under a bad reputation: real strength is protecting the people you love, and even enemies, demons and the guilty can change, while seeing the world as pure good against pure evil can break a person.

content.framing: Mostly heroic combat; cruelty condemned; one revenge torture endorsed
Mixed: delinquency shown as a cover for a good heart

delivery.evidence: Sensui's case against humanity is shown through the Chapter Black tape and the Feast of Human Vices rather than dismissed; Toguro's code is respected even as he loses; the rich patrons are drawn as cartoon villains.
delivery.note: The moral is carried by actions in fights and by a few quiet scenes (the wake, Toguro's sentencing, Sensui's death) rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Protect friends; act from the heart
Humanity is evil and should be wiped out
Strength and honor over a human life
Life as a gamble; cruelty as entertainment

30053.dominant: Classical virtue ethics and Communitarianism (affirmed), Buddhist ideas (as setting), Might makes right (explored and questioned), Bushido / honor code (explored).

160923.heading: Yumeochi: Dreaming of Falling For You
160923.label: From summaries
160923.life_message: Regret over a wasted youth can be faced: a second chance only matters if you treat it as your real life, and the courage and friendships found there have to be carried back into the present.

content.framing: Endorsed as comedy (fan service); romance played straight
Mixed: the roof jump and the dieting shown as dangerous; drinking played lightly

delivery.evidence: Chono's statement that the dream is a second life he does not want to waste (ch. 21) is the clearest statement; the "nothing matters in a dream" view is voiced by Omura and answered by events (ch. 9-14).
delivery.note: Lessons come through character arcs; reviewers say the harem turn and abrupt ending blunt the message.

personified.ideology: Boldness and self-improvement at any cost

160923.dominant: Existentialism (regret, authenticity and a second chance); Hedonism and harem wish-fulfilment (explored).

101120.heading: Yuri Is My Job!
101120.label: From summaries
101120.life_message: Masks keep us safe but cut us off; telling the truth about ourselves, even when it hurts, is what lets real friendship and love grow, while using other people's feelings as tools harms everyone.

content.framing: Mixed: same-sex romance sympathetic; coercion condemned; kisses without consent shown ambiguously

delivery.evidence: Miman built the story around the gap between persona and true self and made the acting visibly exaggerated so readers can tell when a character lies (Wikipedia, Production).
delivery.note: Values come through character drama rather than speeches; reviewers disagree about what the later arcs say about intimacy.

personified.ideology: Being liked by everyone matters most, later unlearned

101120.dominant: Expressive individualism (the true self beneath the mask), Classical virtue ethics (honesty), Postmodernism (performance and meta), Communitarianism.

41593.heading: Yuru Yuri
41593.label: From summaries
41593.life_message: Ordinary school days spent with friends, full of small jokes and small kindnesses, are worth treasuring, and no one should be left out, not even the girl everyone forgets.

delivery.evidence: Short gag chapters with fourth-wall jokes (TV Tropes: chapters 137 and 187; Okazu; UK Anime Network); no character argues a view.
delivery.note: No message is argued; friendship and acceptance are simply the world the jokes happen in.

41593.dominant: Communitarianism (friendship), Hedonism (fun for its own sake), Expressive individualism (gentle).

87213.heading: Yuuna and the Haunted Hot Springs
87213.label: From summaries
87213.life_message: Compassion toward those others would cast out, even a ghost, and loyalty to the people under your roof matter more than power, luck or tradition.

content.framing: Neutral (supernatural action); comic punishment of the hero

delivery.evidence: Kogarashi states his choice of mercy over exorcism in ch. 1; villains such as Byakuei are given grief as a motive (fan wiki); the comedy and fan service carry most chapters (ANN).
delivery.note: The compassion theme is shown by action, not lectures; the fan service is never questioned by the story.

87213.dominant: Pagan/occult (a real spirit world), Communitarianism (the inn as found family), Hedonism (fan service as the hook).

30869.heading: Zatch Bell!
30869.label: From summaries
30869.life_message: Real strength is kindness that protects others: a true king ends needless fighting, and friends grow strong by trusting and sacrificing for each other.

content.framing: Comic; crude gags not endorsed as romance

delivery.evidence: Thompson (ANN) says the early chapters hammer the self-esteem and friendship messages through shouting and repetition, easing later; the villains are rotten enough to cheer against, but Zeno and Koko are redeemed.
delivery.note: The kind-king message is spoken aloud in battle and repeated, especially early, but carried by big emotional scenes rather than lectures.

personified.ideology: Kindness as true strength; a kind king
Intellect and pride turned to loyalty
Envy and power for its own sake
Strength and pride as the right to rule

30869.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (kindness, courage), Might makes right (critiqued), Communitarianism (friends as the source of strength).

116649.heading: The Titan's Bride
116649.label: From summaries
116649.life_message: Love that begins as a claim can grow into a chosen, mutual bond: a partner proves himself through patience, sacrifice and respect, and two people from different worlds can make a family and a home together.

content.framing: Condemned (villains' ambushes); Caius's protective violence endorsed
Endorsed between the leads; Baro's assault framed ambiguously

delivery.evidence: The message rides on romance and sex scenes rather than speeches; court opponents are drawn as obstacles; Baro is given a backstory and a path back.
delivery.note: The story's argument is made by outcomes: each trial ends in deeper love.

personified.ideology: Devoted, protective love and royal duty
Tradition: a fertile bride and a proper heir

116649.dominant: Hedonism (explicit sexual fulfillment), Duty ethics (royal duty and the heir), Progressivism (a same-sex royal marriage), Traditionalism (critiqued, the court).
